claim: SimPy (Sun, Du, Yang, Li and Lo, "AI Coders Are Among Us") was published at ISSTA 2024.
quote: In Proceedings of the 33rd ACM SIGSOFT International Symposium on Software Testing and Analysis (ISSTA '24), September 16-20, 2024, Vienna, Austria.

claim: SimPy rewrites only Python's terminals: it forbids formatting whitespace and newlines and replaces keywords, operators and delimiters with more compact forms, keeping Python's AST.
quote: Compared to the standard Python grammar, we prohibit using tokens popularly hired to style the code appearance, e.g., whitespace and newline, and simplify keywords, operators, and delimiters to a more compact form.

claim: SimPy drops the ':' after compound-statement headers because the block's start marker already delimits it.
quote: However, the block construct initiates with its starting symbol, making the construct itself distinguishable from any previous construct. Hence, removing ':' is safe for this case.

claim: SimPy does not delete `def`: it replaces it, like 77 other terminals, with a dedicated placeholder token (<def_stmt>) added to the tokenizer vocabulary.
quote: SimPy introduces 78 new tokens for the tokenizers to recognize. For example, the "def" keyword of the original Python grammar is replaced by a token

claim: SimPy cuts token count by 10.4% on the GPT-4 tokenizer and by 13.5% on CodeLlama's, over the same Python corpus.
quote: In the experiments, compared with Python, SimPy enables a reduction in token usage by 13.5% and 10.4% for CodeLlama and GPT-4, respectively, when completing the same set of code-related tasks.

claim: On tokenizers trained on code (StarCoder, SantaCoder, Replit-code, CodeT5) SimPy saves 8.6% to 13.8%, StarCoder's 8.6% being the low end.
quote: For tokenizers trained on code corpora, such as Replit-code and StarCoder, SimPy achieved a token reduction ranging from 8.6% to 13.8%.

claim: Across all 14 tokenizers the reduction spans 8.6% to 34.7%; the 34.7% comes only from the inefficient CodeBERT and GPT-2 tokenizers, so the range for modern tokenizers is roughly 9-14%.
quote: The most pronounced impact of SimPy is observed with the least efficient tokenizers, CodeBert and GPT-2, where a remarkable 34.7% reduction in token count was achieved.

claim: SimPy's token counts were measured with each tokenizer's vocabulary extended to include SimPy's placeholder tokens, so every placeholder counts as one token.
quote: In tokenizing the SimPy code, we modify the tokenizers to include tokens of SimPy in their vocabularies.

claim: TinyLlama further trained on the Python dataset (the control) reached 10.00% pass@1 on HumanEval.
quote: | TinyLlama  | Python              | 10.00%   | 13.41%    |

claim: TinyLlama trained on the SimPy dataset alone reached 5.91% pass@1 on HumanEval, below the 10.00% of its Python control.
quote: | TinyLlama  | 100% SimPy          | 5.91%    | 9.76%     |

claim: SimPy's training experiments used only models of about 1B parameters (CodeGen-350M-NL, TinyLlama 1.1B, Pythia 1B); no frontier model was tested.
quote: Our experimental scope in RQ2 is restricted by our computational resources, limiting our evaluation to models with around 1B parameters.

claim: The authors concede SimPy code is hard for humans to read and is meant for agent-only use or behind a converter (DualCode) that shows humans Python.
quote: The source code, when written in AI-oriented grammar, becomes challenging for human interpretation and is therefore not intended for human display.

claim: Token Sugar (Sun et al.) appeared at ASE 2025; the venue is not stated in the arXiv text itself and is taken from the Tokenmaxxing paper's bibliography.
quote: Token sugar: Making source code sweeter for LLMs through tokenefficient shorthand. In 2025 IEEE/ACM 40th International Conference on Automated Software Engineering, ASE '25

claim: Applied statically, Token Sugar's 799 mined shorthands cut 15.1% of tokens on the LeetCode solutions they were mined from and 12.9% on HumanEval's reference solutions.
quote: As shown in Table I, Token Sugar alone achieves a token reduction of 15.1% on LeetCode and 12.9% on HumanEval.

claim: Without training, GPT-4.1 completing sugarized HumanEval prefixes fell from 94.5% to 51.2% pass@1, so the shorthand requires dedicated training.
quote: When provided with a standard Python prefix, GPT-4.1 achieved a baseline Pass@1 of 94.5%. However, when we sugarized the prefix and presented it to the same model, the Pass@1 score dropped dramatically to 51.2%.

claim: Putting Token Sugar examples and their expansions in GPT-4.1's prompt raised pass@1 only to 54.9%, against 94.5% on plain Python.
quote: Next, we ran the same experiment but included examples of Token Sugars and their expanded forms within the prompt, resulting in a Pass@1 score of 54.9%.

claim: Tokenmaxxing ran five models on 100 LiveCodeBench problems in Java, OCaml, Python and Rust with mini-swe-agent and visible tests, 2,000 trajectories in all.
quote: We evaluate four programming languages (Java, OCaml, Python, and Rust) and five models on a 100-problem subset of LiveCodeBench, gathering 2,000 agent trajectories for analysis.

claim: Controlling for problem difficulty, OCaml trajectories used 1.28-1.69 times Python's output tokens, significant (p < 0.001) for all five models.
quote: Across all models, OCaml traces consume significantly more tokens than Python traces (1.28-1.69× vs. Python

claim: The low end of the Rust range, 1.07 times Python (Gemma 4), is not statistically significant (p = 0.480).
quote: | Gemma   | Java vs. Python Rust vs. Python OCaml vs. Python ICC | 0.85× 1.07× 1.44× 0.80 | p = 0.114 p = 0.480 p < 0.001 - |

claim: The high end of the Rust range, 1.57 times Python, is GLM-5.2's (p < 0.001); significant Rust penalties span 1.16-1.57 times.
quote: | GLM     | Java vs. Python Rust vs. Python OCaml vs. Python ICC | 1.34× 1.57× 1.54× 0.73 | p < 0.01 p < 0.001 p < 0.001 -  |

claim: Tokenmaxxing's cost metric is total output tokens (reasoning plus visible output) over the trajectory; input tokens and dollars are not measured.
quote: This is why, like many others, we report the total number of output tokens generated over a single conversation.

claim: The authors argue agentic token cost depends on the reasoning and revision needed to reach a solution, not on the length of the final program.
quote: What matters is not the number of tokens in the final solution, but the amount of reasoning and revision needed to get to the solution.

claim: For Gemma 4 on OCaml, 92% of failed snapshots were compile-time errors: the agent fought the syntax rather than the algorithm.
quote: The agent is fighting OCaml syntax, not the algorithm: 92% of failed snapshots are compile-time errors and 8% are wrong-answer failures.

claim: Agents sometimes solve a problem in Python first and then translate it into the less familiar target language.
quote: Models sometimes solve problems in Python before translating the solution to an unfamliar target language.

claim: GPT-5.5 ran embedded Python to prototype or check invariants on 27% of OCaml problems, 19% of Rust and 18% of Java.
quote: Likewise, GPT-5.5 often embeds Python directly via python3 -c or heredocs to prototype algorithms or validate invariants, especially for OCaml (27% of problems), Rust (19%), and Java (18%).

claim: Ustynov's compressed log format (Format C) uses abbreviated service and event codes plus a schema header.
quote: Format C - Compressed: Abbreviated service/event codes, schema header.

claim: The compressed log file had 17.1% fewer tokens than the human-readable one, yet the session that analysed it used 67.2% more tokens.
quote: Format C achieved 17.1% input reduction but produced 67.2% session cost increase.

claim: Each format was tested in a single fresh Claude Sonnet 4.6 session with the same five diagnostic questions and no extended thinking.
quote: Comprehension was tested by presenting five identical diagnostic questions to claude-sonnet-4-6 in isolated sessions (one per format, no cross-contamination), each starting fresh at 15.1k baseline tokens. No extended thinking was used.

claim: The author attributes the higher session cost to interpretive work moving into the model's reasoning and output.
quote: aggressive compression increased total session cost by 67% despite reducing input tokens by 17%, because it shifted interpretive burden to the model's reasoning phase.

claim: The experiment used one model and one dataset of 200 log events, and the paper does not establish where compression starts to pay.
quote: Single model (claude-sonnet-4-6), single dataset (200 events). The crossover point for compression is not established.

claim: `def` is not removed but replaced by a placeholder token <def_stmt>, one of 78 new vocabulary entries; the colon and parameter parentheses are dropped, and all formatting whitespace and newlines are removed (blocks use <block_start>/<block_end>).
quote: SimPy introduces 78 new tokens for the tokenizers to recognize. For example, the "def" keyword of the original Python grammar is replaced by a token
wiki_says: A Python grammar rewritten for machines (no `def`, no `:`, blocks by markers)

claim: SimPy's 8.6-13.8% (modern tokenizers) was counted with every tokenizer's vocabulary extended by SimPy's placeholder tokens, over whole GitHub files (comments and docstrings included). Variant A was counted on unmodified tokenizers over a paired, handwritten corpus, so the two figures are not directly comparable. SimPy's saving would likely be smaller on stock tokenizers, where a placeholder such as <def_stmt> splits into several tokens, and larger on comment-free function-level code.
quote: In tokenizing the SimPy code, we modify the tokenizers to include tokens of SimPy in their vocabularies.
wiki_says: Even giving up readability, the saving stays at 9–14%, the same order as variant A.

claim: The TinyLlama figures are correct but selective. CodeGen-NL also dropped (4.51% to 2.93%), but Pythia trained only on SimPy rose above its Python baseline (7.01% vs. 5.79%). Training on Python and then on 100% SimPy matched or beat the control for all three models (TinyLlama 10.12% vs. 10.00% pass@1). All figures come from roughly 1B-parameter models on the 164 HumanEval problems, where one problem is 0.61 points.
quote: Interestingly, we observe that the Pythia model, when trained exclusively with 100% SimPy, surpasses the Python baseline on Pass@1.
wiki_says: The models had to be trained on it: training on SimPy alone dropped TinyLlama from 10.00% to 5.91% pass@1.

claim: 15.1% is a static count on the LeetCode solutions the 799 sugars were mined from (in-sample); held-out HumanEval reference code gives 12.9%. Code actually generated by the trained 1-1.5B models saved only 7.7-11.2%, with pass@1 roughly unchanged.
quote: Answer to RQ2: Token sugars are actively and reliably used by LLMs during code generation, causing a negligible difference in Pass@1 performance while yielding up to 11.2% token savings without any desugarization failures.
wiki_says: Mined shorthands cut up to 15.1% of tokens, also requiring training.

claim: The same authors' follow-up measured SimPy at 15.3% on LeetCode solutions and 13.3% on HumanEval reference solutions, which are function-level code like lotml's paired corpus. The 9-14% comes from whole repository files. On comparable code SimPy's saving is therefore about 13-15%, not 9-14%. The tokenizer used for Table I is not named.
quote: More importantly, when used in conjunction with SimPy (which individually achieves 15.3% and 13.3% reductions), Token Sugar brings additional savings, pushing the total reduction to 22.4% on LeetCode and 20.0% on HumanEval.
wiki_says: variant A measures 9–11% fewer and SimPy 9–14%

claim: The multipliers are output tokens only (reasoning plus visible output, summed over the trajectory). Input/context tokens and dollar cost are not measured; the authors justify the choice by prefix caching.
quote: This is why, like many others, we report the total number of output tokens generated over a single conversation.
wiki_says: In agentic use, cost relative to Python was 1.28–1.69× for OCaml and 1.07–1.57× for Rust

claim: The 1.07 lower bound (Gemma 4) is not significant (p = 0.480); the significant Rust penalties are 1.16-1.57 (Sonnet 4.6 1.16, Qwen 1.20, GPT-5.5 1.36, GLM 1.57).
quote: | Gemma   | Java vs. Python Rust vs. Python OCaml vs. Python ICC | 0.85× 1.07× 1.44× 0.80 | p = 0.114 p = 0.480 p < 0.001 - |
wiki_says: agentic cost in Rust was 1.07–1.57 times Python's

claim: Tokenmaxxing never attributes Rust's penalty to ownership or traits. It treats Rust and OCaml as low-resource languages, and Java (garbage-collected, no borrow checker) carries a similar penalty: GPT-5.5 Java 1.30x vs. Rust 1.36x, Sonnet 1.18x vs. 1.16x, Qwen 1.21x vs. 1.20x. The figure cannot support a claim about the weight of ownership.
quote: | GPT-5.5 | Java vs. Python Rust vs. Python OCaml vs. Python ICC | 1.30× 1.36× 1.30× 0.94 | p < 0.001 p < 0.001 p < 0.001 - |
wiki_says: agentic cost in Rust was 1.07–1.57 times Python's ([Tokenmaxxing]). What makes Rust hard for LLMs is the combination — traits, name resolution and ownership

claim: Compile-error loops are documented mainly for the small open models. Gemma 4 on OCaml has 1,196 stuck self-loops and 92% compile-error failures. For the frontier models (GPT-5.5, Sonnet 4.6) the authors describe write-once, test, submit trajectories, and GPT-5.5 has only 13 stuck self-loops on OCaml, yet these models still pay 1.16-1.36x. The paper never splits cost into repair rounds and other work, so 'dominated by repair rounds' goes beyond its evidence.
quote: Most trajectories consist of a single implementation phase followed by verification, indicating that the models typically write the solution once, immediately run ./test.sh, and submit if all tests pass.
wiki_says: driven by loops on code that does not compile and by prototyping in Python — not by surface verbosity; conclusion 3: Agentic cost is dominated by repair rounds.

claim: The authors present Python prototyping as a deliberate strategy, not as waste, and never measure its token share. In their example it pays off: Sonnet's 23 Python turns produce an OCaml solution that passes on the first write. Polishing solutions that already pass is the waste pattern they name besides fighting syntax.
quote: and also more deliberate strategies, such as planning in code comments and prototyping in Python before translating to an unfamiliar target.
wiki_says: driven by ... prototyping in Python

claim: Problem identity explains 80-97% of token-cost variance (ICC); language is a smaller, model-dependent effect. Compile loops are shown as a mechanism, chiefly for Gemma on OCaml, and are not shown to dominate cost. The metric is still worth keeping, but the 'dominate' attribution should go.
quote: The intraclass correlation (ICC) measures what fraction of token-cost variance is explained by problem identity; the high values (0.80-0.97) confirm that problem difficulty dominates, justifying why we control for it.
wiki_says: Loops on code that does not compile, which dominate agentic cost (Tokenmaxxing).

claim: The numbers are right, but 'session cost' is the message-token count of one Claude Code session per format (18.9k vs. 31.6k), not money. All four formats answered 5/5 correctly. The structured format with full, unabbreviated names (B) also used 27% more session tokens (24.0k) than prose. With n=1 per condition, the increase cannot be attributed to abbreviation as such.
quote: | Session tokens (Messages) | 18.9k       | 24.0k         | 31.6k        | 28.3k        |
wiki_says: An abbreviated log format cut input tokens by 17.1% and raised total session cost by 67.2% (log data, one session per condition): compression can move the cost into reasoning.

claim: SimPy's token reductions were measured on 623,887 whole files from GitHub repositories with over 100 stars, comments and docstrings included, which dilutes a grammar-only saving compared with function-level code.
quote: We keep the code files from the repositories with over 100 stars, resulting in 623,887 code files.
bears_on: comparability of SimPy's saving with lotml's paired-corpus measurement

claim: Sequential training (Python first, then the full SimPy dataset) matched or beat the Python-only control on pass@10 for all three small models, so accuracy loss came from training strategy, not from the compressed grammar itself.
quote: Specifically, CodeGen-NL, TinyLlama, and Pythia models trained with Python→100%SimPy achieve Pass@10 scores of 9.15%, 14.02%, and 10.00%, respectively, outperforming the control group's 7.32%, 13.41%, and 9.76%.
bears_on: whether syntax compression hurts accuracy

claim: Partial adaptation fails: fine-tuning on 10-50% of the SimPy data left all three models below their Python control, so a new surface syntax needs a corpus-scale amount of training data, not a few examples.
quote: For instance, TinyLlama (Python→50%SimPy) scored 5.73% in Pass@1 and 11.59% in Pass@10, still trailing behind the TinyLlama (Python) scores.
bears_on: training prior for a new syntax

claim: Teaching SimPy added about 55% more training steps on top of the Python training (100,288 on top of 183,628 for CodeGen), a cost that only model owners can pay.
quote: For example, training CodeGen on the original Python dataset costs 183,628 training steps, and 100,288 additional steps are taken during the further finetuning on the 100% SimPy dataset.
bears_on: training prior; whether lotml can rely on frontier models without training

claim: SimPy keeps single-character symbols and leading spaces because tokenizers merge them into the following token at no extra cost. The same effect explains lotml's finding that removing indentation saves little and braces cost about one token per block.
quote: For example, the whitespace character is combined into its following token by GPT-4, as illustrated by " two" and " int" in Figure 2.
bears_on: indentation/whitespace token cost

claim: The SimPy/Python converter is AST-based, so it only works on grammatically complete code, which limits round-tripping of partial code such as completions or in-progress agent edits.
quote: The converter, we implemented for SimPy, is AST-based, which implicitly requires the input and output code of LLMs under the DualCode framework to satisfy the grammar correctness.
bears_on: transpilation strategy and agent edits on partial code

claim: Only 25.5% of GPT-4 tokens in GitHub Python are syntax elements (keywords and symbols), which caps what any syntax-only redesign can save. Most tokens are identifiers, API names and literals.
quote: found that when tokenized using GPT-4's tokenizer, only 25.5% of tokens correspond to Python syntax elements like keywords and symbols.
bears_on: reachability of the >=20% token target through syntax

claim: Only the combination of syntax compression (SimPy) and semantic shorthand (Token Sugar) crossed 20% (20.0-22.4%). Both need model training, and the result is not human-readable code.
quote: Answer to RQ1: Token Sugar achieves significant token reduction in Python code (12.9-15.1%) while targeting different verbosity sources, and the combined use with SimPy unlocks synergistic reductions (20.0-22.4%).
bears_on: reachability of the >=20% token target

claim: Trained models used the shorthand without losing accuracy: pass@1 was unchanged for Pythia and fell 0.6 points for Llama-3.2 and Qwen-2.5.
quote: Specifically, Pythia maintains identical performance (6.7%), while Llama-3.2 and Qwen-2.5 show only marginal differences of -0.6% and -0.6% respectively.
bears_on: whether compression hurts accuracy once the model is trained on it

claim: The paper separates 'functional verbosity' (constructs such as class definitions that take more tokens than their semantics need) from readability-only verbosity. This matches lotml's finding that its saving comes from deleting declarations, not from shorter keywords.
quote: functional verbosity, where necessary constructs require more tokens than theoretically needed to express the same semantics (e.g., extensive class definitions in object-oriented programming)
bears_on: where token savings come from (declarations vs. keywords)

claim: In generation, the trained models made zero desugarization failures, so even small models emitted the new constructs in valid form once trained.
quote: Finally, across all models, we observe a failure count of zero, indicating that LLMs understand token sugars well and can generate them in a valid format
bears_on: whether models can reliably emit non-standard syntax

claim: Like SimPy, all training results come from models of about 1B parameters (Pythia 1.4B, Llama-3.2 1B, Qwen-2.5 1.5B). The only frontier-model test (GPT-4.1) was untrained and lost 43 points.
quote: The model selection in our experiments is restricted by our computational resources, limiting our evaluation to models with around 1B parameters.
bears_on: external validity for frontier models

claim: Accuracy barely varied by language (except Gemma on OCaml), while output tokens varied strongly. Pass@1 alone hides a language's cost, so the harness has to report tokens alongside correctness.
quote: For the models we explore, accuracy on MiniLCB is not affected very much by language, with the notable exception that Gemma performs much worse on OCaml.
bears_on: evaluation harness metrics

claim: Smaller models spend more tokens after their first passing solution than before it (Gemma, Python: 1,743 to solution, 3,554 after), polishing code that already passes. This cost driver is independent of language syntax.
quote: But, the smaller models (Gemma and Qwen) produce hundreds or thousands more tokens after they find their first working solution.
bears_on: agentic cost drivers; harness metric for tokens after first green

claim: Surface length did not predict agentic cost. Java, the most verbose of the four languages, cost about the same as Rust for Qwen, GPT-5.5 and Sonnet (1.18-1.30x vs. 1.16-1.36x) and was cheaper than Python for Gemma (0.85x, n.s.). OCaml, which is terse, was the most expensive for most models.
quote: We instead make the target language the independent variable: process cost is not surface cost, and the language in which an agent spends the most tokens need not be the one whose programs are longest.
bears_on: syntax compression vs. agentic cost

claim: The penalty follows pretraining representation: The Stack v2 has about 200GB each of Java and Python but 12GB of Rust and less OCaml. A new language starts below OCaml.
quote: After deduplication, The Stack v2 has around 200GB of Java and of Python, but only 12GB of Rust and even less OCaml.
bears_on: training prior

claim: Gemma got out of OCaml compile loops only once it named a concrete language-specific error: fix bug made up 60% of stuck-to-breakthrough edges, and the unchanged algorithm then passed. This supports diagnostics that name the error precisely.
quote: Escape, when it comes, is a language learning event: fix bug dominates breakthrough at 60% (Table 5), the moment the agent finally names a concrete OCaml-specific error and the unchanged algorithm immediately passes.
bears_on: semantic compiler diagnostics and repair loop

claim: When stuck, Gemma re-emitted byte-identical code: 31% of its 1,196 OCaml stuck self-loops were reverts to a broken attempt it had already tried. A harness can detect this cheaply.
quote: This model-lanugage pair has 1,196 self-loops on the stuck state, dominated by revert (31%): the agent rewrites a byte-identical solution that it has already tried, oscillated between 2-3 broken attempts.
bears_on: repair loop; evaluation harness metrics

claim: Error-recovery work (fix bug, debug failure, infra confusion, revert) concentrates in OCaml for every model. 'Infra confusion' (build plumbing, file conventions) reaches 11-12% of OCaml spans for GPT-5.5 and Qwen, so toolchain friction is a cost in its own right.
quote: Across models, error-recovery labels-fix bug, debug failure, infra confusion, and revert-are disproportionately associated with OCaml, suggesting that solving OCaml problems requires more iterative correction.
bears_on: agentic cost drivers; toolchain simplicity

claim: All results come from self-contained competitive-programming problems with visible tests, one scaffold (mini-swe-agent) and a 40-turn limit. The authors warn they may not hold for repository-scale tasks.
quote: Our findings may therefore not generalize to repository-scale software engineering tasks, or to other agent harnesses.
bears_on: external validity of agentic cost evidence

claim: Compression did not change correctness: all four log formats scored 5/5. Only cost and wall-clock time moved (1m36s for prose vs. 7m00s for the compressed format).
bears_on: whether compression hurts accuracy

claim: The paper's 'semantic density' principle counts type annotations, descriptive names and diagnostic error messages as high-value tokens and structural ceremony as waste. This is a position, not a measurement, but it agrees with lotml paying tokens for `! Err` signatures and saving them by deleting declarations.
quote: High-density tokens include: descriptive function/variable names, type annotations, docstrings, business logic expressions, error messages with diagnostic context.
bears_on: token cost of type annotations and error signatures

claim: The author states that the log result has not been tested on code, so it is at best an analogy for programming-language syntax.
quote: Extension to code architecture (file consolidation, anti-pattern rehabilitation) remains theoretically motivated but not experimentally validated.
bears_on: applicability of compression evidence to syntax design

claim: A tool-assisted decompressor (Format D) lowered the reasoning cost but added 5-7 tool calls and an execution error, and still cost more than the human-readable format (28.3k vs. 18.9k). Expansion tools have overhead of their own.
quote: Format D reduced reasoning tax versus raw compressed (28.3k vs. 31.6k) but introduced toolcalling overhead: 5-7 invocations, an execution error (python vs. python3), and an alternativeapproach detour.
bears_on: DualCode-style conversion and agent tool overhead

claim: The paper relays, without data, Ronacher's view that whitespace-based indentation is a problem for LLMs. This is secondhand practitioner opinion bearing on lotml's indentation choice.
quote: Ronacher's subsequent work Ronacher [2026] identifies whitespace-based indentation as problematic for LLMs and notes that understanding code is becoming more important than writing it.
bears_on: indentation vs. braces

claim: The paper relays Haupt's claim that Rust's `fn` costs more tokens than `function`. This contradicts lotml's own measurement (`def` to `fn`: 0 tokens; common abbreviations cost one token) and is unsupported by data in the paper.
quote: observing that LLMs use fewer tokens for common English words than for shorter programmer abbreviations: Rust's fn is less token-efficient than function.
bears_on: keyword and abbreviation token cost

claim: The author flags a training-distribution risk: structures that deviate from what models saw in training may increase hallucination. This is the same concern as lotml's training prior.
quote: Agent-optimal structures (consolidated files, God Objects) are underrepresented in training data.
bears_on: training prior

claim: MultiPL-E translated the HumanEval and MBPP Python benchmarks into 18 additional programming languages (19 in total) and evaluated Codex, CodeGen and InCoder on them.
quote: We use MultiPL-E to translate two widely-used code generation benchmarks, HumanEval [1] and MBPP [2], into 18 languages.

claim: Pass@1 correlates with language popularity, but some niche languages perform as well as more popular ones.
quote: Code generation performance is correlatedwith language popularity, but some niche languages perform as well as more popular languages.

claim: For Codex on MultiPL-HumanEval, pass@1 on MEDIUM, LOW and NICHE languages was reliably lower than on HIGH-frequency languages (p = 0.006, p < 0.001 and p = 0.002).
quote: Although we find reliable differences in Codex pass@1 rates between the MEDIUM, LOW, and NICHE languages when compared to the HIGH category (p = 0.006; p < 0.001; p = 0.002)

claim: Lua was Codex's 9th-best language on MultiPL-HumanEval although it appears in only 0.2% of GitHub activity and is not in the TIOBE top 20.
quote: For instance, Lua is the 9th-best language in our Codex evaluation, although it only appears in 0.2% of GitHub activity and is not in the TIOBE Top-20.

claim: Comparing typed with untyped languages, static type-checking had no overall effect on Codex pass@1 (p = 0.33 on MultiPL-HumanEval, p = 0.23 on MultiPL-MBPP); the paper summarises this as static type-checking neither helping nor hindering.
quote: We observe no overall effect of type annotations on Codex pass@1 rates on MultiPLHumanEval (p = 0.33) or MultiPL-MBPP (p = 0.23).

claim: Removing all type annotations from the Python MultiPL-HumanEval prompts had no significant effect on Codex's pass@1 (p = 0.23).
quote: We run a similar experiment with Codex and Python, where we remove all the type annotations from the MultiPLHumanEval prompts. We find that this has no significant effect on Codex's pass@1 rate for Python (p = 0.23).

claim: Replacing every type in the TypeScript function signatures with Any lowered Codex's pass@1 by 2.5 points (p < 0.001).
quote: We run Codex on a variation of the MultiPLHumanEval TypeScript prompts where all types in the function signature are translated to "Any". We find that the loss of precise types hurts performance on TypeScript (-2.5%; p < 0.001).

claim: Each MultiPL-E compiler translates four things from Python (function signature, simple unit tests, the descriptive comment, and type annotations for typed targets) but never the function body.
quote: Each compiler must be able to translate four components from Python: (1) a function signature (name and arguments), (2) simple unit tests, (3) a comment describing the expected function behavior, and (4) type annotations if the target language is statically typed.

claim: On McEval-Hard, the four instruct models scored about 59-89% pass@1 on high-resource languages, 27-84% on low-resource languages and 0-1% on the no-resource languages Gleam and MoonBit, zero-shot.
quote: The four models achieve pass@1 scores being in the range of ∼59-89% for high-resource languages (depending on the LLM and the language), 27-84% for low-resource, and 0-1% for no-resource.

claim: Once tasks get hard (McEval-Hard), all models consistently fail on Gleam and MoonBit zero-shot; the best result was about 1%, by o3-mini on MoonBit.
quote: as soon as the complexity of the coding task increases (our McEval-Hard benchmark), all LLMs consistently fail in no-resource languages (best pass@1 is 1% by o3-mini on MoonBit).

claim: With five retrieved examples, Gleam McEval-Hard pass@1 rose at most to 1.32% (Qwen 2.5 Coder 32B Instruct, from 0.40% zero-shot).
On MoonBit the best in-context setting was o3-mini with 5-shot prompting, reaching 39% on HumanEval, 46% on MBPP and 12% on McEval-Hard.
quote: o3-mini complemented with a 5-shot in-context learning, which reached pass@1 scores of 39% (HumanEval), 46% (MBPP), and 12% (McEval-Hard).

claim: Few-shot prompting was slightly more effective than RAG over the language documentation, outperforming it in 7 of 12 cases on Gleam and 8 of 12 on MoonBit.
quote: Starting from in-context learning techniques (i.e., 5-shot and RAG), we observe that few-shot is slightly more effective than RAG. Indeed, in 7 out of 12 cases for Gleam and 8 out of 12 for MoonBit, few-shot outperforms RAG in terms of pass@1.

claim: Further pre-training Qwen 2.5 Coder 32B Base on the available Gleam and MoonBit code and documentation reached 12.47% and 25.86% on McEval-Hard, against 3.04% and 10.93% for the fine-tuned instruct model.
quote: For Gleam: on HumanEval, 32.99 (pre-trained) vs 24.74 (fine-tuned); on MBPP, 47.35 vs 34.03; and on McEval-Hard, 12.47 vs 3.04. For MoonBit: on HumanEval, 41.62 vs 34.74; on MBPP, 44.76 vs 37.38; and on McEval-Hard, 25.86 vs 10.93.

claim: EsoLang-Bench evaluated five frontier models (GPT-5.4 xhigh, O4-mini-high, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3-235B and Kimi K2.5) on 80 problems in each of five esoteric languages.
quote: These are GPT-5.4 xhigh [OpenAI, 2026], O4-mini-high [OpenAI, 2025] (OpenAI reasoning model), Gemini 3.1 Pro [Gemini Team, Google DeepMind, 2026] (Google), Qwen3-235B [Qwen Team, 2025] (Alibaba), and Kimi K2.5 [Kimi Team, 2026] (Moonshot).

claim: Every prompt contained the language's full documentation (computational model, complete instruction set, syntax rules and I/O conventions) plus worked examples.
quote: Full language documentation covering the computational model (memory tape, 2D grid, stack, combinators, character/play structure), the complete instruction set, syntax rules, and I/O conventions.

claim: Peak accuracy was 11.2% (GPT-5.4 xhigh with self-scaffolding on Befunge-98), against 100% on the same 80 problems in Python.
quote: Peak accuracy is 11.2% (GPT-5.4 xhigh, self-scaffolding on Befunge-98), compared to 100% on the same 80 problems expressed in Python.

claim: With documentation only (zero-shot), the best cell was 6.2% (O4-mini on Befunge-98), below the 11.2% peak that needed interpreter feedback.
Prepending three solved examples lifted accuracy by only 0.8 percentage points over zero-shot on average, a non-significant difference (Wilcoxon p = 0.505).
quote: The mean cross-language lift from prepending three solved demonstrations is +0.8 pp, against an 89-point gap between mainstream and esoteric performance, and a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test on per-problem solve indicators returns p = 0.505 (n.s.) for few-shot versus zero-shot.

claim: The strongest coding agents (Claude Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.4 xhigh) often avoided writing Brainfuck and Befunge-98 directly, writing Python programs that generate the target code and debugging those generators locally.

claim: On BabelCode code generation across 13 target languages, adherence to the requested language (LCPR) ranged from 74.33% (StarCoder2-15B-Instruct) to 97.60% (Qwen2.5-Instruct-14B) over ten models.
quote: Qwen2.5-Instruct-14B demonstrates the strongest language adherence at 97.60% LCPR, while StarCoder2-15B-Instruct exhibits the lowest fidelity at 74.33% LCPR.

claim: Language confusion is systematic: outputs migrate most notably to Python by default and between syntactically similar language pairs such as C# and Java.
quote: This behavior produces distinct language migration patterns, most notably a strong default to Python and systematic shifts between syntactically similar language pairs (e.g., C#/Java).

claim: On HumanEval-XL, whose prompts name the target language explicitly, nearly all models exceeded 99% LCPR and several reached 100%; the paper ranks explicit language keywords as the most effective mitigation.

claim: In Table IV o3-mini scored 0.18% zero-shot on Gleam McEval-Hard (row: Racket 52.07, Gleam 0.18, MoonBit 1.10), below the wiki's lower bound; the range across the four instruct models is 0.18-0.97%, and 0.40% is Qwen 2.5 Coder 32B Instruct.

claim: RAG was only slightly behind few-shot overall and still lifted hard-task scores well above zero-shot on MoonBit: for GPT-4o on MoonBit McEval-Hard, 0-shot 0.88%, 5-shot 8.06%, RAG 6.12%.
wiki_says: RAG barely better.

claim: The best technique was instruction transfer: adding the instruct-minus-base weight diff to the further pre-trained base model reached up to 26% on Gleam and 33% on MoonBit McEval-Hard at negligible cost; the pre-training figures the wiki cites are for one base model (Qwen 2.5 Coder 32B Base) without instruction following.
quote: This approach considerably outperformed the other techniques, achieving a pass@1 of up to 26% for Gleam and 33% for MoonBit on McEval-Hard.

claim: 11.2% was reached only with self-scaffolding (up to five rounds of interpreter feedback), which the paper calls an order of magnitude above zero-shot for that cell; documentation-only prompting stayed lower, and only Easy-tier problems were ever solved.

wiki_says: Gave five frontier models the full spec of esoteric languages: the best result was 11.2%.

claim: The benefit comes from generating code in any familiar host language, not from Python: JavaScript and Rust generators kept most of the gain.
quote: Thus the critical ingredient is access to a familiar general-purpose host language for constructing target programs, not Python itself
wiki_says: Agents flee to Python. Frontier models write Python programs that generate the code in the target language.

claim: Metaprogramming is a successful adaptation by the two strongest agents, and the causal claim is limited to Brainfuck and Befunge-98, where direct authoring is long and fragile; it is not evidence of a Python pull in general languages.
quote: The metaprogramming claim is specific to Brainfuck and Befunge-98 where direct authoring is fragile, not Whitespace or Shakespeare.

claim: On the same EsoLang-Bench problems under an agentic protocol (language-reference card, file editing, unlimited local interpreter runs, up to three hidden submissions), the mean over four esolangs was 86.9% for Opus 4.6 and 99.7% for GPT-5.4 xhigh, but 24.7% for Haiku 4.5 and 11.3% for Kimi K2.5; the low ceiling belongs to single-shot prompting and to weaker agents.

claim: The >99% figure comes from a different benchmark (HumanEval-XL) compared against BabelCode, not from adding the language name to the same prompts, so dataset and language-set differences are confounded with the keyword.

wiki_says: Naming the language explicitly raised adherence above 99% (also repeated in python-leakage-pilot and evaluation-harness).

claim: Not for every model: on HumanEval-XL (all instruction languages) CodeLlama-13B-Instruct reached 95.97%, StarCoder2-15B-Instruct 93.07% and DeepSeek-V2-Lite 98.92%; the paper says 'nearly all models'.
wiki_says: Naming the language explicitly raised adherence above 99% (same sentence in python-leakage-pilot and training-prior).

claim: In the BabelCode experiment that produced the 74.33-97.60% range, Table III gives each model's dominant migration target: Java for GPT-4.1-Mini (45.38%) and likewise for CodeLlama-13B, GPT-3.5-Turbo and Qwen2.5-14B, JavaScript for Mistral-7B, and Python for only five of ten models. The near-universal Python default was measured on LiveCodeBench, where no language was named.
wiki_says: Adherence ranged from 74.33% to 97.60% across ten models, with 'a strong default to Python'.

claim: MultiPL-E did not measure training-data frequency (Codex's corpus is not public); it grouped languages into four popularity classes from TIOBE rank and GitHub share and tested class differences for Codex with mixed-effects models.
quote: MultiPL-E supports 19 programming languages, which we categorize into four frequency classes (NICHE, LOW, MEDIUM, or HIGH) based on a weighting of TIOBE rank and GitHub frequency (Table 1).
wiki_says: Performance tracks the language's frequency in training ... found a significant correlation with frequency.

claim: The evidence is one model (Codex) and the authors draw 'mixed conclusions' on annotations; they read the TypeScript result as precise types being needed to match the token distribution of typed code seen in training, not as types guiding generation.

claim: A MultiPL-E compiler also translates the signature, docstring terminology and types, and prompt contents matter: removing doctests significantly hurt Codex, and terminology translation had a small but reliable effect.

claim: Running Codex-generated TypeScript without type-checking did not change pass@1 (p = 0.14): the programs the type checker rejects are genuinely wrong, so type errors are real-bug signals rather than noise.

claim: The most common static error theme in every language, UndefinedIdentifier, includes Python-like keywords used in other languages; in Racket, Codex wrote `return`, which is not a Racket keyword.

claim: Codex often generated Markdown for Racket prompts, which the authors attribute to the `#lang racket` file header resembling a Markdown heading: a surface cue in the file header can steer the model to the wrong language.

bears_on: explicit identity: file header and extension design

claim: At temperature 0.8 Codex produced a JavaScript completion whose whole body was executable Python, a direct case of Python leaking into another language's syntax.

bears_on: Python leakage and sampling temperature in the harness

claim: CodeGen did well on TypeScript, absent from its fine-tuning set, which the authors attribute to its similarity to JavaScript: closeness to a well-trained language transfers.

bears_on: whether similarity to Python helps a new language

This significantly lowers Codex's pass@1 rate (-8%; p < 0.001).

claim: In Racket (a NICHE language), Codex produced 2,004 missing-or-unmatched-brace errors, grouped by the authors as 'DoesNotKnowSyntax': in an unfamiliar language, basic syntax errors appear that are almost absent in Python.

bears_on: what kind of errors models make in unfamiliar languages (syntax vs semantics)

claim: Retrieved code examples reduced syntax errors more than retrieved documentation (15.36% vs 8.94% fewer than zero-shot), suggesting models pick up an unfamiliar grammar from examples better than from prose.
quote: This is partially confirmed by the fact that few-shot reduces syntax errors by 15.36% compared to zero-shot, while RAG achieves a smaller reduction of 8.94%.
bears_on: spec design: worked examples vs prose documentation

claim: A hand-checked language manual tailored to the benchmark tasks, given as fixed prompt context to Qwen 2.5 Coder 32B Instruct, reached 15.58/25.07/1.76% (Gleam) and 32.47/39.44/6.61% (MoonBit) on HumanEval/MBPP/McEval-Hard: an optimistic upper bound for spec-in-prompt that still fails on hard tasks.
quote: We obtained a pass@1 of 15.58% on HumanEval, 25.07% on MBPP, and 1.76% of McEval-Hard for Gleam, and 32.47% on HumanEval, 39.44% on MBPP, and 6.61% of McEvalHard for MoonBit.
bears_on: how a new language with a spec in the prompt performs

claim: LLMs consistently did better on Lua than on R despite Lua's fewer repositories, and the authors suggest similarity to a high-resource language (Lua being closer to Python) as the reason.
quote: As already observed in previous studies [6], [35], it is possible that the similarity with a high-resource language can help the model perform well on a low-resource language. For example, in this specific case, Lua is more similar to Python than R.
bears_on: whether similarity to Python helps a new language

claim: Across all benchmarks, no-resource pass@1 stayed between 0% and 20% (average 9%); the non-zero scores on HumanEval and MBPP come from trivial tasks solvable from knowledge of similar languages such as Rust and Java, so 'near zero' holds only for the hard benchmark.
quote: Performance across LLMs and benchmarks stays between 0% and 20%, with an average of 9%.
bears_on: how far a new language starts from zero; similarity to known languages

claim: Fine-tuning and further pre-training cut syntactic failures to under 20% of failures for every model and language, matching the profile of high- and low-resource languages.
quote: Both approaches shift LLM behavior toward what we observed for high- and low-resource languages, with fewer than 20% of failures attributable to syntactic mistakes across all LLM-language combinations.
bears_on: mitigations: training-based approaches vs in-context learning

claim: The authors excluded MultiPL-T because an LLM cannot translate Python into a language it does not know; the synthetic-corpus route needs a translator that works without the model already knowing the target.
quote: In our study, we did not include MULTIPL-T and the approach by Paul et al. [55] as baselines since the former cannot be applied in the context of no-resource languages, given the inability of LLMs to support the automated translation from high- to no-resource languages.
bears_on: synthetic corpus via test-validated translation (transpilation strategy)

claim: LLM-drafted test translations into Gleam and MoonBit needed major manual fixes because the drafting model did not know the languages; building a benchmark for a new language is substantial manual work.

bears_on: evaluation harness: cost of translating benchmarks to lotml

claim: On the relatively-resourced esolangs (Brainfuck, Befunge-98), compile errors were 15-20% and logic errors 35-60%: the model writes parsable code but mistranslates the algorithm into the target's semantics.
quote: Compile errors are 15-20% and logic errors 35-60%, so the model produces parsable code but implements the wrong algorithm.
bears_on: what kind of errors models make in unfamiliar languages (semantics once syntax is acquired)

claim: On the scarcest esolangs (Whitespace, Unlambda, Shakespeare), 70-100% of attempts failed before execution, despite the documentation in the prompt.
quote: 70-100% of attempts fail before execution starts and logic errors are essentially absent because the model rarely produces parsable code in the first place.
bears_on: what kind of errors models make in unfamiliar languages (syntax acquisition)

claim: A separate natural-language critic added nothing over raw interpreter feedback (p = 0.803): concrete execution traces, error messages and crash positions are the useful signal.
quote: a paired Wilcoxon test returns p = 0.803 (n.s.) for TSS versus self-scaffolding, so direct interpreter feedback already captures the benefit and the textual critic adds nothing.
bears_on: compiler feedback in the loop: precise diagnostics over prose explanations

claim: Citing Wang et al. (2025), the paper notes that for Python-derived languages in-context learning helps (Pyth 16.7% to 30.8%) because Python priors bridge the near-identical syntax, unlike the esolangs.

bears_on: whether similarity to Python helps a new language with examples in the prompt

bears_on: limits of a spec in the prompt against the training prior

claim: Only Easy-tier problems were ever solved; every Medium, Hard and Extra-Hard cell was 0% in the static prompting conditions.

bears_on: how a new language with a spec in the prompt performs as task complexity grows

claim: The in-prompt documentation per language was roughly 80 to 140 lines, enough for an author to write verified solutions from it.
quote: The four other languages receive analogously structured documentation of comparable length (between ∼80 and ∼140 lines each)
bears_on: spec length in the prompt

claim: On Brainfuck, generators in Python, JavaScript or Rust gave Opus 4.6 64, 63 and 55 of 80 and GPT-5.4 xhigh 79, 77 and 79 of 80, while forced direct authoring gave 27 and 29 of 80.

claim: The generator helps because it moves implicit, fragile state (cell offsets, pointer position, flags) into named variables and reusable functions: named structure is what makes the low-level target writable.
quote: A host-language generator externalizes this state into named variables and reusable functions, so the same cell allocation, arithmetic, and branching patterns can be emitted consistently across problems.
bears_on: language design: explicit named state over implicit positional state

claim: Written strategy guidance did not help weaker agents, but a small executable helper library did (Sonnet 4.6 12 to 64 on Brainfuck, GPT-5.4 mini 11 to 64 on Befunge-98); Haiku 4.5 stayed flat.

claim: More local interpreter calls helped only agents that already turn feedback into progress; agents near the floor stayed there with many more runs.

bears_on: compiler in the loop: feedback amplifies capable models, does not rescue weak ones

claim: Under the agentic protocol per-language scores ranged 5.0-98.8% on Brainfuck, 5.0-100% on Befunge-98, 31.3-100% on Whitespace and 2.5-100% on Shakespeare across six agents.
quote: Per-language ranges are 5.0-98.8 on Brainfuck, 5.0-100 on Befunge-98, 31.3-100 on Whitespace, and 2.5-100 on Shakespeare.
bears_on: how a new language performs with tools and feedback, and across model tiers

claim: Unfamiliar-language tasks separate agents far more than mainstream benchmarks: the EsoLang standard deviation across six agents was 36.0 against 2.9 on SWE-Bench Verified.

claim: In code translation, where the target language is named and a source program anchors the task, adherence was 98.22-99.73%, far above free generation.

bears_on: Python leakage detection granularity in the pilot and harness
