quote: If a condition expression within a case body is a PelString, Pel interprets it as a natural language condition.

claim: The Pel paper reports no experiment or measurement; its one statement about LLM learnability ('impressive few-shot learnability') is asserted without data.
quote: While Pel has demonstrated impressive few-shot learnability, another promising direction involves fine-tuning LLMs, even small models, specifically for Pel code generation, which could substantially improve code quality and reduce errors.

claim: Quasar separates internal code, which holds program logic and has no effects, from external calls to tools that act on the world.
quote: We propose separating internal code that captures program logic from external calls to tools that interact with the world.

claim: Quasar features are added by annotating external calls with the relevant effects and changing how internal code is executed to track them.
quote: New features can then easily be implemented by (1) annotating external calls with the effects relevant to that feature, and (2) modifying the execution of the internal code to track this information.

claim: Quasar's three demonstrated features are access control with batched approvals, autoparallelization of external calls, and conformal prediction for uncertainty quantification.
quote: access control with batched user queries to improve security, autoparallelization of external calls to reduce latency, and conformal prediction for uncertainty quantification to mitigate hallucinations.

claim: Quasar's software artifact is labelled for COLM 2026.
quote: A software artifact (Mell et al., 2026b) containing both the implementation and figure generation code is available at https://github.com/stephenmell/quasar-colm2026-artifact.

claim: Full Python is the parent language and the Python subset is the child language. 84.8% (28/33) is the best of two configurations (GPT-3.5-turbo); GPT-4-turbo reached 24/33 (72.7%) and the paper's pooled figure is 78%. The number belongs to the whole pipeline (child-language prompt, MAX-SMT type repair, up to five LLM hole-filling calls), on 33 textbook exercises, while the 0/660 figure comes from the elicitation study on a different set (33 regression tests); the parent-language choice was never ablated on its own, and 'parse' means passing all compiler checks, including type checks.
quote: Eudoxus outperforms all baselines in terms of compiler checks (see "Parse Rate" in Table 1), passing all compiler checks on 78% of benchmarks.
wiki_says: The authors chose a Python subset as the parent language and reached 84.8% parse.

claim: The agent's tools are documentation navigation, semantic search and a Cangjie type-lookup index, plus an Execute tool that runs code and a Submit tool that runs public tests; it is not a compiler alone. Most of the jump from zero-shot comes from the documentation: single-time RAG already reaches 40.00 / 46.45 / 59.35 and iterative RAG 47.10 / 52.90 / 65.81, so the agentic loop adds 16-21 points over docs-only retrieval. Sampling at temperature 1.0 with no repeated runs or variance reported, on 155 self-contained HumanEval-derived problems.
quote: | Qwen3-Max         | Single-time RAG                         | 46.45                   |
wiki_says: Shen et al. took generation from 3.23% / 7.74% / 45.16% zero-shot to 63.23% / 73.55% / 81.94% by giving the agent documentation and compiler tools.

claim: The ablation (Qwen3-Max, code generation) does not rank the compiler above the documentation: removing the verification tools drops accuracy 73.55 to 53.55, exactly as much as removing semantic search (53.55), and removing TypeLookup drops it to 57.42. Documentation alone took Qwen3-Max from 7.74 to 46.45. The paper's conclusion is that exploration and verification work only together, so the evidence supports 'docs and compiler are complementary', not 'the compiler is the most important half'.
quote: Without the ability to receive feedback from the execute environment, the accuracy falls dramatically to 53.55%, which is only marginally better than the iterative RAG baseline.
wiki_says: the compiler is the most important half | confirmed and reinforced: docs plus compiler took Cangjie from 3-45% to 63-82%

claim: The MultiPL-T paper does not mention Llama 3. The only downstream adoption it reports is that its datasets entered StarCoder2's pretraining corpus. The Llama 3 statement needs its own citation (the Llama 3 report), not this paper.
quote: The datasets presented in this article are part of the StarCoder2 pretraining corpus as one of several sources of "(Leandro's) High Quality" data.
wiki_says: Llama 3 used the same technique.

claim: MultiPL-T was measured only on languages already in the model's pretraining data, with the low-resource model itself as translator (50-100 samples per function). The authors say it is unlikely to work as-is for languages the model was never trained on, which is lotml's case. For lotml the translator would have to be a rule-based transpiler or a prompted frontier model, neither of which MultiPL-T tested.
quote: MultiPL-T targets low-resource languages, but it is unlikely to work as-is for "no-resource" languages that StarCoderBase is not trained on at all.
wiki_says: A synthetic corpus from test-validated translation ... The Python-to-lotml translator for generating a corpus stops being optional: it is the main lever for open models.

claim: Agnostics reports the cost of that path: MultiPL-T's rejection sampling yields a working program for only about 30% of prompts even with 50-100 attempts, and each target needs a hand-written compiler for test cases and signatures that supports only built-in Python types (no classes) mapped faithfully into the target. Those limits apply to a Python-to-lotml pipeline too, and the wiki should state them.
quote: In MultiPL-T, ≈30% of prompts produce a working program for n ∈ {50, 100} attempts, and the rest are discarded.
wiki_says: The measured path is MultiPL-T's: translate with an LLM and keep only what passes the tests.

claim: The numbers are Ag-LiveCodeBench-X pass@1 (the wiki does not name the benchmark; on MultiPL-E the same 4B models moved only 61->64 Lua and 51->54 Julia). Training also needed a 5,369-problem I/O dataset, a prompt prefix of language tips (written with OpenAI o3 for OCaml and Fortran), and a nonzero base success rate (0.09% was enough). The method failed to improve Qwen 3 1.7B and Llama 3.2 3B. For a language the model has never seen, a compiler and tests are necessary but not shown to be sufficient.
quote: However, we found that Agnostics training on Ag-Codeforces-X does not improve two smaller models, Qwen 3 1.7B and Llama 3.2 3B Instruct, perhaps due to the problems being too difficult for models of this size.
wiki_says: Agnostics trained Qwen3-4B with only an input/output verifier and a short per-language configuration: Lua 11->23%, Julia 10->22%, OCaml 1->7%. A compiler and tests are enough.

claim: Quasar measures tooling benefits from effect annotations on external calls. Batched approvals cut user interactions by 26% on both GQA and AgentDojo, and autoparallelization cut running time by 18% (GQA) and 27% (AgentDojo). Variance is large because only about half of the tasks can be batched or parallelized. On BrowseComp-Plus the cuts were 97% fewer approvals and a 93% speedup. The caveat is that tool authors attach the annotations to external functions, and the LLM writes plain Python, so this is evidence for tooling, not for models writing effect annotations.
quote: On the GQA dataset, QUASAR reduces running time by 18%±23.
wiki_says: There is no evidence that effect annotations help LLMs or tooling - the search found no study.

claim: The table leaves out the decisive point for lotml: models do not write Quasar. They write a restricted Python subset (no classes or inheritance) that a transpiler compiles to Quasar, because models struggle to generate Quasar directly. Restricting generation to the subset kept accuracy close to unrestricted Python (GQA 71.4 vs 71.8). The third feature, conformal prediction for uncertainty quantification, is also missing from the table.
quote: Instead, our strategy is to have the LLM generate Python and then transpile this Python code to QUASAR using an existing compiler (Mell et al., 2026a).
wiki_says: Quasar: separates internal logic from tool calls with effect annotations, for access control and parallelization.

claim: Quasar does report measurements: task accuracy when generating through the Python subset against unrestricted Python, reductions in approvals and latency, and conformal coverage. None of them shows that a new surface syntax helps the model, because the model writes Python. 'None with evidence that the design helps the model write code' is accurate; 'none with measured evidence' is not.
quote: We show that generating QUASAR code via transpilation retains task performance comparable to that of Python, and we present several strategies for improving transpilation success.
wiki_says: no language has been designed for LLMs | outdated: BAML, MoonBit, Pel, NanoLang, Zero, Quasar - none with measured evidence

claim: A five-iteration self-repair loop with UCLID5 compiler feedback produced zero programs passing compiler checks for both GPT-4-turbo and GPT-3.5-turbo: when the model has no prior for the language, compiler feedback alone does not rescue it; the parent language plus deductive repair did.
quote: | Self-repair (GPT4t)         | 0            |
bears_on: compiler in the loop versus a familiar parent language for a zero-corpus language

claim: The parent language was chosen by an elicitation study rather than by taste: models asked to use a non-existent Python verification API wrote consistent code, falling into three categories, and the child language was fitted to the 'object-oriented' category, judged easiest to translate to UCLID5.
quote: When asked to write Python code that used a non-existent formal verification API, however, the LLM outputs were more consistent.
bears_on: method for choosing lotml's surface syntax: elicit what models naturally write before fixing the grammar

claim: SPEAC argues that repairs too aggressive for human users (e.g. inserting missing declarations, retyping variables from their uses via MAX-SMT) are appropriate when the 'user' is an LLM.
quote: The second key idea in our approach is that program analyses and repair that are overly aggressive for human users may be suitable for LLM "users."
bears_on: automatically applicable compiler fixes for Python habits (training-prior item 6)

claim: The two Eudoxus versions produced compiler-clean programs for 30/33 distinct problems, while all 11 baseline variants together managed 6/33.
quote: Even more interesting, the two versions of Eudoxus generated programs that passed all compiler checks for 30/33 unique problems; the 11 versions of the baselines together generated programs that passed all compiler checks for only 6/33 unique problems.
bears_on: size of the parent-language effect on a very low-resource target

claim: Passing compiler checks is not correctness: 33 of 52 compiler-clean Eudoxus programs scored 4 or 5 on a 1-5 scale, graded by a single author (a stated threat to validity).
quote: On the other hand, 33/52 programs (24 unique problems) that pass compiler checks produced by Eudoxus scored four or higher.
bears_on: evaluation harness: syntactic validity must be paired with executed or graded semantics

claim: SPEAC critiques MultiPL-T-style corpus generation: it only works where the model can already translate into the target reliably, and assumes a general-purpose target.
quote: This approach is restricted to languages where the LLM is able to translate to the language reliably but unable to generate code from natural language.
bears_on: bootstrapping a corpus for a language the model has never seen

claim: Grammar prompting and grammar-constrained decoding are dismissed for real languages because context-free grammars cannot capture context-sensitive languages, and static-analysis decoding assumes a linear, no-backtracking process.
quote: This approach works well for simple languages but cannot capture most non-trivial programming languages, which are context-sensitive.
bears_on: constrained decoding covers only syntax

claim: The deductive repair is cheap relative to the model: 0.9 s of MAX-SMT repair versus 7.2 s of LLM calls per task with GPT-3.5-turbo (1.8 s versus 35.1 s with GPT-4-turbo).
quote: Eudoxus with GPT3t took an average of 0.9 seconds (SD 0.6) in repair steps and 7.2 seconds (SD 4.6) in LLM calls.
bears_on: latency budget of a repairing semantic compiler

claim: Internal inconsistency: the introduction cites 9.1% for the fine-tuned GPT-3.5-turbo baseline, but Table 1 reports 2/33 (6.1%) for it; cite the table if the baseline is used.
quote: | Fine-tuned GPT3t            | 2/33         |
bears_on: citation accuracy

claim: Removing the Cangjie-specific TypeLookup tool (type or class name in, members and docs out) cut Qwen3-Max code-generation accuracy from 73.55 to 57.42; the authors single out language-specific type checkers and fetchers as highly effective agent extensions.
quote: This underscores a key insight for practical applications: equipping ILA agents with language-specific extensions, such as type checkers or fetchers, is a highly effective strategy for boosting both performance and efficiency.
bears_on: semantic compiler: a type/symbol lookup query (digest) for agents

claim: Documentation search must be semantic, not keyword-based, because a model unfamiliar with the language asks conceptually related but lexically different questions; removing SemSearch cut accuracy from 73.55 to 53.55.
quote: This design choice is crucial since an LLM, being unfamiliar with the target language, may generate conceptually-related but lexically-different queries.
bears_on: what documentation tooling an agent needs to write an unfamiliar language

claim: The fine-tuned Java-to-Cangjie translator compiled 85.45% of outputs but was functionally correct on only 61.21%, below ILA-agent with every model (64.24-76.36); compile rate overstates the quality of a fine-tuned low-resource model.
quote: it exhibits a severe deficit in functional correctness, even when achieving a high compilation pass rate.
bears_on: fine-tuning a corpus versus inference-time docs plus verification; compile rate is not a quality metric

claim: In program repair the agent starts by running the buggy code and uses the error message to direct documentation lookup, so diagnostics are the entry point into the docs.
quote: The agent often first runs the buggy code to obtain the resulting error message, which then inform a more focused exploration phase.
bears_on: diagnostics that point into the documentation

claim: An Execute tool that runs arbitrary snippets lets the agent test isolated language constructs before writing the full solution; agents rarely go from exploration straight to Submit without Execute first.
quote: This is critical for verifying unfamiliar language knowledge in a low-stake, exploratory manner.
bears_on: agent tooling: a snippet runner or REPL alongside the compiler

claim: The method presumes well-structured official documentation and informative execution feedback, and was tested on one statically typed language with self-contained tasks only.
quote: We assume the existence of well-structured documentation and the execution environment that provide informative feedback, highlighting a symbiotic relationship between AIdriven tools and the language ecosystem itself.
bears_on: documentation and diagnostics as part of the language deliverable

claim: The documentation was parsed into chunks following its table of contents, exposed through ViewStruct/ViewDetail navigation; removing these structural views cut accuracy from 73.55 to 65.81.
quote: We automatically parse the documentation into structured chunks based on its table of contents and chapter divisions.
bears_on: shape of the lotml documentation: hierarchical, chunkable by section

claim: Test validation is the active ingredient: fine-tuning StarCoderBase-15B on unvalidated Racket translations gave 11.6 pass@1 (base 11.8), against 21.0 with validated data.
quote: | StarCoderBase-15B |       11.8 |        21.0 |            11.6 |
bears_on: corpus bootstrap: an unvalidated translated corpus is worthless

claim: Showing the original Python in the translation prompt raised pass@50 for Racket (34.7 to 56.8) and Lua (51.4 to 68.5) but lowered it for OCaml (26.1 to 23.9); the authors speculate Python misleads the model when the target is further from Python.
quote: As shown in Table 7, adding the original Python to the prompt substantially increases the likelihood of a successful translation to Racket and Lua, but slightly decreases the likelihood of a successful translation to OCaml.
bears_on: Python-like syntax with different semantics: Python context can mislead translation

claim: Simply training longer on the language's natural data from The Stack barely helped Racket and OCaml and hurt Lua, and self-instruct produced buggy programs (four of five in a sample).
quote: Nevertheless, we get poor results for all: the performance of these fine-tuned models barely increases for Racket and OCaml and even decreases for Lua.
bears_on: corpus bootstrap: more raw data or self-generated data does not substitute for validation

claim: Translated-from-Python data slightly degraded idiomatic style: Racket style score fell from 89.5% to 85.2%, with more nested ifs and iteration where recursion was idiomatic.
quote: We find that the base model achieves a style score of 89.5% and the finetuned model 85.2%.
bears_on: a Python-derived corpus carries Python idioms into the target language

claim: For typed targets, types inferred from the Python tests were put into the target signature, because with type annotations the model is far more likely to produce a function of the expected type.
quote: With type annotations, the LLM is far more likely to produce a function with the expected type.
bears_on: mandatory signatures, and typed Python as the source of a lotml corpus

claim: On a 14-problem benchmark using user-defined types, higher-order functions and libraries, the OCaml-tuned 15B model regressed (50.6 to 42.9), suggesting single-function synthetic data can overfit; the authors suggest mixing in natural data.
bears_on: a corpus of isolated functions may not teach program-level structure

claim: Generating the datasets took about 9,984 A100 GPU-hours, the largest share of roughly 550 GPU-days spent on the project.
quote: Dataset Generation: ~9,984 hours generating the MultiPL-T training sets.
bears_on: cost of bootstrapping a corpus by LLM translation

claim: The authors expect source-target proximity to matter: for Rust they would rather translate from C++ than Python.
quote: However, we speculate that it would be more effective to modify MultiPL-T to support a source language closer to Rust, such as C++.
bears_on: parent language: a source close to the target eases translation

claim: RL started from almost nothing: a base success rate as low as 0.09% was enough to start learning, and configuring OCaml and Fortran took an hour each.
quote: The prefix only needed to slightly raise the model's train split performance; base accuracy as low as 0.09% was enough for the model to start learning (see §4.3). Configuring the two languages took 1 hour each.
bears_on: RL for a zero-corpus language: the spec in the prompt only has to get the first successes

claim: For near-zero languages the prompt prefix was built by sampling faulty programs from the base model and asking o3 to distil the model's misconceptions into 10-20 sentences of advice.
quote: For OCaml and Fortran, we let a base model generate several faulty snippets, and asked a capable LLM (OpenAI o3) for advice based on the snippets with the following prompt.
bears_on: writing the lotml spec and diagnostics from observed model errors (Python habits)

claim: Distillation lost to RL: fine-tuning Qwen 3 4B on 1,987 Fortran solutions from Sonnet 4 Thinking (teacher 12%) reached only 2-3%, while Agnostics reached 15%.
quote: Table 5 shows the resulting models reach scores far lower than the 15% of Qwen3-4B-CF-Fortran (Table 2).
bears_on: corpus bootstrap: distilling from a frontier model versus RL with a verifier

claim: Partial rewards were exploited: rewarding programs that run without error, or that pass only public tests, taught models to emit empty programs or hard-code public tests, so the reward is binary on all tests.
quote: In both cases the models were very likely to learn how to exploit the reward, e.g., by producing empty programs or by hard-coding the public tests
bears_on: verifier design for any lotml RL loop: no credit for merely compiling

claim: Training removed shallow errors: OCaml programs with syntax errors fell from 55% to 35% and builtin misuse from 60% to 32%, while visible logic flaws rose from 18% to 25%.
quote: More programs have syntax errors (55% vs 35% after training), more programs misuse builtin functions (60% vs 32%), and so on.
bears_on: which errors dominate in an unfamiliar language: standard-library misuse as much as syntax

claim: Rejection sampling would be too sparse on hard tasks: during training the Fortran model succeeded 6.64% of the time (11,400 verified programs), the base model 0.09% (158 programs).
quote: During Agnostics training, Qwen3-4B-CF-Fortran generated a correct answer to a train split problem only 6.64% of the time, generating 11400 verified programs overall.
bears_on: RL versus MultiPL-T-style rejection sampling for bootstrapping

claim: Specialization costs other low-resource languages: the Lua-trained Qwen3-4B kept Python roughly flat (34.34 to 32.96) but fell from 10.00 to 6.55 in Julia and 10.00 to 3.00 in R, despite the text's claim that training does not lower other languages.
bears_on: cost of specializing an open model on lotml

claim: MultiPL-E needs a roughly 500-line prompt and test translator per language, while I/O-specified tasks reuse one verifier; Ag-LiveCodeBench-X is also much harder than MultiPL-E.
quote: Each MultiPL-E programming language requires a ≈500 LOC prompt and test translator, considerably more effort than writing an Agnostics configuration file.
bears_on: evaluation harness: I/O-specified tasks versus translating HumanEval/MBPP signatures and tests

claim: Pel adopts pipes so the model can write the inner call first and decide on the outer one afterwards, matching left-to-right generation; the benefit is argued, not measured.
quote: Unlike traditional nested function calls bar(foo(a)) where the LLM needs to plan the bar( call before generating foo(a), Pel's pipes allow the LLM to generate (foo a), then decide to pipe it into bar after the fact
bears_on: syntax for left-to-right generation (pipes, method chains)

claim: Pel's argument against Python as an action language is that its grammar (hundreds of EBNF lines) is too large to restrict feature-by-feature in constrained decoding.
quote: Modifying the grammar of languages like Python to disable features at the generation level is impractical due to their complexity (e.g., Python's EBNF grammar spans hundreds of lines).
bears_on: tension between a Python-like syntax and grammar-constrained decoding

claim: Pel errors carry the failing function's signature, types and docstring, and an LLM helper agent proposes a rewrite from that context.
quote: When an error occurs, the associated PelException captures not only the error message and location but also contextual information, often derived from the docstring of the Pel function where the error originated.
bears_on: diagnostics that embed the signature and documentation of what was misused

claim: The REPeL keeps the environment after an error and offers Common Lisp-style restarts (rewrite all, rewrite from the error, rewrite one expression), so expensive earlier agent calls are not lost.
quote: the REPeL does not simply crash; it preserves the state of the environment before the error and presents the user (or an automated system) with restart options:
bears_on: agent tooling: resumable execution after a compile or runtime error

claim: Pel deliberately diverges from Python's truthiness (PelNil is neither true nor false) and declares lists 1-indexed, yet its own examples index from both 0 and 1; it never measures whether models carry Python habits into these differences.
quote: Importantly, unlike Python's None, PelNil does not evaluate to false in conditional contexts. Its truthiness is undefined.
bears_on: semantic divergence from Python and unmeasured leakage risk

claim: Pel asserts that uniform S-expression syntax improves in-context learning but gives no measurement.
quote: This uniformity makes the language easier for LLMs to learn (better incontext learning) and parse.
bears_on: which language features designers chose for LLMs, and whether they measured any benefit

claim: Pel parallelizes independent top-level expressions automatically from a def/use dependency graph, which its immutability makes simple.
quote: Pel's functional nature and emphasis on immutability simplify this dependency analysis.
bears_on: colorless concurrency through dependency analysis

claim: Models could not write Quasar's own syntax: they have never seen it and struggle to generate it, so Quasar keeps Python as the surface language and transpiles.
quote: A key challenge is that LLMs have never seen it before, and we find that they struggle to generate it directly.
bears_on: role of a Python-like surface syntax for a language with no corpus

claim: Instructing GPT-5 to stay inside the transpilable Python subset barely changed accuracy (GQA 71.4 vs 71.8 for unrestricted Python; AgentDojo 63.4 vs 64.5) and execution success (97.9 vs 99.6; 82.8 vs 76.3).
bears_on: cost of restricting a model to a Python subset with different semantics

claim: Feeding the transpiler's static errors back in a multi-turn loop raised accuracy above unrestricted Python (GQA 72.3, AgentDojo 67.7) without executing faulty code, so no side effects.
quote: Importantly, this feedback is based only on static program information; in contrast, traditional multi-turn feedback based on Python interpreter errors requires running the code, which can result in undesirable side effects from unsuccessfully executed code.
bears_on: a static-diagnostics loop (semantic compiler) instead of run-and-fix

claim: The subset leaves out classes and inheritance on the grounds that code actions perform actions rather than build complex software.
quote: However, many practical code actions do not use the unsupported language features of Python (e.g., classes and inheritance); intuitively, LLMs are trying to perform actions, not write complex software.
bears_on: lotml's feature set: no classes

claim: Quasar is functional (single assignment) but accepts Python's imperative updates inside if/for by compiling them into expression-level conditionals and folds, instead of asking the model to write immutable code.
quote: QUASAR is functional, while Python is imperative. Thus, in QUASAR, variables cannot be changed once they have been defined.
bears_on: immutable-by-default semantics: compile Python-style mutation away rather than forbid it (the pilot saw models reassign immutable locals)

claim: Gains grow with task complexity: on 80 BrowseComp-Plus tasks with Recursive Language Models, approvals fell 97% and runtime 93%.
quote: We see large improvements on this dataset: there is a 97%±1 reduction in the number of user approvals required and a 93%± 4 speedup.
bears_on: measured benefit of effect and capability metadata for agent tooling

claim: The approval, latency and conformal analyses include only programs that compile and execute in Quasar, so they say nothing about failures.
quote: We only include programs in our analysis that successfully compile and execute in QUASAR (i.e., no compilation or execution errors), but we include programs regardless of whether their output matches the ground truth label.
bears_on: evidence quality of measured benefits

claim: Across six open-weight models generating TypeScript for HumanEval and MBPP, on average 94% of compilation errors came from failing type checks rather than syntax.
quote: In our evaluation of LLMs (§5), on average 94% of compilation errors result from failing type checks.

claim: In the same evaluation, syntax errors were on average 6% of the compilation errors in generated TypeScript.
quote: For instance, in our evaluation of state-of-the-art open-weight LLMs (§5), syntactic errors make up on average 6% of all compilation errors in generated TypeScript code.

claim: The evaluation used six instruction-tuned open-weight models of 2B to 34B parameters (Gemma 2 2B/9B/27B, DeepSeek Coder 33B, CodeLlama 34B, Qwen2.5 32B), no closed frontier model.
quote: We use 6 different open-weight LLMs, covering 3 LLMs of varying parameter sizes from the same model family and 4 models of a similar size from different model families

claim: The benchmarks were the MultiPL-E TypeScript translations of HumanEval (159 tasks) and MBPP (384 tasks).
quote: The benchmarks for these tasks are based on TypeScript-translated tasks from HumanEval [12] and MBPP [5], contained in the MultiPL-E dataset [13], with 159 and 384 instances each.

claim: For synthesis and translation together, type-constrained decoding reduced compilation errors by 75.3% on HumanEval and 52.1% on MBPP, averaged over the six models.
quote: In contrast, type constraining reduces compilation errors by more than half, i.e., by 75.3% and 52.1% on HumanEval and MBPP respectively.

claim: For synthesis and translation together, only 9.0% (HumanEval) and 4.9% (MBPP) of the non-compiling instances were due to syntax, the ceiling of an idealized syntax-only constrainer.
quote: For synthesis and translation, in the unconstrained setting (Vanilla), on average only 9.0% and 4.9% of the non-compiling instances in HumanEval and MBPP respectively are due to syntactic errors (Syntax)

claim: In the repair task, type constraining raised pass@1 by 37.0% relative to unconstrained decoding, on average over models and datasets.
quote: employing type constraining improves LLMs' pass@1 rate, achieving an average increase by 3.5% in synthesis, 5.0% in translation, and 37.0% in repair tasks.

claim: In the repair task, type-constrained sampling resolved 53.7% more compilation errors than vanilla decoding.
quote: On average, using type-constrained sampling, 53.7% more compilation errors are resolved than using vanilla LLM decoding.

claim: The median time per synthesis instance rose by 39.1% (HumanEval) and 52.1% (MBPP) on average over the models.
quote: On average over the evaluated models, we observe a relative increase of 39.1% and 52.1% in HumanEval and MBPP respectively.

claim: The overhead was measured on an unoptimized Python implementation that the authors expect a systems-oriented implementation to improve.
quote: Moreover, this is measured on an unoptimized, Python-based implementation and could be significantly improved by a more system-oriented implementation

claim: In RustRepoTrans (v6), compilation errors were 92.3% of failed translations to Rust, against 58.3% to 83.3% for other target languages in Pan et al.
quote: In RustRepoTrans, compilation errors account for 92.3% of failures, significantly higher than the 58.3% to 83.3% observed in other benchmarks.

claim: The failure analysis covers the 1,748 translations from seven LLMs that failed at least one test, over 375 C, Java and Python to Rust tasks with repository context.
quote: We collected all unsuccessful translations from LLMs in RQ1 (Section IV-B), resulting in 1,748 code samples that failed to pass all test cases.

claim: By raw count of rustc error messages, the most frequent code was E0599 (method not implemented for the type), with 4,079 occurrences.
quote: E0599        |       4,079 | This error occurs when a method is used on a type which doesn't implement it.

claim: E0425 (unresolved name) was second, with 2,095 occurrences.
quote: | E0425        |       2,095 | An unresolved name was used.

claim: E0277 (type does not implement a required trait) was fourth, with 976 occurrences.
quote: E0277        |         976 | You tried to use a type which doesn't implement some trait in a place which expected that trait.

claim: The authors attribute many of the top error codes to the use of nonexistent, unimplemented, unresolved or undeclared elements.
quote: Many of these stem from using nonexistent, unimplemented, unresolved, or undeclared elements, highlighting the hallucination phenomenon also seen in other repository-level code generation tasks

claim: The corpus is 86,726 code samples with compilation or runtime errors, generated by seven LLMs in four compiled languages (C++, Java, C, Rust).
quote: we analyzed a corpus of 86,726 code samples that contained compilation or runtime errors. These samples were generated by seven LLMs across four compiled languages.

claim: The problems are 1,651 contest-style problems from IBM's Project CodeNet, taken from the PROBE dataset.
quote: This dataset is made up of 1,651 programming-contest-style problems from IBM's Project CodeNet dataset [25], grouped into four difficulty levels.

claim: Under the baseline prompt, 16.7% of Rust compilation-error labels were ownership and lifetime errors and 6.1% trait or type-bound errors.
quote: Rust shows a distinct pattern, with 16.7% of errors related to "Ownership and lifetime" and 6.1% to "Trait/type bound" issues.

claim: The 16.7% is 2,165 of 12,942 Rust compilation-error labels in the baseline-prompt table.
Asking the LLM simply for revised code snippets did not work in RustAssistant's real-world evaluation.
quote: We tried a naive approach where we asked the LLM to simply give us the revised code snippets. This approach did not work in our real-world evaluation.

claim: With revised snippets instead of the changelog, RustAssistant's accuracy on the top-100 crates fell below 10% (commit-level, GPT-3.5, Table 4).
quote: As Section 5 will show (Table 4), the accuracy of RustAssistant tanked below 10%, making the tool unusable.

claim: On the 50 Stack Overflow programs, RustAssistant with GPT-4 reached a peak fix rate of 74% (37 of 50, one completion).
quote: RustAssistant is able to achieve a peak fix percentage of 74% demonstrating that these benchmarks are harder.

claim: With GPT-4, RustAssistant fixed 92.59% of the micro-benchmarks, 72% of the Stack Overflow programs and 73.63% of the GitHub commits.
quote: With GPT-4, we find that RustAssistant is able to fix 92.59% of the micro-benchmarks, 72% of the Stack Overflow programs, and 73.63% of the GitHub commits.

claim: The 270 micro-benchmarks are hand-written programs, one per error code, covering 270 of the 506 official Rust error codes.
quote: (a) 270 microbenchmarks that we have written ourselves, covering 270/506 official Rust error codes [50]

claim: On the micro-benchmarks, fix rates were fairly consistent across the six error-code categories, ownership and lifetime included.
quote: The performance of the models is fairly consistent across categories, suggesting that there are no specific error codes that are easier or harder for the models to fix.

claim: The micro-benchmark error codes were grouped into six categories: Syntax, Type, Generics, Traits, Ownership and Lifetime.
quote: We further classified each of the errors codes into one of the six categories: Syntax, Type, Generics, Traits, Ownership, and Lifetime.

claim: The two pairs come from different task sets. 75.3%/52.1% is synthesis plus translation, where the syntax ceiling is 9.0%/4.9%. 9.0%/4.8% is the synthesis-only caption, where types cut 74.8%/56.0%. Pair like with like.
quote: Type constraining reduces compiler errors by 74.8% and 56.0% in the synthesis of HumanEval and MBPP problems respectively, compared to only 9.0% and 4.8% ideal improvement on the two datasets respectively through syntax-only constraining.
wiki_says: Constraining by types cut 75.3% (HumanEval) and 52.1% (MBPP) of compilation errors; constraining syntax alone would, in the ideal case, cut 9.0% and 4.8%.

claim: The 37% is a relative pass@1 increase, averaged over models, on repairing the models' own non-compiling synthesis outputs given the compiler error. It is not 37 percentage points. The compile-error figure for repair is 53.7% more errors resolved.
quote: Additionally, it enhances functionally correct repair of non-compiling code relatively by 37% on average.
wiki_says: Repair improved by 37%.

claim: The figure is for TypeScript only, from six open-weight models of 2B to 34B parameters on HumanEval/MBPP. The authors expect stronger models to make fewer typing errors on these datasets. It does not cover 'typed code' in general.
quote: Stronger LLMs, such as the latest OpenAI models [33], may make fewer typing errors on the HumanEval and MBPP datasets.
wiki_says: 94% of LLM compile errors in typed code are type errors; syntax is about 6%.

claim: The 94% is the complement of the syntax share. Syntax was detected with the oxc toolchain and counted per non-compiling instance, so 'type checks' covers every non-syntactic tsc rejection, including undeclared identifiers (the paper's own example), wrong arity and missing returns. The TypeScript and Rust findings therefore do not conflict: unresolved names are inside the 94%.
quote: We compute syntactic correctness using the Oxidation toolchain [52] as the official TypeScript compiler does not clearly distinguish between syntactic and semantic errors.
wiki_says: Types, not syntax: 94% of compilation errors result from failing type checks (TypeScript); separately, unresolved names lead in Rust.

claim: The cited version (v6, pinned in sources.json) reports 92.3% (1,614 of 1,748 failed translations, seven LLMs). 94.8% does not appear anywhere in it and probably comes from an earlier version.
quote: our experiments of seven representative LLMs show that LLMs struggle with repositorylevel context code translation, with compilation errors reaching 92.3%
wiki_says: When translating to Rust (RustRepoTrans), compile errors are 94.8% of failures.

claim: v6 reports 92.3% of failures as compilation errors, with 0% runtime errors and 7.7% functional errors.
quote: In RustRepoTrans, compilation errors account for 92.3% of failures, significantly higher than the 58.3% to 83.3% observed in other benchmarks.
wiki_says: Even so, compile errors are 94.8% of failures when translating to Rust (RustRepoTrans).

claim: By count, E0599 comes first (4,079) and E0425 second (2,095). E0308 type mismatch (1,035) is third, ahead of E0277 (976), so it is not far behind. The heading 'Unresolved names lead' should read 'missing methods and unresolved names lead'.
quote: | E0308        |       1,035 | Expected type did not match the received type.
wiki_says: The most frequent codes are unresolved name (E0425), missing method (E0599), unresolved import (E0432) and missing trait (E0277); type mismatch (E0308) is far behind.

claim: E0432 is ninth with 287 occurrences, behind E0609 (906), E0433 (639), E0061 (343) and E0252 (290). The counts are of error messages, at an average of 7.7 per failed translation, so cascades inflate them.
quote: | E0432        |         287 | An import was unresolved.
wiki_says: E0432 (unresolved import) is among the four most frequent codes.

claim: The denominator is wrong. 86,726 counts samples with compilation or runtime errors across four languages and two prompts. The 16.7% is 2,165 of 12,942 Rust compilation-error labels under the baseline prompt only. Labels are multi-label and were assigned by GPT-4.1-mini, with 0.91 exact-match accuracy on Rust.
wiki_says: In 86,726 errors from seven models on CodeNet, ownership and lifetimes were 16.7%.

claim: In this paper's Rust data, type mismatches ('Incompatible parameter types', 43.4%) dominate, followed by missing imports (20.5%) and ownership (16.7%). Trait/type-bound errors are only 6.1% and undeclared variables 3.8%. 'Names and traits dominate' fits only RustRepoTrans's repository-context translation, not this self-contained setting.
quote: The "Incompatible parameter types" error was more prevalent in Java (43.0%) and Rust (43.4%) than in C++ (20.3%) and C (21.9%).
wiki_says: Corrected: ownership is 16.7% of errors; names and traits dominate.

claim: The largest Rust-specific excess is type mismatches, a genuine absolute increase that the authors attribute to Rust's strict type system and low training-data share. Trait/type-bound errors are a small class (6.1%).
quote: In contrast, Rust exhibits a substantially higher absolute number of incompatible parameter type errors (5,555), indicating a genuine increase rather than a relative effect.
wiki_says: What makes Rust hard for LLMs is the combination: traits, name resolution and ownership.

claim: In this paper's feedback data, ownership/lifetime errors had one of the two highest not-fixed shares (33.6%, with incompatible parameter types at 33.7%), although their full-fix rate (12.9%) is close to the others'.
wiki_says: RustAssistant fixes those categories [ownership and lifetimes] at the same rate as the others.

claim: The equal-rate result holds only for the synthetic micro-benchmarks: one hand-written program per error code. The Stack Overflow set was deliberately concentrated on memory- and thread-safety errors, and it was harder (GPT-4 peak 74% against 92.59%).
quote: To limit the effort, we concentrate on memory-safety and thread-safety issues, two areas in which the Rust type system is stricter than C/C++.
wiki_says: RustAssistant fixes those categories [ownership and lifetimes] at the same rate as the others.

claim: The comparison mixes conditions. 'Below 10%' is GPT-3.5 at commit level on the top-100 crates; 74% on SO is GPT-4. The paper's own 10%-to-74% contrast is on micro-benchmarks with GPT-3.5, and its 10% end is already a changelog (FixedCode only, P1), not whole revised snippets. Line numbers, the echoed original code and the fix description raised it to 73.70%.
quote: We demonstrate the features that were needed to help the model communicate code changes, bring accuracy up from a mere 10% to nearly 74%.
wiki_says: Asking for the whole revised snippet dropped accuracy to 'below 10%'; a changelog format with original and fixed lines reached about 74% on the Stack Overflow cases.

claim: Below 10% is the share of commits fully fixed. Per error, the revised-snippet prompt (P0) still fixed 32.22% (N=1) and 41.30% (N=5) of errors with GPT-3.5, against 44.76% and 55.03% for the full changelog prompt.
wiki_says: Asking for the whole revised snippet dropped accuracy to 'below 10%'.

claim: The arXiv v1 text names no venue for this paper. Its only ISSRE mention is the authors' earlier 2025 paper, so the venue cannot be checked against the source.
quote: in 2025 IEEE 36th International Symposium on Software Reliability Engineering (ISSRE), 2025, pp. 264-275.
wiki_says: Nogueira, Vieira and Campos, ISSRE 2026.

claim: A conventional type checker cannot drive constrained decoding: the decoder needs a completion engine that answers whether a prefix can still be completed into a well-typed program.
quote: Note that commonly used grammar and type checkers can not be used as a completion engine for constrained decoding.
bears_on: type-system: types checkable on prefixes; compiler architecture

claim: The authors suggest that new languages build their compilers as incremental completion engines, so constrained generation comes for free alongside parsing and type checking.
quote: their compilers as an incremental completion engine, which additionally enables automatic adoption for constrained code generation, besides conventional grammar parsing and type checking.
bears_on: semantic-compiler and constrained-decoding: one front end serving the parser, checker and decoder

claim: To make the constrainer work, the authors made TypeScript stricter. Parameters and return types must be annotated, every variable must be annotated or initialized, and callbacks to reduce need an annotated accumulator. Without these, generated code often failed to compile.
quote: We have identified three situations where generated code often fails to compile without type annotations, prompting us to enforce them.
bears_on: type-system: mandatory signatures, local inference, annotation of empty collections

claim: The TypeScript subset excluded features that block left-to-right typing, among them destructuring assignment, unannotated uninitialized declarations, return-type inference, literal types and enums. It also excluded use of functions before declaration, user-defined classes and type declarations, and general generic functions.
quote: Destructuring Assignment Uninitialized, Unannotated Variable Declarations Return Type Inference Literal Types Enums
bears_on: type-system: which features make prefix type checking hard; forward references; return-type inference

claim: Self-referential members such as valueOf or clone produce unbounded chains of higher-order types. The type-reachability search therefore needs a pruning heuristic and becomes incomplete, so it can reject well-typed code.
quote: Some programming languages define self-referential default members, e.g., clone in Java or valueOf in TypeScript, which are nullary functions that return a value of the same type as the callee
bears_on: type-system and constrained-decoding: keep the member/trait graph finite for type search

claim: A case study failure is TypeScript inferring never[] for an empty array literal used as an accumulator. The constrainer fixed it by forcing an annotation, the same case as lotml's `var xs: [int] = []`.
quote: TypeScript infers special type never[] for the empty array, disallowing inserting curr of type number through push.
bears_on: type-system: annotation required for empty collections under local inference

claim: Sample-and-check needs one completion-engine call per token in 99.4% of cases. The prior approach of masking the whole vocabulary timed out on every benchmark instance.
quote: In our experiments, their implementation results in timeouts for all benchmark instances, with a timeout of 5 minutes per instance.
bears_on: constrained-decoding: implementation strategy and cost of a type-aware constrainer

claim: The reported Types results are an emulation, because the implementation covers only a TypeScript subset. Samples that compiled unconstrained are kept as is; only failing ones are resampled under constraints. Constrained decoding also needs next-token distributions, which closed APIs do not expose.
quote: Concretely, if a sample compiles correctly without any constraining, we report it as-is. Otherwise, we report the result of a constrained resample.
bears_on: constrained-decoding: how far the 75%/52% figures transfer; frontier-model availability

claim: A failed Rust translation carried 1 to 193 compiler errors (mean 7.7, median 3). The authors see rustc's report-everything behaviour as making repair harder, which argues for root-cause-first ordering and cascade suppression.
quote: In unsuccessful translations, the number of compilation errors ranged from 1 to 193 (average: 7.7, median: 3), complicating debugging.
bears_on: semantic-compiler: report every error but order by root cause; suppress cascades

claim: Dependency-related errors, meaning unresolved functions and variables from the surrounding repository, account for 67.6% of failures.
quote: Dependencyrelated errors, including function and variable resolution issues, account for 67.6% of failures, highlighting the challenge of interconnected code.
bears_on: semantic-compiler: name/import diagnostics with did-you-mean and suggested imports

claim: By manual cause, function-difference errors lead at 38.6%, then variable differences (24.9%) and data-type misinterpretation (16.1%). Hallucinated cross-language APIs outweigh type confusion.
quote: At a more detailed level, the top three error causes are Function Differences Misinterpretation (38.6%), Variable Differences Misinterpretation (24.9%), and Data Type Misinterpretation (16.1%).
bears_on: which error classes dominate LLM compile failures in Rust with repository context

claim: Borrow-checker errors appear inside the 'variable state' cause, together with undeclared variables and privacy. They are not a separate dominant class.
quote: Common issues include treating undeclared variables as declared, making simultaneous mutable borrows, using the same variable as both mutable and immutable, and incorrectly treating private variables as public.
bears_on: memory-model: weight of ownership errors; mutability diagnostics

claim: Source-language syntax leaks into the Rust output: chained assignment, goto and the C ternary operator.
quote: Examples include using chained assignments (allowed in Python, C, and Java), attempting to use the goto keyword from C, or employing an unsupported operator "condition ? expr1 : expr2" in Rust.
bears_on: training-prior and lotml-syntax: prior leakage from familiar languages

claim: Repository context lowers Pass@1 by 16.2 to 30.8 points and DSR@1 by 26.3 to 38.4 points against function-level CodeTransOcean. One compiler-feedback round raised the best model from 51.5% to 62.1%.
quote: Our benchmark's repository-level context poses greater challenges for LLMs, reducing their Pass@1 and DSR@1 scores by 16.2% to 30.8% and 26.3% to 38.4%, respectively
bears_on: evaluation-harness: include multi-module tasks; value of a compile-feedback round

claim: Missing imports dominate C++ (56.6%) and C (35.5%) but not Java (8.1%) or Rust (20.5%). The authors credit Java's implicit java.lang and Rust's prelude, so a prelude removes a whole error class.
quote: For C and C++, "Missing import" is by far the most common classification, accounting for 56.6% of C++ compilation errors and 35.5% of C compilation errors.
bears_on: module system and prelude design

claim: After feedback, errors needing a non-local fix were fully fixed far less often than local ones such as missing imports (12.4% to 15.4%). Examples are undeclared variables (5.3%), incompatible parameter types (7.8%) and undeclared functions (7.9%).
quote: In contrast, "Undeclared variable" (5.3%), "Incompatible parameter types" (7.8%), and "Use undeclared function" (7.9%) are fixed completely far less often.
bears_on: semantic-compiler: diagnostics for non-local errors need related locations and suggested fixes

claim: Rust's debug-mode overflow checks turn arithmetic overflow into the largest Rust runtime-error class (about 44%). The same faults pass silently in C, C++ and Java.
quote: Finally, "Numeric-overflow" errors appear mostly in Rust (43.9%), with few instances in Java (5.6%), C (4.9%), and C++ (4.0%).
bears_on: type-system: one checked-overflow semantics in every build

claim: Rust fails to compile far more often than the other three languages: 23,416 of 52,669 compile failures.
quote: Across the two prompting techniques, a total of 52,669 samples failed to compile: 9,953 in C++, 6,996 in Java, 12,304 in C, and 23,416 in Rust
bears_on: cost of strict static checking for first-pass compile success

claim: The setting is single-file competitive programming with no IDE or tooling. Authors warn it may amplify some errors and miss multi-file dependencies, so the distribution may not carry over to agentic, repository-scale work.
quote: In this study, we evaluate LLMs in a competitive-programming setting without IDE assistance, compiler or runtime feedback beyond standard diagnostics, or human-in-the-loop intervention
bears_on: how far the 16.7% ownership share generalizes to lotml's agent setting

claim: Code-specific fine-tuning lowers how many errors a model makes but not which kinds, so error-class priorities hold across model variants.
quote: This suggests that code-specific fine-tuning primarily reduces the frequency of errors rather than altering their nature.
bears_on: training-prior: diagnostics priorities are stable across model variants

claim: In the GPT-3.5 prompt ablation, each feature of the changelog output format raised accuracy substantially. The features were line-number prefixes, echoing the original code and a fix description.
quote: It demonstrates that the addition of each new feature to the changelog format raises accuracy by a significant margin.
bears_on: fix format for LLM repair: anchored, verifiable patches

claim: Echoing the original lines makes a patch self-verifying: the tool rejects any changelog whose OriginalCode or line ranges do not match the file.
quote: This part is defensive because it is a repetition of the input; RustAssistant rejects the changelog if the OriginalCode segment fails to match the actual original code.
bears_on: semantic-compiler: patches anchored to content, rejected on mismatch

claim: Writing a free-text description of the fix before the code improved accuracy markedly (P3 to P4).
quote: It is interesting that the simple act of describing the fix (going from P3 to P4), helps the model accuracy significantly.
bears_on: fix/diagnostic format: a rationale field before the patch

claim: Grouping an error with the errors its fix introduces, and giving up on a group that stops progressing, mattered greatly. Without grouping, fixes cascaded into ever more errors.
quote: Without grouping, RustAssistant would fix errors in a random order, which increased the chances of it getting stuck with an error that it could not fix, leading to a ever-increasing blow-up of code changes and resulting errors.
bears_on: semantic-compiler: root cause first, cascade tracking, giving up cleanly

claim: rustc's related locations (notes) were what RustAssistant used to choose the code shown to the model. Diagnostics should carry secondary spans.
quote: The Rust compiler, for instance, not just points to the error location, but to related locations as well.
bears_on: diagnostic format: children/related spans

claim: The LLM sometimes ignored rustc's own suggested fix. It also loosened qualifiers (removing const) where developers tightened them, so machine-applicable suggestions are better applied by the tool than delegated to the model.
quote: This is an interesting case since the LLM chose to ignore the suggestion in the error message.
bears_on: semantic-compiler: apply MachineApplicable fixes without a model round (check --fix)

claim: On 346 Clippy lints, the LLM loop fixed 74.86%, against 31.50% for Clippy's pattern-based auto-fix. Rule-based auto-fix alone covers a minority of cases.
quote: RustAssistant is able to fix 2.4x more errors than Clippy ' s own auto-fix option, achieving a peak accuracy of nearly 75%.
bears_on: semantic-compiler: scope of check --fix versus model repair

claim: Self-Debugging allowed up to 10 debugging turns, and the successful debugging processes mostly ended within 3 turns.
quote: We set the maximum number of debugging turns to be 10, though empirically the successful debugging processes mostly end within 3 turns.

claim: On MBPP, Codex (code-davinci-002) without self-debugging scores 61.4%.
On MBPP, Codex with simple feedback (a correct/wrong verdict, decided by running the one visible unit test) scores 68.2%.
On MBPP, Codex with unit-test feedback plus a model-generated line-by-line trace scores 70.8%; the trace is written by the model, not produced by running the code.
Across tasks, models generally benefit from richer self-debugging feedback, especially when execution information is in the feedback.
quote: For all tasks, models generally benefit from richer feedback for SELFDEBUGGING, especially when the execution information is present in the feedback.

claim: On HumanEval, most models lose 60-80% of their per-attempt debugging effectiveness (relative to the first attempt) within 2-3 attempts.
quote: most models lose 60-80% of their debugging capability within just 2-3 attempts, despite iterative debugging being a critical capability for practical code generation systems

claim: Restarting from the original problem statement at a DDI-computed point, inside the same attempt budget, improved final HumanEval accuracy for most, not all, evaluated models.
quote: The results reveal that strategic fresh starts can significantly improve debugging performance across most models without requiring any additional computational resources.

claim: Compared with i.i.d. resampling at an equal sample budget, self-repair gains are often modest, vary between subsets of the data, and are sometimes absent.
quote: We find that when the cost of carrying out repair is taken into account, performance gains are often modest, vary a lot between subsets of the data, and are sometimes not present at all.

claim: The primary experiment ran 2,400 trials (ten complete runs) with qwen2.5-coder:14b driven by the aider agent.
quote: Our primary experiment comprises 2,400 trials across ten complete runs, using qwen2.5coder:14b via ollama and aider on dedicated GPU hardware.

claim: With test-suite feedback only (untyped mode), qwen2.5-coder:14b succeeded in 24.6% of trials on the min-no-loc chaff bin and 41.2% on the min-with-loc chaff bin.
With the minimal type error (min-no-loc on the first chaff bin, min-with-loc on the second), qwen2.5-coder:14b succeeded in 34.6% and 47.8% of trials.
With the full unification stack (all mode), qwen2.5-coder:14b succeeded in 40.7% and 63.4% of trials on the two chaff bins.
More detailed type-error messages generally improved the agent's fix rate, with a significant ordered trend for qwen2.5-coder:14b.
quote: We find concrete evidence that more detailed error messages generally improve an agent's ability to fix type errors.

claim: Of 872 typed-mode trials whose final submission type-checked, 854 (97.9%) also passed all semantic tests, on single-error programs.
quote: Across all typed modes and all 10 runs, there were 872 trials in which the agent's final submission was type-correct (i.e., the oracle's type-check step passed). Of those, 854 also passed all semantic tests-a rate of 97.9%.

claim: The authors suggest considering two error-reporting modes: a terse human mode and a detailed AI mode.
quote: Our results suggest it is worth considering offering two reporting modes: a terse human mode and a detailed AI mode.

claim: Detailed execution feedback does not always improve multi-turn code generation; the authors attribute this to reduced diversity of generated programs, which costs performance at large sample budgets.
quote: Interestingly, detailed execution feedback prompts do not always translate to improved performance (Section 5.2). We show that this can be attributed to reduced diversity of generated programs which results in performance drops for large sample budgets.

claim: Simple execution feedback (binary pass/fail or failed tests) gave the best performance for most models on competitive-programming benchmarks.
quote: This matches our experimental results: simple execution feedback (e.g., binary, failed tests) provides optimal performance for most models (Appendix D.2).

claim: Test feedback ranked first in the Python replication, but that ranking was not observed in the exploratory Java extension, where simple and JUnit test feedback did not differ significantly.
quote: while test feedback remains the strongest feedback type in our Python replication, the same ranking is not observed in our Java extension, as simple and JUnit-based test feedback do not differ significantly.

claim: The trace is a line-by-line execution trace written by the model itself, not one obtained by running the code; it carries no more information than the code explanation. It is not evidence for runtime traces or richer compiler output.
quote: Note that both the execution trace and the line-by-line explanation come from model generation instead of code execution, thus the trace feedback does not require more information than the pure code explanation feedback; i.e., no access to intermediate execution states.
wiki_says: MBPP with Codex reached 70.8 "with a trace", presented as richer feedback.

claim: The ordering is not monotonic across models and tasks: on TransCoder, Codex scores 87.9 with +Trace against 91.6 with unit-test feedback alone, and GPT-4 on MBPP scores 80.6 (UT), 80.4 (+Expl.), 80.2 (+Trace). On Codex MBPP, the bare correct/wrong verdict gives +6.8 points; unit-test content and the trace add only +2.6 more.
wiki_says: Richer feedback yielded more (MBPP with Codex: 61.4 baseline, 68.2 simple, 70.8 trace).

claim: Fresh starts improved final accuracy for most models, but not uniformly: in Table 2, codestral:22b (89.02 to 88.41) and devstral:24b (94.51 to 93.90) got worse at the 50% threshold, and the gain depends on the threshold chosen. The text also says six models were evaluated while Table 2 lists nine. Single benchmark (HumanEval), fixed six-attempt budget.
quote: Additionally, while our fresh start interventions demonstrate performance improvements across almost all evaluated models, the magnitude of these improvements critically depends on the selected effectiveness threshold θ.
wiki_says: Starting over recovers the lost debugging capability.

claim: The 'capability' is the normalised per-attempt effectiveness (new problems solved at each attempt relative to the first), not accuracy, and the decay constants come from HumanEval only; the authors say lambda and t_theta are dataset-specific and need calibration.
quote: Due to computational constraints, our current validation focuses on HumanEval variants, though the underlying exponential decay phenomenon has been observed across broader programming contexts including other benchmark datasets
wiki_says: "Most models lose 60-80% of their debugging capability within just 2-3 attempts", stated without scope.

claim: The study measures a single repair step (initial programs, then feedback, then repairs) and how to split a sample budget between initial samples and repairs; it does not measure the number of rounds. Its central finding, that feedback quality is the bottleneck, is not reported by the wiki.
quote: We call the tree of interleaved text and programs produced by this procedure-rooted in the specification ψ, then branching into initial programs pi, each of which branches into feedback fij and then repairs rijk-a repair tree, T (Figure 2).
wiki_says: Olausson et al. is cited under "The repair loop saturates in two or three rounds".

claim: Each pair is not a range but two disjoint chaff bins (28 min-no-loc chaffs, 32 min-with-loc chaffs), for one model, qwen2.5-coder:14b. The wiki omits the proximate mode (32.9/60.9), which is below min in the first bin and close to all in the second.
quote: Each cell shows a/b, where a is the percentage (%) of that mode's trials on the 28 min-no-loc chaffs and b is the percentage on the 32 min-with-loc chaffs.
wiki_says: Repair at 24.6-41.2% with tests only, 34.6-47.8% with the minimal type error, 40.7-63.4% with the full unification stack.

claim: Because of a bug, the 'min' mode printed either no location or one location depending on the chaff, so the two numbers come from two different modes (min-no-loc, min-with-loc), and the second already includes a location.
quote: Our goal was to have this mode report only the type error with no error locations, but due to a bug that we discovered while re-checking our data analysis, this mode prints zero error locations
wiki_says: 34.6-47.8% "with the minimal type error".

claim: The trend comes from one 14B open model on ten small programs with single-error chaffs. With claude-haiku-4.5 every mode succeeded in 87.9-99.7% of trials and the min-no-loc trend was not significant; the authors state the results cannot be generalised.
quote: We have used only one language, small programs, a single model, single-error chaffs, ten runs, and so on. The results can in no way be considered generalizable.
wiki_says: Detailed diagnostics help (the ablation numbers are given without naming the model).

claim: Per-chaff results show striking inversions (e.g. avl-tree-1, avl-tree-3, poly-arith-1, leftist-heap-4, huffman-6, dijkstra-2) where more verbose messages did worse.
quote: This statistical trend, however, masks real variation under the hood. The variation shows that we cannot uniformly assume that one mode of reporting will always be better than the other.
wiki_says: The averaged trend is reported as if it held per error.

claim: The authors warn the figure reflects chaff design: each program had exactly one injected type error, so undoing it restores the original program.
quote: The 97.9% figure may say more about our chaff design than about any fundamental property of typed languages in general.
wiki_says: 97.9% of the repairs that passed the type check also passed the tests (no caveat).

claim: Zheng et al. vary runtime execution feedback (binary, failed tests, failed and passed tests, LDB debugger traces) on competitive-programming problems with Llama 3.x and GPT-4o, not compiler diagnostics; the differences between feedback types are small, and the authors attribute failures to not understanding the algorithm rather than to bugs.
quote: We posit that for challenging problems presented in the competitive programming benchmark, models generate wrong code not because the code is buggy by accident but because models do not understand how to solve the problem correctly.
wiki_says: Detailed feedback does not always help, cited as a caveat on detailed compiler diagnostics.

claim: The authors explicitly do not attribute the difference to language: the Java extension uses LLM-generated mutations, a different model (GPT-4o-mini vs GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet), JUnit instead of pytest, and 100 instances; no pairwise difference among logical-mutation feedback types is significant. The defensible statement is that the Python ranking was not reproduced in a confounded Java setting.
quote: Our Java exploratory extension should not be interpreted as a direct Java-Python comparison.
wiki_says: The ranking of feedback types varies by language.

claim: On Spider, one debugging turn captured almost all of the gain: accuracy improved by at most 0.1% after the first turn.
quote: Note that typically one debugging turn is sufficient, and the accuracy improvement after one turn is within 0.1%.
bears_on: how many repair rounds a compiler loop should budget

claim: On TransCoder the major improvement also came from the first debugging turn, about 12 points over greedy decoding.

claim: On the full SWE-bench test set (2,294 instances), 1,185 (51.7%) of SWE-agent with GPT-4 Turbo trajectories contain at least one failed edit, where a failed edit is an edit command rejected because it raised a linting error.

quote: E111, E112, E113 are indentation errors. E999 denotes a syntax error and an E902 occurs if flake8 cannot read the source file.

quote: Details such as including the correct indentation level, inserting delimiters at specific points in a line, and adhering to stylistic preferences of the codebase all require some amount of planning or calculation.
bears_on: edit-format design for the harness (search-and-replace vs line-range vs diff) and indentation sensitivity

claim: The lint guard has a cost: it rejects intermediate states. To remove a function parameter, the agent must change the header and every use in one edit, or remove the uses first. Otherwise the header-only edit trips an undefined-name check and is reverted. The authors frame adding a guardrail as a trade-off between the errors it prevents and the workflows it blocks.
quote: The editing guardrail has a drawback. To a certain degree, it forces some edits to be done in a particular order.
bears_on: what `check` on every edit should reject (syntax only) versus report (semantic errors); atomic refactorings in the compiler

claim: The guard assumes the original file was clean, so any lint output is attributed to the edit. A compiler-backed check-on-edit for lotml would need the same 'introduced by this edit' baseline, i.e. diagnostics diffed against the pre-edit state, to avoid blocking edits in files that already have errors.
quote: A fair and verified assumption we make when considering this feature is that the original codebase associated with each task instance is well-formed.
bears_on: agent-computer interface of `check --json`: report new versus pre-existing diagnostics

claim: Recovery degrades with repetition. Successful recoveries take about 2.2 consecutive failed attempts; unsuccessful ones average 5.59. Across all instances there are 810 successful recoveries against 555 unsuccessful. Once an agent is stuck on an edit error, more rounds rarely help, which argues for diagnostics that fix the error in the first round.
quote: with 810 successful recoveries versus 555 unsuccessful ones. While the number of consecutive failed edit attempts resulting in a recovery remains steady (2.2), it increases significantly for unsuccessful recoveries (5.59).
bears_on: diagnostic quality and applicable fixes (`check --fix`); value of one-round repair

claim: The 3-point lint ablation is close to run-to-run noise. Six runs of the default configuration on SWE-bench Lite ranged from 17.33% to 18.67% (mean 17.94), and the ablations themselves are single runs.
bears_on: how much weight the 18.0 vs 15.0 result can carry; sample sizes for the lotml harness

claim: Silent success confuses agents. SWE-agent prints an explicit 'ran successfully and did not produce any output' message, and after an accepted edit it shows the updated region instead of nothing. An ACI for a compiler should report an explicit 'no errors' result rather than empty output.
quote: however, if no output is generated, a specific message ("Your command ran successfully and did not produce any output") is included to enhance clarity.
bears_on: what `check` returns on success; agent-computer interface for the compiler

claim: Going directly from file-level localization to edit locations, skipping the skeleton step, was both less accurate and costlier than the hierarchical default (Table 2). Agentless attributes this to the model becoming confused by large context.
quote: We first observe that by directly going from file-level to the edit locations, both the cost and performance are worse. The reason is that the model can become confused when providing a large context
bears_on: digest as an index before bodies; context an agent needs

claim: Agentless edits with a Search/Replace format rather than regenerating code, claiming small edits are cheaper and more reliable; this claim is asserted, not measured in the paper. Search/Replace requires the search block to match the file exactly, whitespace included, which is where indentation-sensitive syntax can bite.
quote: This simple diff format avoids generating the complete code and instead focuses on producing small edits, which are not only more cost-efficient, but also more reliable and accurate (less chances for hallucination).
bears_on: editing test with search-and-replace edits on the indented vs braces variant

claim: To compare candidate patches, Agentless parses old and new code into ASTs and unparses them into a canonical source format with docstrings removed. Surface differences such as spaces, newlines and comments then vanish before majority voting, effectively a canonical formatter used as an equivalence check.
quote: More specifically, to standardize the patch, we begin by parsing both the old and new code (after applying the patch) into abstract syntax trees. Next, we unparse the trees into a canonical source code format with docstrings removed.
bears_on: canonical formatter; one canonical form per program

claim: Patch selection, not generation, is the bottleneck: 126 issues (42.0%) were solved by at least one sampled patch, well above what the selected patch achieved.
quote: if we consider all patch samples (instead of only selecting one patch) for each issue, the total number of possible issues that AGENTLESS can solve is 126 (42.0%).
bears_on: value of execution and test feedback alongside compile feedback

claim: Execution feedback carries the selection. Majority voting alone gave 77 fixes and adding regression tests gave 81. The largest gain came from adding LLM-generated reproduction tests.
quote: We see that by only using majority voting, we can already achieve 77 correct fixes. By adding the existing regression tests, and filter for candidate patches with the lowest amount of regression errors, we can improve performance to 81 issues resolved.
bears_on: value of execution and test feedback alongside compile feedback

claim: Agentless is matched by closed-source agents when the issue gives a location clue, but loses when none is given. There, agents with code-search tools do better, which argues that a skeleton or digest alone does not replace search for issues without anchors.
quote: However, the closed-source agent tools perform better compared to AGENTLESS in the case where no location clue is provided. This highlights an advantage of agent-based tools in solving these more complex problems where they are able to use complex code search tools.
bears_on: digest versus semantic and textual queries (LSP/MCP)

claim: Error-correction rounds alone barely help code built on hallucinated types and functions. Combined with retrieved types they multiply performance by 4, and with types plus headers by 1.5. Compiler feedback and static context are complements, not substitutes.
quote: But given the scaffolding effect of relevant static information, they act multiplicatively, increasing performance by a factor of 4 for types without headers, and a factor of 1.5 for both types and headers.
bears_on: repair loop design; what context accompanies diagnostics

claim: Error rounds matter more in the low-resource language: the with-versus-without-error-rounds ratio was about 2 in Hazel and about 1.2 in TypeScript. lotml, a new language, sits on the Hazel side for syntax errors that do not transfer from Python.
quote: In Hazel, the ratio of tests passing with-versus-without error rounds was about 2, whereas for TypeScript it is about 1.2.
bears_on: value of rich diagnostics for a low-resource language

claim: A diagnostic that only partly described a Hazel parse error was still enough for GPT-4 to fix it: knowing a syntax error existed sufficed. This is weak evidence that, for syntax errors, error location and presence matter more than message detail.
quote: One phenomenon of note was that sometimes even poor error messages proved effective; the error in Figure 11 is an at-most partially accurate characterization of the syntax error, but knowing there was a syntax error proved sufficient for the model to correct it
bears_on: rich versus terse diagnostics (open question in semantic-compiler)

claim: Two correction rounds usually sufficed to eliminate static errors, and further rounds showed diminishing returns, so the authors capped the loop at 2.
quote: However, we have noticed that 2 rounds are often sufficient to eliminate static errors, and that rounds in excess of 2 tend to show diminishing returns, so we have capped the maximum number of rounds at 2.
bears_on: repair-loop round limit

claim: The authors recommend that a language server report the full list of static errors rather than only the first one encountered.
quote: Ideally, it would produce a list of errors, rather than just the first error encountered, as is supported by Hazel's total type error localization and recovery system [87].
bears_on: `check --json` returns every diagnostic

claim: Digest format matters. Writing bodiless headers with an ellipsis made models, especially StarCoder2, emit '...' instead of code; the authors switched to omitting the body entirely.
quote: Interestingly, we originally used ellipsis (...) in place of the body, but this resulted in an increased chance the model (especially the smaller StarCoder2 model) would itself emit the token ... in lieu of a full completion.
bears_on: digest format: how to elide bodies

claim: LLMs writing a low-resource ML-family language borrowed syntax and library functions from the nearby high-resource languages (OCaml, Elm). The authors countered with a 'crash course' prompt listing differences from those languages and few-shot examples. This is the same prior-leakage pattern lotml expects from Python.
quote: We have found that when asked to write Hazel code, contemporary LLMs fail to follow Hazel's syntax and semantics, often borrowing syntactic forms and library functions from OCaml and Elm.
bears_on: semantic Python leakage; a negative-characterization tutorial in the compiler (ChatLSP aiTutorial)

claim: Retrieved headers can hurt. For StarCoder2-15B, two programs (BO and TO) degraded after headers were added, because completions used type-appropriate but irrelevant headers. Smaller models appear more sensitive to irrelevant context.
quote: However, two examples, BO and TO, experienced degraded performance after the inclusion of headers. After close examination of the headers and the output programs, we discovered that the completions tending to use type-appropriate but in-fact irrelevant retrieved headers.
bears_on: digest scope; relevance filtering of context

claim: Under BasePrompt the medium context (signature plus docstring, no body) made many models emit empty functions; over 31% of StarCoder2's outputs were empty. Bodiless dependency stubs looked exactly like the target the model had to complete.
quote: Particularly, Starcoder-2 is heavily impacted by this issue, as over 31% of its generated results are empty functions, revealing a significant weakness of the model.
bears_on: digest format: bodiless entries must not look like stubs to fill

claim: Three rounds of test-error feedback raised pass@1 by over 10 points for GPT-3.5 and over 7 for WizardCoder, but not at all for CodeLlama-13b-Python. The benefit of feedback rounds depends on the model.
quote: We observe that GPT-3.5 and WizardCoder demonstrate a high capacity for debugging with improvement of over 10% and 7% in pass@1, respectively, while CodeLlama fails to take advantage of this process.
bears_on: repair loop: compile errors versus test failures

claim: In WizardCoder's debugging rounds, SyntaxError and AttributeError were fixed in the first round; the remaining errors were mostly assertion failures, i.e. wrong behaviour rather than ill-formed code.
quote: Furthermore, fundamental issues like SyntaxError or AttributeError were promptly rectified during the initial round.
bears_on: repair loop: compile errors versus test failures

claim: Pretrained models often pass tests while re-implementing dependencies already in context, a technical-debt pattern pass@k does not see. RepoExec adds the Dependency Invocation Rate to measure it.
quote: Pretrained LLMs generate functionally correct code but often fail to effectively utilize the provided dependencies, occasionally reimplementing dependencies already present in the given context.
bears_on: harness metrics beyond pass@k; whether the digest leads agents to reuse existing functions

claim: RepoExec provides only one level of dependency (direct callees), so its context comparison says nothing about transitive context.
quote: In this work, we currently consider one level of dependency context, specifically the dependencies directly called from the target function.
bears_on: how far the digest must reach (direct vs transitive dependencies)
