claim: After instruction tuning on dependency-annotated data, small (signature-only) context matched full context, suggesting the signature-only gap is partly learnable rather than inherent.
quote: Notably, performance improves significantly with small context, matching results from full context, enabling more efficient processing and reducing computational costs.
bears_on: digest sufficiency; bodies on demand

claim: Location-only results are the costly part of LSP references. Adding ±2 source lines to each reference raised rename pass@1 from 0.67 to 0.83, cut tokens by 19%, and cut file reads per episode from 15.2 to 3.2.
quote: It helps substantially and via the predicted mechanism: vs. B, pass@1 0.67→0.83, site-recall 0.930→0.958, tokens -19%, and file-reads/episode 15.2 → 3.2 (below grep's 4.3) - the location-only arm wastes its turns reading each file back to see the call site.
bears_on: what a compiler query returns: include the source line inline with every location

claim: A cold index silently returns incomplete references. pyright's find-references at a definition returned only the definition until the referencing files were opened. Warming has a real time cost, so a warmed or pre-built index is a prerequisite.
quote: pyright resolves references lazily per file, so a cold find references issued at a definition - the natural query for a rename - returns only the definition (1 result) until the referencing files are opened
bears_on: incremental compiler index for MCP/LSP queries; never return partial references silently

claim: Whether semantic references beat grep depends on how ambiguous the identifier is, not on the language. Within one repository the LSP's F1 benefit rises as grep precision falls: zero for a unique name (precision 1.00) and +0.550 for a heavily colliding one (precision 0.07).
quote: As grep's precision falls, the LSP's benefit rises, nearly monotonically - same repo, same language, same model. decodeBase64 (grep precision 1.00) gets zero benefit; parseAccept (grep precision 0.07, essentially drowned in false positives) gets +0.550.
bears_on: semantic vs textual queries; naming conventions in lotml

claim: Agents seldom use semantic tools on their own: 0-6% on localization, but 45-57% on reference-shaped tasks. Forcing semantic-first on localization lowered success. Exposing a tool is not enough; it has to fit the task class.
quote: it defaults to grep on localization (semantic-tool use 0-6%) but reaches for the LSP about half the time on reference tasks (45-57%), unprompted.
bears_on: MCP/LSP tool surface; whether agents will call compiler queries

claim: On reference-completeness the LSP raised precision to 1.00 (grep 0.76) at a ∼19% token premium, but recall did not improve in any arm. The missed call sites were due to agent thoroughness, which better retrieval did not fix.
quote: on reference-completeness the LSP buys precision (1.00 vs 0.76, zero false call sites) but not token savings (a ∼19% premium) and cannot raise the recall ceiling set by agent thoroughness
bears_on: value of a `references` query; atomic rename in the compiler instead of agent-driven multi-site edits

claim: Backend completeness varies widely: pylsp (jedi) found about a third of the cross-file references pyright found (5 of 15 vs 14 for one function). A semantic query is only as good as the analyzer behind it.
quote: pylsp (jedi) returns only ∼ 13 of cross-file references on dynamic Python (5 of 15 for to native string vs. pyright's 14)
bears_on: compiler-backed (complete) references versus heuristic analyzers

claim: On single-file bug-fix edits with real tests, grep-only was best (pass@1 0.83), against 0.58 with free LSP access and 0.75 with forced LSP. LSP tools gave no edit-correctness benefit there.
quote: Grep-only leads (pass@1 0.83); adding (C, 0.58) or forcing (D, 0.75) the LSP does not help, and the LSP again carries a token premium.
bears_on: whether to prioritize LSP/MCP (R16, v2) over check-on-edit

claim: Outlines is an open-source Python library that guides generation with regular expressions and context-free grammars by precomputing an index from finite-state-machine states to vocabulary tokens.
quote: This framework leads to an efficient approach to guiding text generation with regular expressions and context-free grammars by allowing the construction of an index over a language model's vocabulary.

claim: The paper's method is implemented in the open-source Python library Outlines and claims little overhead per generated token.
quote: It adds little overhead to the token sequence generation process and significantly outperforms existing solutions. An implementation is provided in the open source Python library Outlines [Louf and Willard].

claim: XGrammar was published at the 8th MLSys Conference, 2025.
quote: Proceedings of the 8 th MLSys Conference, Santa Clara, CA, USA, 2025. Copyright 2025 by the author(s).

claim: Combined with an inference engine that overlaps CPU mask generation with GPU decoding, XGrammar reports near-zero end-to-end overhead for structured generation.
quote: Combined with an LLM inference engine, it can generate near-zero overhead structure generation in end-to-end low-LLM serving.

claim: On MLC-LLM with Llama-3.1 8B, enabling XGrammar left time per output token almost unchanged on the JSON Schema and JSON-grammar tasks (Table 2).
quote: Additionally, we examine the overhead of XGrammar's constrained decoding in end-to-end scenarios by measuring performance on the MLC-LLM engine with and without XGrammar. As shown in Table 2, enabling XGrammar enhances output quality with nearly zero overhead in TPOT.

claim: XGrammar is open source and integrated into major open-source LLM serving frameworks.
quote: We are open-sourcing XGrammar and integrating it into major open-source LLM frameworks.

claim: SynCode reduced the number of syntax errors in generated Python and Go code by 96.07% on average relative to unconstrained generation (CodeGen-350M, WizardCoder-1B and LLaMA-7B on HumanEval and MBXP).
quote: Furthermore, SynCode reduces the number of syntax errors in generated Python and Go code by 96.07% on average compared to standard generation.

claim: The syntax errors SynCode left in Python and Go were all programs cut off by the maximum token limit, not grammar violations.
quote: All of the errors were because the LLM failed to generate a complete program within the maximum token limit.

claim: SynCode handles Python's indentation outside the context-free grammar, with a mechanism that tracks the acceptable indentation for the next token and masks tokens that violate it.
quote: To support languages with indentation, such as Python and YAML, SynCode has a mechanism that tracks acceptable indentation for the next token, effectively masking tokens that violate indentation constraints at a given point.

claim: SynCode's Python grammar (from the Lark repository) declares _INDENT and _DEDENT with %declare, so the indentation tokens are synthesized outside the grammar rules.
quote: %import common.WS_INLINE 165 166 %declare _INDENT _DEDENT 167 %ignore WS_INLINE

claim: Grammar-constrained decoding, and constrained decoding in general, can distort the LLM's distribution: outputs are grammatical but their likelihoods are not proportional to the model's.
quote: In this paper we demonstrate that GCD techniques (and in general constrained decoding techniques) can distort the LLM's distribution, leading to outputs that are grammatical but appear with likelihoods that are not proportional to the ones given by the LLM, and so ultimately are low-quality.

claim: The paper names the problem grammar-aligned decoding (GAD) and proposes ASAp, which converges to the grammar-conditioned LLM distribution as more samples are drawn.
quote: By updating this bound when more samples are observed, the decoding algorithm converges to the desired probability distribution-i.e., it samples outputs from the LLM-induced probability conditioned on the outputs being accepted by the grammar.

claim: Grammar-Aligned Decoding was peer-reviewed at NeurIPS.
quote: The authors would like to thank NeurIPS anonymous reviewers for their insightful feedback and helpful discussions.

claim: Monitor-Guided Decoding appeared at NeurIPS 2023.
quote: To appear in 37th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2023) as

claim: MGD runs a monitor that queries static analysis (a language server over LSP) at trigger points during decoding and turns its suggestions into token masks.
quote: A monitor observes the code generated by an LM and queries static analysis at pre-defined trigger points. The suggestions returned by the static analysis are converted to masks which are used for reshaping the logits

claim: On Java method completion (DotPrompts, score@6), MGD raised the compilation rate by 21.77-24.69% relative for the four open models and by 18.52% relative for text-davinci-003.
quote: All the models with MGD outperform their respective base models on Compilation Rate, by a relative improvement ranging between 21.77%- 24.69%. TD-3-MGD outperforms TD-3 by a relative margin of 18.52%.

claim: Near-zero end-to-end overhead was measured only on JSON Schema and an unconstrained-JSON grammar (MLC-LLM with Llama-3.1 8B; in-browser WebLLM on JSON-mode-eval). The only programming-language grammar, a Python DSL, ignores indentation and was measured only at mask level, where its per-token latency is several times JSON's (see findings). Nothing in the paper measures an indentation-sensitive or full programming-language grammar end to end.
quote: The Python DSL covers basic control flow (if, for, while) and data types (str, int, float, bool) but ignores indentation.
wiki_says: XGrammar is listed among engines for constraining lotml code with an unqualified "near-zero overhead".

claim: It is an average reduction (not removal) over three small 2023-era models (350M-7B) on HumanEval/MBXP, using a hand-trimmed subset of each grammar that leaves out features such as Python lambdas. Computed from Table 3, the per-cell reductions average about 95.7% and the pooled reduction is about 96.1%, so 96.07% cannot be reproduced exactly from the table. The leftover errors are truncated programs, not violations of the grammar.
quote: The grammar has commonly used features of the language such as control flow, and loops, and excludes some features such as Python's support for lambda functions.
wiki_says: SynCode "removes 96.07% of syntax errors in Python and Go".

claim: SynCode treats indentation as a non-context-free fragment handled by a decoding-time indentation tracker that masks tokens, not as lexer machinery. It reports no cost for it. Go, a brace-delimited language, also needed non-CFG handling (optional semicolons inserted at line ends). The paper's evidence against indentation is residual indentation errors (Table 7), not cost.
quote: SynCode can handle non-context-free fragments of PLs, such as indentation in Python and end-of-scope markers in Go.
wiki_says: "SynCode needed extra lexer machinery for Python", under the heading that significant indentation makes the constrainer more expensive.

claim: GAD is the name of the problem. The algorithm, ASAp, removes the bias only asymptotically, over repeated samples of the same prompt (2,000 per benchmark). The authors call slow convergence its key limitation: on some benchmarks KL divergence barely improves, and ASAp has no strong effect on solving downstream tasks.
quote: The key limitation of our work is the current slow convergence of the ASAp algorithm. In some benchmarks, even after 2,000 iterations the KL divergence barely improves
wiki_says: Grammar-Aligned Decoding "corrects" the distortion.

claim: The gains are relative, not percentage points (e.g. CodeGen-350M 52.43 to 65.37), at score@6, on Java only. With a standard prompt they are 21.77-24.69% for the open models and 18.52% for text-davinci-003. Combined with prompt augmentation or fill-in-the-middle they shrink to 13.18-17.70%, so 19-25% understates the spread.
wiki_says: MGD "raised the compilation rate by 19-25%".

claim: Outlines' CFG support extends the FSM index to LALR(1) parsers. The paper only sketches this extension and evaluates no grammar-constrained generation; its one benchmark is regex timing against Guidance.
quote: More importantly, our indexing approach can also be extended to CFGs and LALR(1) parsers to allow for efficient guided generation according to popular data formats and programming languages (e.g. JSON, Python, SQL, etc.).
bears_on: grammar class for the published lotml grammar (LALR(1) compatibility)

claim: The only performance evidence is a single timing sample per max_tokens value against Guidance on one regex. There is no accuracy or validity evaluation at all.
quote: The value of max\_tokens is varied and the timings are recorded with timeit for a single loop and single repeat value (i.e. only one sample is collected for each value of max\_tokens).
bears_on: strength of evidence behind listing Outlines as an engine for lotml

claim: For a slightly augmented Python grammar, a naively built Outlines index (unreduced DFAs) was about 50 MB.
quote: In our tests using a slightly augmented version of the Python grammar, we find that even naively constructed indices (i.e. ones containing unused and redundant parser and FSM state configurations) are still only around 50 MB.
bears_on: memory cost of constraining with a full programming-language grammar

claim: For parser-guided generation, REDUCE operations make the index depend on parser stack configurations, so it needs a trie over stack values. The CFG case is harder than the regex case for the same reason XGrammar later calls context-dependent tokens.
quote: Ultimately, each parser configuration that permits a complete parse of a vocabulary string is added as an entry in the index for the PDA, and, in this case, the index will need to be a trie data structure in order to allow queries against the parser's stack values.
bears_on: what grammar properties make constraining slow

claim: Per-token mask latency grows with grammar complexity: under 40 us for JSON but under 200 us for XML and the (indentation-free) Python DSL.
quote: XGrammar consistently achieves the lowest latency across all tasks, with under 40 µs per token for JSON Schema and CFG (JSON), and under 200 µs for XML and Python DSL.
bears_on: per-token overhead of a programming-language grammar

claim: The runtime cost sits in context-dependent tokens, those that finish a rule and need the full stack to validate. They were under 1% of the vocabulary for JSON, which is why the mask cache works. Grammars where rule ends admit many continuations push more tokens into this slow path.
quote: Experiments show that context-dependent tokens account for only a minor proportion, amounting to less than 1% (1134 out of 128k) for the Llama-3.1 model using JSON grammar.
bears_on: what grammar properties make constraining slow

claim: Grammar ambiguity (non-determinism, epsilon edges) multiplies parallel stacks, and each stack must check its context-dependent tokens and merge masks. Deterministic grammars are cheaper to constrain.
quote: The increase in the number of stacks increases the computation as we need to check the context-dependent tokens for each stack and merge the token masks.
bears_on: lotml grammar should be deterministic/unambiguous

claim: Near-zero overhead holds only while CPU mask generation is faster than the GPU forward pass. vLLM's grammar backend degraded noticeably at larger batch sizes.
quote: In practice, the time for mask generation is less than the time for LLM inference, so the mask generation process will not become the bottleneck of the generation process.
bears_on: conditions under which constraining is free

claim: XGrammar's quality evaluation measures only syntactic correctness of function-call JSON and XML, not task or functional accuracy.
quote: We measure the syntactic correctness of the generated function calling outputs and XML code using LLaMA-3.1 8B.
bears_on: whether constraining changes functional accuracy

claim: Per XGrammar, Outlines' grammar mode considers only the most recent lexer token, so it can misjudge LLM tokens that span several lexer tokens. SynCode avoids this but pays heavy offline preprocessing.
quote: but it only considers the most recent lexer token, which may lead to incorrect judgments when LLM tokens span across multiple lexer tokens (Appendix A in (Koo et al., 2024)).
bears_on: engine choice and correctness for lotml

claim: SynCode requires an unambiguous LALR(1) or LR(1) grammar.
quote: The grammar needs to be unambiguous LALR(1) or LR(1) grammar for using the respective base parsers.
bears_on: grammar class for the published lotml grammar

claim: SynCode's soundness and efficiency assume a lexer with 1-character lookahead and no backtracking, so earlier lexical tokens never change type.
quote: We assume lexical analysis with a 1-character lookahead and no backtracking. This assumption is crucial for the efficiency of SynCode algorithm.
bears_on: lotml lexical design (tokens decidable with 1-char lookahead)

claim: Even brace-delimited Go needed a programmatic non-CFG rule for optional, automatically inserted semicolons. Explicit delimiters help only if terminators are also mandatory.
quote: For instance, in Go, semicolons are optional and may be automatically inserted at the end of non-blank lines.
bears_on: explicit delimiters vs indentation; avoid automatic semicolon insertion

claim: In few-shot Python (Table 7), SynCode eliminated or nearly eliminated syntax errors but left indentation errors behind (LLaMA-7B: 40 to 5, an 88% cut). The indentation tracker is less complete than the CFG constraint.
quote: | Llama-7B       | Indentation  |         40 |         5 | 88%  |
bears_on: cost and reliability of constraining an indentation-based syntax

claim: Without constraints, only 6% of Python and 25% of Go samples had syntax errors. The authors attribute Go's higher rate to less training data and argue constraints help most for under-represented languages, which is lotml's case.
quote: On average, of all standard generated samples, 6% and 25% have syntax errors for Python and Go, respectively.
bears_on: syntax is the smallest share of errors; value of a published grammar for a new language

claim: Grammar constraining gave only a slight improvement in functional correctness on HumanEval (pass@1 and pass@10, Python and Go), never a large one.
quote: We observe that augmenting LLMs with SynCode has a slight improvement in functional correctness over standard generation.
bears_on: whether constraining changes functional accuracy

claim: Offline mask-store cost scales with the number of grammar terminals and the vocabulary. For the Python and Go grammars (94 and 87 terminals) it took several minutes and up to about 2 GB per model.
quote: We see that generating the store requires less than 2GB of memory and several minutes across the evaluated models and grammars.
bears_on: grammar size (terminal count) and constraining cost

claim: SynCode's Lark EBNF supports ignore terminals: comments and whitespace are allowed anywhere in Python at the cost of one trivial accept sequence each. This matches the 'free comments anywhere' requirement.
quote: Our EBNF syntax adopted from Lark allows one to provide ignore terminals as part of the grammar. Lark ignores those terminals while parsing. In the case of Python, this includes comments and whitespaces.
bears_on: free comments in the constrained output; Lark dialect

claim: SynCode's published Python grammar also uses Lark terminal priorities (HEX_NUMBER.2 etc.). Together with %declare _INDENT _DEDENT, these are features OpenAI's Lark subset rejects, so the grammar is not portable to OpenAI as-is.
quote: DEC_NUMBER: /0|[1-9]\d*/i 159 HEX_NUMBER.2: /0x[\da-f]*/i 160 OCT_NUMBER.2: /0o[0-7]*/i
bears_on: grammar dialects (llguidance Lark subset vs full Lark)

claim: In the toy example, prompted for binary strings ending in 1, GCD produced them only 30% of the time. An early token that the grammar allows can trap sampling in a region whose only completions are unlikely.
quote: However, we observe that GCD [8] generates strings ending with a 1 only 30% of the time-i.e., GCD has effectively ruined the LLM's ability to follow the prompt by biasing sampling towards 00000, an incorrect output.
bears_on: what grammar properties make constraining lossy

claim: Correcting the distortion did not reliably improve correctness: ASAp yielded correct samples 38% more often than GCD on INV-BV but 73% less often on solvable SLIA benchmarks (geomean).
quote: ASAp produces correct samples 38% more often than GCD (geomean), whereas for SLIA benchmarks that both tools can solve, ASAp produces correct samples 73% less often than GCD (geomean).
bears_on: whether constraining (and de-biasing it) changes functional accuracy

claim: The evaluation is small: 15 SLIA, 15 INV-BV and 6 constituency-parsing problems on Mistral-7B, each sampled 2,000 times.
quote: we randomly select 15 SLIA problems, 15 INV-BV problems, and 6 CP problems.
bears_on: practicality of distribution-aligned decoding for lotml

claim: MGD cost a mean 83.16% decoding-time slowdown on CodeGen-6B. The authors note their implementation is unoptimized.
quote: We observe a mean slowdown of 83.16% in decoding time for CodeGen-6B with MGD.
bears_on: per-token cost of type-aware constraining

claim: Prefix static analysis in IDEs is heuristic, both imprecise and incomplete, so a monitor can block valid code or allow invalid code.
quote: Though these heuristics are well-engineered and are widely used, they can be both imprecise (they can give incorrect suggestions) and incomplete (they can leave out correct suggestions).
bears_on: a type system checkable exactly on prefixes; the 'valid continuations at the cursor' API

claim: The main monitor fires only at an object dereference ('obj.') and restricts the following identifier to the members of the inferred type. It is targeted type guidance, not whole-program type constraining.
quote: This is the pre-condition pre we use. We employ a static analysis Aφ which returns all the type-consistent identifiers that can be referenced through obj.
bears_on: scope of the compiler's 'expected type at the cursor' API

claim: With MGD a 1.1B model beat text-davinci-003 on compilation rate and next-identifier match. Semantic constraints can substitute for model scale.
quote: With MGD, SantaCoder-1.1B achieves better compilation rate and next-identifier match than the much larger text-davinci-003 model.
bears_on: value of type constraints over syntax constraints

claim: Identifier accuracy falls sharply as identifiers span more subtokens, and MGD recovers much of it. Long or rare names are a decoding hazard.
quote: We show that the ability of LMs to accurately predict the identifier name decreases sharply with an increase in identifier complexity, while augmenting them with MGD improves their performance.
bears_on: lotml naming and tokenization

claim: MGD's library includes an approximate mode for black-box models with limited logit masking, a possible route on hosted APIs that accept no grammar.
quote: It also supports an approximate mechanism for MGD of black-box LMs with limited logit-masking support.
bears_on: constraining lotml on Claude/Gemini, which accept no grammar

claim: MGD measures compilation and agreement with ground truth, not functional correctness. The authors put pre/post-conditions out of scope and say testing is still needed.
quote: Satisfying functional-correctness specifications like pre/post-conditions and invariants is beyond the scope of this work.
bears_on: whether constraining changes functional accuracy

claim: In Let Me Speak Freely?, Claude 3 Haiku scored 86.51 on GSM8K answering in plain text, and 86.99 when simply asked to answer in JSON with no schema in the prompt (Table 1).

The 23.44 GSM8K score for Claude 3 Haiku is the 'JSON + schema constraint' cell of Table 1, a format-restricting instruction that writes a schema into the prompt, with a standard deviation of 22.9 across nine prompt variants.
Removing the schema from the prompt (asking only for JSON, XML or YAML) raised average GSM8K scores and lowered prompt sensitivity for Claude 3 Haiku, GPT-3.5 Turbo and LLaMA 3 8B Instruct.
quote: Table 1 illustrates the effects of removing the schema restriction on the GSM8K dataset. We observe significant improvements in average scores and lower standard deviations across different prompt perturbations for Claude 3 Haiku, GPT-3.5 Turbo, and LLaMA 3 8B Instruct.

claim: The answer-before-reasoning key order the paper reports concerns GPT-3.5 Turbo in JSON mode on the Last Letter task, where 100% of responses put the answer key first, turning chain-of-thought into direct answering.
quote: Upon inspection, we found that 100% of GPT 3.5 Turbo JSON-mode responses placed the "answer" key before the "reason" key, resulting in zero-shot direct answering instead of zero-shot chain-of-thought reasoning.

claim: Let Me Speak Freely? finds that stricter format constraints generally cause larger degradation on reasoning tasks.
quote: Furthermore, we find that stricter format constraints generally lead to greater performance degradation in reasoning tasks.

claim: Let Me Speak Freely? (Tam et al.) was published in the EMNLP 2024 Industry Track, as CRANE's bibliography records; the paper's own converted text does not state the venue.
quote: Let me speak freely? a study on the impact of format restrictions on large language model performance. In Dernoncourt, F., Preot¸iuc-Pietro, D., and Shimorina, A. (eds.), Proceedings of the 2024 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing: Industry Track

claim: In JSONSchemaBench's quality experiment, every open-source engine tested (Guidance, Outlines, Llamacpp, XGrammar) scored at least as high as unconstrained generation on the three reasoning tasks, and strictly higher on GSM8K.
quote: The results in Table 8 show that the constrained decoding, regardless of the framework, achieves higher performance than the unconstrained setting.

claim: Unconstrained ('LM only') Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct scored 80.1% on GSM8K in JSONSchemaBench's quality experiment.
With Guidance constraining the output, the same model scored 83.8% on GSM8K, the best of the five settings (XGrammar 83.7%, Llamacpp 82.4%, Outlines 81.6%).
The quality experiment used a single model, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, with the setup and prompts of the .txt rebuttal (Kurt 2024b).
quote: For our experiments, we use the Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct model to measure task performance. We follow the original setup and prompt specifications from Kurt [2024b], with full details provided in Appendix F.

claim: JSONSchemaBench summarizes the quality effect as a consistent improvement of up to 4% on downstream tasks, GSM8K included.
quote: (3) Constrained decoding consistently improves the performance of downstream tasks up to 4%, even for tasks with minimal structure like GSM8k.

claim: JSONSchemaBench reports that the .txt rebuttal attributed the decline in Let Me Speak Freely? to inadequate prompting, missing context and poorly crafted schemas.
quote: Kurt [2024b] argued that the performance decline observed in previous studies [Tam et al., 2024] comes from inadequate prompting, insufficient contextual information, and poorly crafted schemas.

claim: CRANE improved accuracy by up to 10 percentage points over the best baseline on GSM-Symbolic and FOLIO, with open models from 1.5B to 32B parameters.
quote: showing up to 10% points accuracy improvement over baselines on challenging symbolic reasoning benchmarks GSM-symbolic and FOLIO

claim: CRANE was published at ICML 2025 (PMLR 267).
quote: Proceedings of the 42 nd International Conference on Machine Learning, Vancouver, Canada. PMLR 267, 2025.

claim: In practice CRANE adds only start and end delimiters to the output grammar and turns constrained decoding on between them, leaving the reasoning outside the delimiters unconstrained.
quote: To avoid this, we augment the output grammar with specific delimiter symbols S1 and S2 that mark the start and end of the constrained generation.

claim: CRANE's theoretical result is that augmenting a restrictive output grammar with production rules for intermediate reasoning steps preserves the model's expressivity under constrained decoding.
quote: We further demonstrate that augmenting the grammar G with specific additional production rules enables the LLM to generate the intermediate reasoning steps while ensuring that the final output always adheres to the intended output structure.

claim: Biagiola et al. report that an incomplete constrainer pushes the model into low-probability regions, causing frequent time-outs and reducing functional correctness by up to 97%.
quote: Incompleteness pushes the model into low-probability regions of the program space, causing the generation to frequently time out, and reducing functional correctness by up to 97%.

claim: The 97% is a relative drop measured against constrained decoding with the complete grammar, not against free generation.
quote: When incomplete, performance drops, by up to 97% relative to the complete-constrainingmodel baseline.

claim: The 97% case is Qwen-3-Coder-Next-80B generating TOML, whose exact match fell from 62.5% with the complete grammar to 1.9% when the grammar forbade the optional space before '='; Gemma-2-2B fell from 48.1% to 28.6% under the same grammar.
quote: For Gemma-2-2B, exact match drops from 48.1% to 28.6%, while for Qwen-3-Coder-Next-80B the reduction is far more pronounced, reaching 97%.

claim: The incomplete grammar behind the 97% (c-space=) differs from the complete TOML grammar by a single lexeme in one production rule.
quote: c-space = : forbids spaces only before the = symbol (e.g., foo= 1). This is the smallest constrainer, changing the original grammar by a single lexeme in a production rule.

claim: Under the c-space= grammar, Qwen-3-Coder-Next-80B reached 1.9% exact match and 2.9% syntactic correctness, with 86.5% of generations hitting the time limit.
The constrainers in the incompleteness experiment were GGML BNF (GBNF) grammars executed through llama.cpp.
quote: All constrainers are implemented as GGML BNF grammars [14], which are used by llama.cpp to perform constrained decoding.

claim: In the TypeScript study (RQ0), unconstrained decoding matched or beat the type-constrained decoder of Mündler et al. on functional correctness in every configuration, significantly in all but two.
quote: RQ0 (Effectiveness): Unconstrained decoding consistently achieves the best functional correctness across all the configurations.

claim: Misalignment means a constrainer that is incomplete (rejects programs of the target language) or unsound (accepts programs outside it); incompleteness biases and distorts the model's distribution.
quote: Misalignment is caused by the constrainer being incomplete-rejecting programs that belong to the target-or unsound-allowing programs that are not part of the target.

claim: The 23.44 is not JSON mode. It is the '+ schema constraint' cell of Table 1 (Section 5.1): a format-restricting instruction with a JSON schema written into the prompt. The paper reports JSON-mode (constrained decoding) scores only for GPT-3.5 Turbo, Gemini 1.5 Flash and LLaMA 3 8B, since JSON mode was an OpenAI/Gemini API flag, and a TGI feature for the open models. Asked for JSON without the schema, Claude 3 Haiku scored 86.99, above its 86.51 in text. The 23.44 also carries a 22.9 standard deviation across prompt variants.
quote: The JSON-mode scores for GPT 3.5 turbo, Gemini 1.5 Flash and LLaMA 3 8B are presented in Table 11.
wiki_says: GSM8K fell from 86.51 to 23.44 for Claude 3 Haiku in JSON mode

claim: The key-order explanation is given for GPT-3.5 Turbo in JSON mode on Last Letter, not for Claude 3 Haiku on GSM8K. The paper names no specific cause for the Claude drop. Its own Table 3 shows a 60.07% parse-error rate for Claude 3 Haiku answering GSM8K in JSON, against 1.85% for XML and 0.0% for YAML. It also reports that a corrective re-formatting prompt raised Claude 3 Haiku's JSON scores (Figure 5).
quote: | Claude-3-Haiku | JSON XML YAML   | 3.48 0.0 0.0              | 60.07 1.85 0.0      |
wiki_says: the cause given is that answers put the answer key before the reasoning key

claim: The only true grammar-constrained decoding the paper tests (gpt-4o-mini Structured Outputs, labelled JSON-Schema) lost 2.86 points on GSM8K against natural language (91.71 vs 94.57) and beat natural language on Last Letter (86.07 vs 83.11). The authors summarize that NL is only 'slightly better' in 2 of 3 reasoning tasks. The large drops come from prompt-only format instructions and the older JSON mode.
wiki_says: Formats that hurt reasoning: in Let Me Speak Freely? ... GSM8K fell from 86.51 to 23.44 (cited as evidence about constraining)

claim: On GSM8K all four open-source engines beat the unconstrained baseline, but on Shuffle Objects Llamacpp tied it (52.6% vs 52.6%). The quality test covered only the four open-source engines, not OpenAI or Gemini, and one model, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. The gains were small: at most 3.7 points on GSM8K and 3.3 points on the other two tasks.
wiki_says: in JSONSchemaBench, every engine beat free generation

claim: The 'LM only' baseline is not free-form natural language. It is the same JSON prompt and reasoning-first {"reasoning", "answer"} schema taken from the .txt rebuttal, generated without enforcement. The comparison isolates enforcement of an already reasoning-friendly format, so it does not test the format restriction that Let Me Speak Freely? measured.
quote: For the task of Shuffle Objects, and GSM8K, we use the same prompt and JSON schema from the dottxt's "let me speak freely" rebuttal.
wiki_says: free generation (GSM8K with Llama 3.1 8B: 80.1 free, 83.8 with Guidance)

claim: Reasoning rules in the grammar are only the theoretical construction (Ga -> R G). The CRANE algorithm leaves reasoning unconstrained and applies the grammar only between delimiters (<< and >> on GSM-Symbolic), switching back to free generation after the end delimiter. 'Up to 10 points' is measured against the best baseline (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, 31 vs 21 on GSM-Symbolic). Against the purely constrained baseline the gain reaches 18 points (31 vs 13). The models were open, 1.5B to 32B parameters, run with greedy decoding, and CRANE needs logit access.
quote: Importantly, we know that enforcing the output grammar G from the beginning can limit expressivity. Instead, we impose grammar constraints judiciously to avoid restricting the LLM's reasoning capabilities.
wiki_says: CRANE (ICML 2025) added up to 10 points by including reasoning rules in the grammar

claim: The 97% comes from one model (Qwen-3-Coder-Next-80B) on one task: TOML documents (TomlModeEval, 100 problems), a configuration format rather than a programming language. A llama.cpp GBNF grammar forbade only the optional space before '='. The figure is exact match relative to the complete grammar (62.5% to 1.9%). Free generation, also at 62.5%, did win in that case. For Qwen-2.5-32B, however, the same incomplete grammar tied free generation on exact match and beat it on similarity.
quote: Qwen-2.5-32B appears less sensitive to this feature: exact match remains essentially unchanged at 39.7% vs. 40.3% (nc), though the similarity score still shows a meaningful increase.
wiki_says: when the constrainer rejects valid programs, functional correctness drops "by up to 97%" and free generation wins

claim: Not every incompleteness hurts. Grammars that forbade TOML comments or dotted keys lost nothing against the complete grammar for any of the three models. The damage depends on whether the model strongly prefers the rejected construct, as with the optional space before '='. The paper's general claim rests on that case and on the TypeScript type constrainer, which lacks forward references, imports and user-defined types.
quote: By contrast, removing other features, such as comments (c-comment) or dotted keys (c-dotted), does not reduce functional correctness relative to the complete constrained strategy (c), and this holds consistently across all evaluated models.
wiki_says: a grammar that rejects valid programs is worse than none

claim: The 97% is a single-model worst case (Qwen-3-Coder-Next-80B) on TOML generation with a syntax-only GBNF grammar, measured as relative exact-match loss against the complete grammar. The risk table should state those conditions. It should also note that the type-constrained TypeScript case lost roughly 2 to 10 points of functional correctness against free generation.
quote: We chose TOML because it is widely adopted, has a simple syntax and semantics, and includes several derived forms [12].
wiki_says: an incomplete constrainer cut correctness by up to 97%

claim: Biagiola et al. replicated the type-constrained TypeScript decoder of Mündler et al. that the page cites: six LLMs on HumanEval and two on MBPP, three temperatures, 10 runs, about 57k and 47k programs. Type constraints raised compile rates for weaker models but lowered functional correctness in every configuration (e.g., Qwen-2.5-32B on HumanEval at temperature 0.1: 72.3% constrained vs 82.3% free). The cause was an incomplete constrainer that lacks forward references, imports and user-defined types. Type constraints reduce compile errors, not necessarily wrong programs.
quote: While type-constrained decoding improves type-syntax correctness, this does not show better functional correctness.
wiki_says: Types are worth more than syntax ... a 'valid continuations and expected type at the cursor' API ... for type constraints, the step that actually reduces errors

claim: Format restriction hurt reasoning tasks but helped classification. Restricting the answer space to valid labels reduced answer-selection errors, so the effect depends on whether the output is a free derivation or a choice from a small set.
quote: These findings suggest format restrictions' impact on LLM performance is task-dependent: stringent formats may hinder reasoning-intensive tasks but enhance accuracy in classification tasks requiring structured outputs.
bears_on: when grammar constraints help vs hurt functional correctness

claim: Parse failures do not explain the drops. LLaMA 3 8B had a 0.148% parse-error rate in JSON on Last Letter yet a 38.15-point gap, which points to the format interfering with generation itself.
quote: In the LLaMA 3 8B setting, the parsing error rate for the Last Letter task in JSON format is only 0.148%, yet there exists a substantial 38.15% performance gap as seen in Table 1.
bears_on: when grammar constraints help vs hurt functional correctness

claim: Answering freely in natural language and then converting to the format (NL-to-Format) scored nearly the same as unrestricted answers. Decoupling reasoning from format compliance preserves accuracy.
quote: Comparing NL-to-Format with unrestricted Natural Language responses, we observe nearly identical performance across most models, as both derive answers from the same initial natural language response.
bears_on: whether the model should reason freely (comments, scratchpad) before or inside constrained output

claim: The authors single out key order (reasoning before answer) and the decoupling of reasoning from format as the factors that keep capability under structured output. For code, this argues for letting free reasoning, such as comments, precede the constrained construct.
quote: The order of keys in structured outputs and the decoupling of reasoning from format adherence emerge as important factors in maintaining LLM capabilities while providing structured responses.
bears_on: free comments in the published grammar; reasoning before code

claim: The study used only small, older models (GPT-3.5 Turbo, Claude 3 Haiku, Gemini 1.5 Flash, LLaMA 3 8B, Gemma 2 9B) and simple two-field outputs. The authors flag that stronger models were excluded, so the large drops may not carry over to frontier models; gpt-4o-mini already showed small gaps.
quote: First, due to cost constraints, we were unable to include results frommore powerful language models such as LLaMA 70B or GPT-4o in our experiments.
bears_on: weight of this evidence for frontier models generating lotml

claim: A cheap repair step (re-prompting to fix outputs that failed to parse) recovered part of the loss for the two models with the most parse errors. This is an alternative or complement to constraining.
quote: By prompting Claude-3-Haiku to reformat any output with parsing errors for both Claude 3 Haiku and LLaMA 3 8B (the two models with the highest percentage of parsing errors), we observed improved scores in JSON and YAML formats
bears_on: repair loop vs constrained decoding in the evaluation harness

claim: JSONSchemaBench names the failure the alignment paper later measures: an over-constrained engine, one that rejects valid instances, limits the model's expressive power and can hurt downstream accuracy.
quote: Over-constrained grammar engines risk limiting the expressive power of LMs, potentially preventing the generation of valid responses and negatively impacting downstream task performance.
bears_on: publishing a grammar that accepts exactly the compiler's language

claim: The benchmark tests a constrainer with both positive and negative instances: it must allow every valid instance and block every invalid one, checked by walking each tokenized instance through the engine's mask. lotml's grammar tests can reuse this protocol, with corpus programs as positives and known-invalid programs as negatives, run per engine.
quote: For the purpose of evaluating coverage, we assert that an engine must successfully generate each valid instance and block generation of each invalid instance to "pass" a test case.
bears_on: how to test the published grammar against the compiler

claim: Engines diverge widely on the same specification: the best supported twice as many real-world schemas as the worst. A grammar published in three dialects needs conformance tests on each target engine, not only on the reference parser.
quote: (2) Frameworks demonstrate significant differences in their actual support for real-world JSON schemas, with the best framework supporting twice as many schemas as the worst.
bears_on: the three grammar dialects (Lark/llguidance, GBNF, EBNF)

claim: Engines fail differently. XGrammar rarely fails to compile but was under-constrained in 38 of 43 test categories, while Outlines and Llamacpp fail mostly at compile time and are over-constrained more often than under-constrained.
quote: In contrast, XGrammar minimizes compilation errors but shows the highest number of under-constrained failures, indicating a trade-off favoring permissiveness.
bears_on: the three grammar dialects; soundness vs completeness per engine

claim: Hosted providers support only a conservative subset of JSON Schema: OpenAI declared coverage was 0.30 on GitHub Easy against Guidance's 0.90. Hosted grammar features should be treated as a constrained subset and tested.
quote: While closed-source implementations have low empirical coverage, they have very high compliance rates, indicating that their providers have taken a more conservative strategy, implementing only a subset of JSON Schema features that they can reliably support.
bears_on: hosted APIs that accept a grammar (OpenAI Lark subset)

claim: Constrained decoding need not cost latency. Guidance cut time per output token below the unconstrained baseline (6.37 ms vs 15.40 ms on GlaiveAI) by fast-forwarding tokens the grammar forces, while Outlines spent 3 to 8 s compiling each schema.
quote: (1) Constrained decoding can speed up the generation process by 50% compared to unconstrained decoding.
bears_on: cost of constraining; deterministic keywords that a grammar can fast-forward

claim: Under-constraining hands responsibility back to the model, which often still produces valid output. A permissive grammar paired with a full compiler check is a legitimate design, if documented.
quote: Another reason is under-constraining effectively delegates responsibility to the LM, which may produce valid output despite a lack of strict constraints.
bears_on: soundness vs completeness of the published grammar

claim: On FOLIO the constrained baseline used a Prover9 grammar whose COMMENT terminal lets the model write free text after each formula, and it beat unconstrained chain-of-thought for all three models (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B 39.41% vs 32.02%). Comments in the grammar act as a reasoning channel. They are allowed only at line ends here, not anywhere.
quote: The Prover9 grammar divides FOL formulas into Predicates, Premises, and Conclusions and allows intermediate reasoning in comments
bears_on: free comments in the published grammar so the model can reason inside constrained output

claim: FOLIO numbers for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct: unconstrained CoT 32.02% accuracy and 57.14% compiling; grammar-constrained (with comments) 39.41% and 86.21%; CRANE 46.31% and 85.71%.
quote: | Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct    | Unconstrained CoT Constrained CRANE | 32.02 39.41 46.31 | 57.14 86.21 85.71 | 371.52 549.75 449.77 |
bears_on: when grammar constraints help vs hurt functional correctness

claim: A grammar admitting only the final answer often scored below unconstrained chain-of-thought on GSM-Symbolic (Qwen2.5-1.5B: 22% vs 26%; CRANE 31%), so constraining the answer alone throws away reasoning.
quote: Similarly, with the Qwen2.5-1.5BInstruct model, CRANE achieves 31% accuracy-5 percentage points higher than an unconstrained generation with CoT and 9 percentage points higher than a constrained generation.
bears_on: whether letting the model reason freely inside constrained output matters

claim: The expressivity proof covers only grammars with a finite language (answer sets such as yes/no). It does not cover infinite languages such as a programming language's programs, so it does not by itself show that a full-language grammar hurts reasoning.
quote: First, Proposition 3.1 only demonstrates a reduction in expressivity when the language L(Gc) is finite. This leaves open the question of whether Proposition 3.1 can be extended to grammars G where L(G) is infinite.
bears_on: applicability of the restrictive-grammar argument to a lotml program grammar

claim: For a general-purpose language whose grammar can start with almost any identifier, the decoder cannot tell where reasoning ends and code begins. CRANE needs explicit delimiters, such as code fences, to switch the constraint on.
quote: For instance, grammar for generalpurpose programming languages such as Python can allow any text string at the start (e.g. program starting variable names) making it hard to detect the end of reasoning string.
bears_on: how lotml code is delimited in model output when constrained

claim: CRANE needs access to output logits, so it cannot run on hosted models that do not expose them.
quote: Second, CRANE for constrained decoding relies on existing tools (Ugare et al., 2024b) that require access to output logits, rendering CRANE inapplicable to models that do not expose logits.
bears_on: constraining lotml generation on hosted APIs

claim: CRANE also enforced a semantic constraint, that generated expressions use only variables defined in the problem, on top of the context-free grammar. Constraints on identifiers in scope work alongside syntax.
quote: we enforce syntactic constraints via the context-free grammar provided in Appendix C.5.1 and apply the semantic constraint ensuring that generated expressions contain only valid problem-defined variables.
bears_on: scope- and type-aware constraints beyond the grammar

claim: The trade-off is real: switching constraints off for reasoning lets slightly more syntax errors through than purely constrained output, in exchange for much higher functional correctness.
quote: Although, for several instances, CRANE produces slightly more syntax errors than a purely constrained generation, it offers a substantial improvement in functional correctness over this baseline.
bears_on: when grammar constraints help vs hurt functional correctness

claim: Alignment is the relation among three languages: what the model is likely to generate (L_M), the real language (L_T) and what the constrainer permits (L_C). Constrained decoding helps only when they align. For a new language such as lotml, where the model's prior favours Python-like constructs, misalignment can also come from the model side (an inference, not tested in the paper).
quote: The central thesis of this paper is that constrained decoding is beneficial to code generation only when there is alignment between these three languages.
bears_on: what alignment between the grammar and the real language means

claim: Forbidding optional whitespace that the model habitually emits was the most damaging restriction, far worse than forbidding comments or dotted keys. Models attach meaning even to aesthetic spacing, so a constraint grammar must accept every whitespace variant the compiler accepts and must not encode the canonical formatter's layout.
quote: Moreover, optional spaces are more impactful than comments or dotted keys, showing that models attribute semantics to all syntactic constructs, including aesthetic spacing.
bears_on: whitespace in the published grammar; OpenAI's advice to make whitespace explicit

claim: With a complete grammar, constraining helped most for the weakest model and least for strong ones: Gemma-2-2B gained 54% (relative), Qwen-2.5-32B 2.5%.
quote: When the constrainer is complete, constrained decoding significantly outperforms its unconstrained counterpart (by 2.5% for a 32B model and up to 54% for a 2B model).
bears_on: when grammar constraints help vs hurt functional correctness

claim: For the strongest model (Qwen-3-Coder-Next-80B), even a complete grammar gave no benefit, because it almost never made syntax errors unconstrained. The value of a syntax grammar shrinks for frontier models.
quote: c and nc are equivalent for Qwen-3-Coder-Next-80B, where the unconstrained model makes syntax mistakes in only 0.2% of cases, excluding timeouts.
bears_on: expected benefit of the published grammar for frontier models

claim: Forward references, meaning use before definition, cannot be checked on a token prefix without backtracking, so practical type constrainers drop them and become incomplete. Language rules that make prefixes checkable decide whether type-level constraining can be complete.
quote: For instance, features such as forward referencesi.e., using a variable, function, or class before it is defined-cannot be enforced at the token level without backtracking, as the validity of an earlier token may only become apparent much later in the sequence.
bears_on: a type system checkable on prefixes; declaration order in lotml

claim: When soundness and completeness cannot both be had, the authors recommend prioritizing soundness and then shrinking the incompleteness by finetuning or enlarging the constrainer. A syntax-only grammar for a language with a reference parser can be complete, as their complete TOML grammar was, and that complete constrainer helped.
quote: We argue, however, that soundness (Figure 3.b) should be prioritized over completeness to benefit from the guarantees of constrained decoding: if the constrainer is sound, all the solutions generated under constrained decoding are guaranteed to be correct, according to the user-defined constraints.
bears_on: requirement that the grammar accept exactly the compiler's language

claim: Incompleteness can be measured directly by running model-generated programs that the real compiler accepts through the constrainer. For Gemma-2-2B, 982 of 4,231 compiling TypeScript solutions (23%) were rejected.
quote: Among the 4,231 unconstrained solutions that compiled, 982 failed the incremental type-checking pass of the TypeScript constrainer.
bears_on: how to test the published grammar against real model output

claim: A complete syntax grammar does not stop semantic errors. TOML conflicting keys still occurred: 19 of Gemma-2-2B's 411 errors and 66 of Qwen-2.5-32B's 102.
quote: Also, the complete constrainer does not prevent type errors such as duplicate keys: across 10 runs (1000 generated programs per model), Gemma-2-2B produces 411 type-syntax errors of which 19 are conflicting key errors
bears_on: syntax vs semantic constraints; the compiler's continuation/type API

claim: On the rbtree benchmark (42 million insertions into an unshared red-black tree), Koka's purely functional implementation compiled to C came within 10% of C++ using the in-place std::map.
quote: Surprisingly, the purely functional Koka implementation is within 10% of the C++ performance.

claim: On rbtree, Java (G1, default settings) came close to C++ in time but used almost 10 times Koka's peak memory (1.7 GiB against 170 MiB).
quote: Java performs close to C++ here but also uses almost 10× the memory of Koka (1.7GiB vs. 170MiB, Figure 9).

claim: On rbtree, Koka with drop/reuse specialization and reuse analysis disabled ("no-opt") was more than 2 times slower than optimized Koka.
quote: This benchmark also shows the potential effectiveness of the reference count optimizations where the "no-opt" version is more than 2× slower.

claim: On benchmarks with heavy sharing (deriv, nqueens), Perceus's reuse and specialization optimizations are less effective.
quote: However, in benchmarks with lots of sharing, like deriv and nqueens, the optimizations are less effective.

claim: Making every reference-count operation atomic, instead of using Koka's thread-shared flag, slowed the single-threaded benchmarks by 5% (rbtree) to 59% (nqueens).
quote: We observed a slowdown from 5% (rbtree) up to 59% (nqueens) across our benchmarks.

claim: Perceus inserts precise reference-counting instructions over a core language with explicit control flow, so cycle-free programs are garbage free, which in turn enables reuse analysis and guaranteed in-place updates.
quote: Starting from a functional core language with explicit control-flow, Perceus emits precise reference counting instructions such that (cycle-free) programs are garbage free, where only live references are retained.

claim: Koka compiles to standard C11 and, because it uses reference counting, needs no runtime system (no collector) and links directly with C/C++ libraries.
quote: The use of reference counting means no runtime system is needed and Koka programs can readily link with other C/C++ libraries.

claim: The benchmarked Koka compiled its generated C code with gcc using a customized version of the mimalloc allocator.
quote: Koka 2.0.3, compiling the generated C code with gcc 9.3.0 using a customized version of the mimalloc allocator [27].

claim: Koka ships no cycle collector: only mutable references can form cycles, and breaking them is left to the programmer, as in Swift.
quote: Since mutable references are uncommon in our setting, we leave the responsibility to the programmer to break cycles by explicitly clearing a reference cell that may be part of a cycle.

claim: On the const_fold benchmark, Lean 4 was 5 times as fast as OCaml (ocamlopt 4.10) even though it incurred more cache misses per second.
quote: Note that Lean is 5x as fast as OCaml on const\_fold even though it triggers more cache misses per second.

claim: On const_fold, Lean spent 17% of its runtime deallocating memory while OCaml spent 90% in its GC; Lean's figure excludes time spent updating reference counts.
quote: Using const\_fold as an example again, Lean spends only 17% of the runtime deallocating memory, while OCaml spends 90% in the GC.

claim: At the time of the paper, the new Lean compiler had a single backend that emits C, with an LLVM backend in progress.
quote: At the time of writing, the compiler supports only one backend where we emit C code.

claim: Lean infers borrowed parameters with a heuristic: a parameter is kept owned if it, or one of its projections, is reset or passed to a function that takes it owned; otherwise it is borrowed and needs no inc/dec.
quote: We say a parameter x should be owned if x or one of its projections is used in a reset, or is passed to a function that takes an owned reference.

claim: Lean's reset/reuse instructions reuse the memory cell of a non-shared value for a new constructor value, so map over an unshared list allocates no memory.
quote: We remark that if the list referenced by xs is not shared, the code above does not allocate any memory.

claim: Lean's pure IR cannot create cyclic data structures, so reference counting's inability to reclaim cycles does not arise and no collector is needed.
quote: We remark that in Lean and λpure, it is not possible to create cyclic data structures.

claim: Swift parameters default to borrowed ("+0"/guaranteed), and the compiler may change the calling convention only locally, inside individual modules.
quote: Parameters default to borrowed in Swift, but the compiler may locally change the calling convention inside individual modules.

claim: In the Swift 3.1.1 runtime, reference-counting operations took on average 42% of execution time in client programs and 15% in server programs, 32% across all programs.
quote: performing RC operations takes on average 42% of the execution time in client programs, and 15% in server programs. The average across all programs can be shown to be 32%.

claim: About 93% of RC operations in the Swift client programs and about 87% in the server programs went to objects whose counter was only ever updated by one thread.
quote: Similarly, about 93% of the RC operations in client programs, and about 87% of those in server programs are to private objects.

claim: Biased reference counting biases each object to one thread and keeps two counters: the owner updates its counter non-atomically, other threads update a second counter atomically.
quote: BRC leverages this by biasing each object towards a specific thread, and keeping two counters for each object - one updated by the owner thread and another updated by the other threads.

claim: Swift avoids reference cycles with weak references rather than a cycle collector.
quote: Swift uses weak references to avoid cyclic references, an approach popular in previous literature [11, 16].

claim: In strict mutable value semantics, references are second-class: created only implicitly at function boundaries and never stored in variables or object fields.
quote: In the discipline's strictest form, references become second-class citizens: they are only created implicitly, at function boundaries, and cannot be stored in variables or object fields.

claim: The implementation strategy allocates fixed-size values on the stack and uses copy-on-write for dynamically sized containers.
quote: Fixed-size values are allocated on the stack, thereby enabling numerous off-the-shelf compiler optimizations, while dynamically sized containers use copy-on-write to mitigate copying costs.

claim: Because references can be neither assigned to variables nor stored in fields, all values form disjoint trees rooted in variables, so reference cycles cannot form.
quote: As such, they can neither be assigned to a variable nor stored in object fields, and all values form disjoint topological trees rooted in the program's variables.

claim: The synthetic evaluation timed 1,344 randomly generated (fuzzer-built, single-threaded) programs over 20 independent runs in Swift, Swiftlet, Scala Native and C++.
quote: We report results for a data set measuring the execution time of 1344 randomly generated programs across 20 different independent runs.

claim: Swift was the fastest implementation in the overwhelming majority of the synthetic benchmarks.
quote: In contrast, Swift is the fastest language in the overwhelming majority of the benchmarks.

claim: In median normalized time by write ratio, Swift was slower than C++ only for programs where more than 90% of memory accesses were mutations.
quote: Swift proved slower than C++ only for programs with extremely large number of mutating operations (> 90%), providing compelling empirical evidence in favor of copy-on-write

claim: An inout parameter lets the callee mutate the caller's value, and the ampersand at the call site marks that the argument will be mutated (it is not C's address-of).
quote: Note that the ampersand featured in the call expression is not the "address-of" operator from C/C++. Instead, it signals in code that the argument is to be mutated-conceptually "copied out" of the callee upon return.

claim: Non-inout parameters are immutable and semantically passed by value, so the compiler may pass an alias to the caller's value instead of a copy, as long as the alias does not escape the callee.
quote: Therefore, in terms of a concrete operational semantics, arguments can be passed as aliases to values stored at the call site rather than being copied.

claim: Under mutable value semantics, arbitrary graphs are represented as arrays of vertices holding arrays of destination indices, i.e. the arena-and-index idiom.
quote: For example, a vertex set might be represented as an array, each element of which contains an array of outgoing edge destination indices.

claim: The >2x slowdown is reported for rbtree only, the unshared best case for reuse; "no-opt" disables drop/reuse specialization and reuse analysis, not reference-count optimization in general, and on deriv no-opt Koka is only slightly slower.
quote: It is also interesting to see that the "no-opt" Koka is only just slightly slower than optimized Koka here.
wiki_says: Without the counting optimizations Koka is more than 2 times slower.

claim: rbtree has no shared subtrees, so reuse fires on every insertion; the authors acknowledge the benchmark may be biased toward reference counting, attribute part of the result to 8-byte versus 16-byte allocation alignment, and have no C++ baseline for the shared variant rbtree-ck. They frame all results as evidence of viability, not as absolute comparisons.
quote: it has been suggested that rbtree is biased to reference counting as it has no shared subtrees and thus reuse analysis can use in-place updates all the time.
wiki_says: Koka's purely functional red-black tree came within 10% of C++'s std::map (also ADR 0003: 'Perceus brought Koka within 10% of C++ on a red-black tree'), presented as general evidence.

claim: The 10x figure is with default JVM settings; tuning parameters reduced it to about 1.5x, at the cost of making Java slower.
quote: This can be reduced to about 1.5× by providing tuning parameters on the command line but that also made it slower on our system.
wiki_says: Java came close in time using almost 10 times the memory (1.7 GiB against 170 MiB).

claim: On const_fold, disabling borrow inference made Lean faster (0.90 of base) while disabling reuse made it 1.64x slower; the paper attributes the gap over OCaml mainly to time OCaml spends in GC, and its conjecture that fewer cache misses explained the speed was refuted. Borrow inference helped binarytrees and deriv instead.
wiki_says: Borrowed-parameter inference plus reset/reuse: Lean was 5 times faster than OCaml on const_fold (ADR 0003: 'Lean 4 with reuse and inferred borrowing was 5 times faster than OCaml').

claim: The two percentages are not comparable: Lean's figure measures only object deletion, because inc/dec are inlined and cannot be timed, so time spent updating reference counts is excluded. The paper's own Fig. 7 table (as converted) lists the const_fold Lean deletion share as 1~3%, not 17%.
quote: This comparison is not entirely precise since it does not include the amount of time Lean spends updating reference counts, but it seems to be the most plausible explanation for the difference in performance.
wiki_says: Lean spent 17% of its time deallocating against OCaml's 90% in collection.

claim: Five of the seven client programs are single-threaded, so 100% private trivially; the client average of about 93% is pulled down by the one multithreaded outlier, Regex-Redux, where only about half of RC operations were private. The figures say little about how much sharing a genuinely concurrent program has.
quote: The outlier is Regex-Redux, where nearly 50% of the RC operations are on shared objects, and 12% use the shared counter.
wiki_says: 87-93% of the operations touched objects private to one thread (cited under 'Atomic counting' as evidence that most operations need not be atomic).

claim: The 32% is total RC overhead in the Swift 3.1.1 runtime of 2018, averaged over client (42%) and server (15%) programs; the atomic part alone, measured by removing CAS on the subset of programs that still ran, was about 25% of execution time.
quote: We will show later that, on average, not using atomic operations reduces the average execution time of the programs by 25%.
wiki_says: Swift spent 32% of its time counting (memory-model places the same figure under 'Atomic counting').

claim: Biasing is to the OS thread that allocated the object (thread ID in the header); ownership transfer is left to future work, so a green thread that migrates would hit the slow atomic path for every object it allocated before migrating. Biased counting is therefore a poor fit for migrating tasks, while Lean and Koka avoid atomics without biasing by marking values thread-shared only when they are passed to a new task.
quote: First, when an object is allocated, BRC saves the ID of the thread allocating the object in the RCWord, effectively biasing the object.
wiki_says: Green threads that migrate between OS threads force reference counting to be atomic or biased.

claim: The C++ side is a generated translation that passes data structures by value and forbids mutable references across function boundaries, so every read of a std::vector element copies it; C++ loses on read-heavy programs because of those copies, not because optimized C++ is slower. Swift was also compiled with -Ounchecked.
quote: Indeed, each read of std::vector copies an entire element, potentially causing repeated copies in deeply nested data structures.
wiki_says: Swift was the fastest in the 'overwhelming majority' and only lost to C++ with more than 90% mutations.

claim: The >90% threshold comes from median normalized times per write-ratio bucket (Figure 15); the same section says C++ is usually the fastest in write-dominated programs, so individual programs below 90% writes also favor C++.
quote: On the other hand, C++ is usually the fastest implementation in programs that are dominated by writes.
wiki_says: Swift only lost to C++ with more than 90% mutations.

claim: The authors expect a tracing GC to beat reference counting when reuse does not fire and the program allocates many short-lived objects; OCaml's bump-pointer minor heap was close on rbtree for that reason.
quote: More generally, we expect a GC to do better when reuse optimization is not triggered, and there is lots of short-lived object allocation.
bears_on: cost of reference counting vs tracing GC; allocation-heavy benchmarks must be reported separately

claim: Koka avoids atomic counts without copying: objects start unshared and are marked thread-shared (recursively, once) only when passed to a new thread, and the fast path tests a sign bit instead of using atomics.
quote: In particular, when starting a new thread, the argument passed to the thread is marked as thread-shared.
bears_on: non-atomic counting per task; alternative to copying or moving values between tasks

claim: Precise counting requires explicit control flow: Koka compiles exceptions into explicit error returns, because unwinding would leak values whose drops were moved into callees.
quote: In Koka, we guarantee that all control-flow is compiled to explicit control-flow, so our reference count analysis does not have to take non-linear control-flow into account.
bears_on: error-handling design (exceptions vs result values) as a precondition for Perceus-style counting

claim: Perceus deliberately has no borrowing: adding borrowed parameters would forfeit garbage-freedom, so 'Perceus-style reuse plus Lean-style borrow inference' is a trade-off to tune, not two free wins.
quote: We would like to integrate selective "borrowing" into Perceus - this would make certain programs no longer be garbage free, but we believe it could deliver further performance improvements if judiciously applied.
bears_on: combining reuse with borrow inference; default parameter convention

claim: Reuse can raise peak memory: on cfold the unoptimized build used 11% less memory because reuse tokens hold cells for later reuse.
quote: The "no-opt" version of Koka also uses 11% less memory; this is because the reuse analysis essentially holds on to memory for later reuse.
bears_on: predictable memory use of reuse analysis

claim: FBIP reuse is predictable enough to program against: the programmer can match each pattern to a same-size constructor in the branch and know the update will be in place when the value is unique.
quote: Importantly, a programmer can rely on this optimization happening, e.g. they can see the match patterns and match them to constructors in each branch.
bears_on: predictable performance; semantic-compiler diagnostics reporting where reuse fails

claim: The authors attribute Swift's weaker counting performance partly to the language: some Perceus optimizations need static guarantees (immutability, tracked thread sharing) that Swift lacks.
quote: As discussed for example in Section 2.7.2, some of the optimizations we perform are difficult to do in Swift as the static guarantees of the language are not strong enough.
bears_on: why lotml's ban on stored mutable references matters for counting cost

claim: A mutable reference cell shared between threads needs more than atomic counts: read-and-dup races with write-and-drop, requiring double-CAS, hazard pointers or locks.
quote: To make this work correctly, we need to perform both operations atomically, either through a double-CAS [9], using hazard pointers [15, 33], or using some other locking mechanism.
bears_on: any shared mutable cell or channel between tasks; keeping stored references out of the language

claim: Forcing atomic reference counting on all values (-ST) slowed Lean's benchmarks by 1.13x (qsort) up to 2.31x (unionfind), a larger range than Perceus's 5-59%.
bears_on: cost of atomic counting; non-atomic counting per task

claim: Lean tags values single-threaded by default and marks everything reachable as multi-threaded at Task.mk/Task.bind; task creation then costs time proportional to the unmarked values reachable from the closure.
quote: Note that task creation is not a constant time operation in our approach because it is proportional to the number of single-threaded values reachable
bears_on: passing values between tasks without copying; task-spawn cost

claim: Borrowing and reuse compete: a borrowed parameter saves inc/dec but can never be reset, so its cell cannot be reused in place; the inference is a heuristic, not an optimum.
quote: Our heuristic is based on the fact that when we mark a parameter as borrowed, we reduce the number of RC operations needed, but we also prevent reset and reuse as well as primitive operations from reusing memory cells.
bears_on: borrow inference vs reuse; default parameter convention

claim: Borrow inference breaks down at partial application and closures: the result may escape, so Lean wraps such functions in an owned-signature wrapper.
quote: Partially applying constants with borrowed parameters is also problematic because, in general, we cannot statically assert that the resulting value will not escape the current function and thus the scope of borrowed references.
bears_on: where inference fails: closures, higher-order functions, polymorphic interfaces

claim: Borrow inference can destroy tail calls, because a dec of the owned argument is emitted after the call; Lean had to force owned parameters in tail-call positions.
quote: However, the previous example shows that our function for inserting reference counting instructions may insert dec instructions after a constant application, and consequently, destroy tail calls.
bears_on: interaction of borrow inference with loops and tail calls

claim: Reuse was fragile enough that Lean's developers needed a static analyzer to check that constructors are guarded by reuse, plus runtime counters of shared vs unshared resets, and sometimes rewrote code (inlining balance1) to get reuse.
quote: We address the first question using a simple static analyzer that when invoked by a developer, checks whether reuse instructions are guarding constructor applications in a particular function.
bears_on: semantic-compiler diagnostics; 'inference alone is not enough'

claim: When trees are shared (rbmap_10, rbmap_1 keep old versions as backtracking does), reuse stops firing and Lean slows down sharply, with deallocation time rising.
quote: As expected, Lean's performance decreases on these two variants since the tree is now a shared value, and the time spent deallocating objects increases substantially.
bears_on: when reuse fails: sharing

claim: A well-tuned tracing collector stayed competitive: MLton (whole-program, tracing GC) beat or tied Lean on several benchmarks, including the most sharing-heavy one.
quote: However, Lean still outperforms all systems but MLton on rbmap\_1.
bears_on: cost of reference counting vs tracing GC

claim: Polymorphism costs boxing in Lean's runtime: an unboxed scalar must be boxed before being passed to a polymorphic function.
quote: The unboxed value support has restrictions similar to the ones found in GHC. For example, to pass an unboxed value to a polymorphic function we must first box it.
bears_on: generics implementation (monomorphization vs boxing) and its interaction with counting

claim: Swift's optimizer statically removed up to 97% of RC operations, yet the remainder still cost 32% of execution time on average, so a percentage of eliminated operations says little about cost.
quote: Specifically, we found that Swift removes up to 97% of RC operations in our programs.
bears_on: evaluating claims like Lobster's 95% of operations removed

claim: In a best-case single-threaded microbenchmark, an atomic (CAS) increment took 13.84 ns against 5.77 ns non-atomic, 2.40x slower.
quote: As shown in the table, the increment operation takes 13.84 ns in O and 5.77 ns I . Hence, the use of atomic operations slows down the operation by 2.40x.
bears_on: cost of atomic counting

claim: Swift pays for atomics even in single-threaded programs because separate compilation stops the compiler from proving objects thread-private: a module boundary is what forces the conservative choice.
quote: However, as argued in Section 1, the Swift compiler does not know this because Swift compiles components separately. Hence, Swift is forced to use atomic operations always for correctness.
bears_on: inference stops at boundaries; making thread-locality a language guarantee

claim: Biased counting recovered 22.5% of client execution time and 7.3% of server throughput, coming within 3.7% of the unsafe no-atomics configuration.
quote: Overall, we find that, on average, BRC improves the execution time of client programs by 22.5%, and the throughput of server programs by 7.3%.
bears_on: whether a runtime technique is needed if the language already guarantees non-atomic counting per task

claim: Even with its static optimizations, Swift's immediate (non-deferred) counting is about 20% slower than deferred reference counting, which trades that time for memory overhead.
quote: While Swift's non-deferred RC with optimization is fast, it is still slower than DRC (about 20% [21]).
bears_on: reference-counting design space: immediate vs deferred reclamation

claim: BRC has no ownership transfer: objects stay biased to their allocating thread, and transfer is left to future work.
quote: It is possible to apply such ownership transfer techniques to BRC. In future work, we plan to implement similar techniques to better support various program behaviors.
bears_on: green threads migrating between OS threads; colorless concurrency runtime

claim: Closures are a hole in Swift's value semantics: implicit by-reference captures reintroduce aliasing, and exclusivity violations are caught only at runtime. Swiftlet captures by copy (immutable) to keep the guarantee static.
quote: By contrast, Swift does not require captures to be explicitly declared, and its implicit captures are by-reference, so closures introduce reference semantics.
bears_on: closure capture semantics; no stored references; cycles

claim: inout passed as an interior pointer interacts badly with copy-on-write: the callee cannot tell whether the pointer lands in shared storage, so the caller must defensively copy non-unique buffers before the call.
quote: Hence, the callee has no way to determine whether or not that pointer refers to a value inside of a shared buffer. As a result, the caller is compelled to copy non-unique storage defensively.
bears_on: cost of inout on collections with copy-on-write

claim: Naive copy-on-write is slow: most of Swiftlet's gap to Swift came from uniqueness checks that a dedicated optimizer would remove by reasoning about reference counts statically.
quote: Manual modification of the LLVM bitcode generated by our compiler reveals that unnecessary reference counter checks account for most of the performance loss that we observed.
bears_on: compiler effort required for value semantics to perform; Python and C targets

claim: Exclusivity for inout is checked syntactically: the same access path may not appear twice among a call's inout arguments, and array indices that cannot be proved distinct are rejected.
quote: These restrictions ensure that aliases can be prevented simply by verifying that the "path" to a value (i.e., a list of member accesses and/or array subscripts) never appears twice in inout arguments to a single function call.
bears_on: inout checking rules and the errors the semantic compiler must explain

claim: Alias-for-copy only works for immutable bindings: assigning to or from a var generally requires a copy (or copy-on-write), so a callee that copies a parameter into a var to mutate it pays for a copy.
quote: Any assignment involving a mutable binding, on the left- or right-hand side typically requires a copy, because the value might be mutated later.
bears_on: copy cost of the default convention; warning when a copied parameter is mutated and discarded

claim: Moves can be inferred for temporaries and for the last use of a value, so an explicit sink convention is needed mainly as an API contract, not for basic copy elimination.
quote: Note that the same optimization could be applied on the last use of a value.
bears_on: sink/consume parameter convention

claim: The paper's evidence is single-threaded; concurrency with MVS is left as future work, though MVS excludes data races by construction.
quote: This paper focuses on a single threaded execution model, yet concurrent and parallel applications have become ubiquitous.
bears_on: colorless concurrency on top of value semantics

claim: Swiftlet omits protocols and generics; how to compile generic value types (monomorphization vs type erasure with boxing) is left open.
quote: One challenge, in particular, is to choose between monomorphisation and type erasure (Griesemer et al. 2020).
