bears_on: generics implementation; polymorphic interfaces where borrow inference fails

claim: Swift was benchmarked with -Ounchecked, which disables overflow and bounds checks, so the results do not show the cost of the checked arithmetic lotml plans for its C target.
quote: Benchmarks were compiled with the most aggressive optimization level: -O3 for C++, -Ounchecked for Swift, and release -full for Scala Native.
bears_on: performance target; checked arithmetic on the C target

claim: MVS parameter passing maps onto Rust's borrows: inout is operationally a mutable borrow and the optimized pass-by-value is an immutable borrow, enforced syntactically instead of by a lifetime-aware type system.
quote: Mutable borrows are operationally identical to inout arguments, and immutable borrows correspond to the way we optimize pass-by-value semantics.
bears_on: parameter conventions; training prior from Rust and Swift

claim: Diff formats that locate edits by line number score far below rewriting the whole code, because models cannot emit exact line numbers and offsets, even when the source is shown to them numbered.
quote: This poor performance stems from the inherent fragility: LLMs struggle to generate precise line numbers and offsets, and this issue persists even when the input code is explicitly numbered.

claim: Removing line numbers is necessary but not sufficient: content-anchored diffs still trail full-code rewriting because their hunks are arbitrary line fragments, which are unnatural for a model pre-trained on well-formed code.
quote: We attribute the remaining performance gap to a form of fragmented hunks. In these conventional diff formats, the hunks consist of arbitrary line fragments.

claim: Diffs that rewrite whole syntactic units found through the AST (a control block or a function) were more accurate than line-level content diffs on every base model tested.
quote: The main results in Table 2 demonstrate that BLOCKDIFF and FUNCDIFF consistently outperform the line-level CONTENTDIFF across all base models.

claim: For the stronger fine-tuned models, rewriting only the changed functions was on average more accurate than rewriting the whole file.
quote: With the more capable Qwen2.5-Coder models, the average accuracy of FUNCDIFF even exceeds the FULLCODE baseline.

claim: Large models shown a new block-diff format with a single example often fell back to standard unified diffs, which then failed to apply: an edit format outside the training prior is not learned from the prompt.
quote: This phenomenon occurs since they struggle to learn the precise BLOCKDIFF format from a single example and frequently default to generating standard unified diffs, which inevitably leads to application failures during the patching process.

claim: On Diff-XYZ, search-replace was the most effective edit representation for larger models across applying, reversing and generating diffs; unified-diff variants stayed usable but consistently behind.
quote: The results in Table 5 show that search-replace is the most effective representation overall, especially for larger models, achieving strong results across all three tasks.

claim: Search-replace wins because it has no global constraints (line numbers, hunk lengths, context counts): each replacement stands alone, so one bad edit does not invalidate the others.
quote: Each replacement stands on its own, so an error in one edit does not invalidate the rest. Larger models are better at locating distinctive anchors and ordering small, local edits, which increases parse/apply success.

claim: As open Qwen2.5-Coder models grow they approach GPT-4o at applying a given diff, but none comes close at generating one: writing a well-formed diff takes much more capacity than applying it.
quote: In contrast, none of the open-source models achieve comparable performance on Diff Generation. This gap suggests that handling diff syntax and formatting requires substantially more capacity than simply applying edits.

claim: Without a format description in the system prompt, GPT-4.1 frequently emitted V4A, the patch format it was trained on, instead of the unified diff it was asked for.
quote: This effect is especially noticeable for GPT 4.1, which, without explicit instructions, frequently outputs diffs in V4A, the format it was trained to produce, rather than unified diff (see Figure 11 in Appendix B).

claim: On SWE-bench Verified (Python), replacing string-replacement edits with edits addressed to named AST entities cut tool-level edit errors per instance by 76-88% for GPT-5, GPT-5-mini and Qwen3-Coder-480B.
quote: For capable models (GPT-5, GPT-5-mini, and Qwen3-Coder-480B), CODESTRUCT reduces errors per instance by 76-88%, indicating that AST-based operations are substantially more reliable than text-based string matching in this regime.

claim: With the text-based interface on Python repositories, the authors report edit errors as dominated by string-replacement failures from exact text matching and whitespace sensitivity.
quote: Text-based interface: Errors dominated by string replacement failures (exact text matching issues, whitespace sensitivity)

claim: The structured edit takes the indentation from the target node, re-indents the model's replacement itself and rejects any edit that leaves a syntax error, so in an indentation language the model never has to reproduce the surrounding indentation.
quote: The tool automatically preserves formatting by computing the local indentation context and validating the modified AST before committing the change. Edits that would introduce syntax errors are rejected, ensuring post-edit syntactic validity via AST validation.

claim: GPT-5-nano gained 20.8 points on SWE-bench Verified with structured edits, as runs ending without any valid patch fell from 46.6% to 7.2%: the model had the right intent but could not express the edit as text.
quote: Models that frequently fail to produce valid patches under text-based interfaces benefit most: GPT-5-nano improves by 20.8% as empty-patch failures drop from 46.6% to 7.2%.

claim: For most model configurations, structured reads and edits came with 12-38% fewer tokens and up to 33% lower inference cost.
quote: For most configurations, these accuracy improvements coincide with reduced token consumption (12-38%) and lower inference cost (up to 33%).

claim: On HumanEval+, MBPP+ and APPS+ (Python, whole programs), incorrect indentation caused 0.0% of failures in every closed-model cell except GPT-3.5 on APPS+ (1.2%).

On RWPB, real-world functions from recent GitHub repositories, incorrect indentation broke 2.1% of tasks for StarCoder2, GPT-4 and GPT-3.5, 2.9% for Phi-3 and 0.7% for Llama-3, and none for DeepSeekCoder, DeepSeek-V3, DeepSeek-R1 or Claude-3.
Across nine models on three standard Python benchmarks, syntax bugs are the smallest class of failure and functional bugs the largest.
quote: Among the three primary bug types, syntax errors constitute the smallest proportion, whereas functional bugs are the most prevalent.

claim: Given the interpreter's error and a bug taxonomy, GPT-4 fixed all of its syntax bugs in the first repair round, against 23% of runtime and 23% of functional bugs.
quote: The syntax bugs are completely fixed in the first iteration. For runtime bugs, 23% of error codes are corrected in the first iteration and 16% in the second iteration. For functional bugs, 23% are fixed in the first iteration and 3% in the second iteration.

claim: Removing layout that does not change the AST shortens Java, C# and C++ files by 13.2-14.7% of GPT-4o tokens but Python files by only 4.0%, because Python's indentation and newlines are syntax.
quote: With the same measurement, we observe a surprisingly non-marginal token reduction for all three languages, with 14.7% for Java, 13.2% for C#, and 13.2% for C++. In contrast, Python only shows a modest reduction of 4.0%.

claim: Across ten models and four languages on fill-in-the-middle tasks, stripping formatting from the input never lowered pass@1 by more than 4.2%, and none of the drops was significant.
quote: Specifically, across all models and languages, we do not observe a Pass@1 drop higher than 4.2% after removing the code format in the input

claim: Models keep writing formatted code whatever the input looks like: output tokens fell by only 2.5% on average (at most 11.5%), so the saving is on the input side.
quote: Specifically, output code token reduction averages 2.5% across all models and languages, with the highest reduction being 11.5%, achieved by Gemini-1.5 in Java.

claim: Prompting a model to emit minified code is fragile: Gemini-1.5 deleted spaces the syntax needs and its C++ pass@1 fell from 67.2% to 11.1%.
quote: For example, Gemini-1.5 often removes elements in a way that violates syntax rules, leading to a sharp decline in Pass@1 (e.g., from 67.2% to 11.1% in C++).

claim: The comparison is wider than one token per block. With explicit delimiters, layout that leaves the AST unchanged can be stripped from code given to the model as context: 14.7% of tokens in Java files and 13.2% in C# and C++, against 4.0% in Python, whose indentation and newlines are syntax; in fill-in-the-middle tests the stripped input cost no significant accuracy. The saving is input-side only (models keep formatting their output unless prompted or fine-tuned), and the paper measured completion, not editing or lotml. So braces do buy a modest input-token option that significant indentation forecloses.
quote: With the same measurement, we observe a surprisingly non-marginal token reduction for all three languages, with 14.7% for Java, 13.2% for C#, and 13.2% for C++. In contrast, Python only shows a modest reduction of 4.0%.
wiki_says: Replacing indentation with braces costs one token per block: the choice between them is not a token question.

claim: Line-number diffs almost always applied, because the authors' patcher skipped consistency checks, yet pylint showed they had damaged the code: a patch that applies is not an edit that worked.
quote: In contrast, while number-indexed formats maintain nearly perfect patch success rates due to the absence of strict consistency verification, subsequent linter checks reveal significant damage to the resulting code.
bears_on: lotml `patch` must re-parse and type-check the result before reporting success, not only report that it applied

claim: Their patcher, used on Python, falls back to progressively relaxing whitespace and blank-line matching when no exact match exists, following aider; the authors treat this tolerance as a standard part of content-addressed patching.
quote: It attempts to find a plausible match by progressively relaxing constraints on whitespace and blank lines when an exact textual match is unavailable (Gauthier, 2023a).
bears_on: the editing harness's tolerant application mode and the tolerant matcher in `patch`

claim: Patch-application failures concentrated in the minimal-anchor line format: the model tends to write the shortest anchor, and the shortest anchor is often not unique in the file.
quote: Only CONTENTDIFF frequently encounters patch application failures, since the model is more likely to generate minimal anchor content that is not unique within the source code.
bears_on: how `patch` resolves anchors: by symbol, or with a uniqueness error that names the duplicate matches

claim: On JavaScript (trained on CommitPackFT, tested on HumanEvalFix-JS), AST-block diffs beat line-level diffs by a wider margin than on Python. The training data differ, so this is not a controlled indentation-versus-braces comparison, but it gives no sign that braces make line-level diffs safer.
quote: The results in Table 4 demonstrate that BLOCKDIFF and FUNCDIFF exhibit an even more pronounced advantage over the line-level CONTENTDIFF in JavaScript.
bears_on: adr:0005-significant-indentation: whether braces would make diff-based editing more reliable

claim: On today's short, function-level benchmarks, diffs did not save latency, and line-level content diffs were slower than rewriting the whole code, because the anchors make up most of the output. The saving appears only on long files.
quote: As illustrated in Figure 4, we observe that purely diffbased formats do not provide a substantial latency advantage, especially CONTENTDIFF whose average latency even exceeds that of FULLCODE.
bears_on: token cost of edits; whether `patch` should also accept a whole-function rewrite

claim: To keep diffs free of non-semantic noise, the authors ran Black over every Python source and target before computing edits; a canonical formatter is what makes diffs carry only the intended change.
quote: For Python datasets, we further format both the source and target code with Black (Foundation, 2018) to minimize the impact of non-semantic modifications.
bears_on: `fmt` as the canonical form that edits and diffs are computed against

claim: Small models can mistake unified diff's one-character line markers, including the leading space that marks a context line, for ordinary code characters. The paper does not break this down by language, but in an indentation language the context marker is the same character as indentation.
quote: Small models may confuse single-character udiff markers (+, -, leading space) with ordinary code characters.
bears_on: patch format for an indented language: avoid whitespace as a structural marker

claim: Swapping +, - and space for explicit ADD/DEL/CON tags made diffs worse across most settings: more explicit markers did not make the format easier for models.
quote: In contrast, udiff-l performs poorly across most settings, suggesting that verbose line markers make the format harder for model rather than easier.
bears_on: the intuition that explicit markers are easier for models than implicit structure

claim: Dropping line numbers from hunk headers did not help either: even though the patcher ignored them, the numbers acted as scaffolding that kept hunks in file order. This complements, rather than contradicts, the To Diff or Not to Diff result, where line numbers that had to be correct were the failure.
quote: Even though our application step does not rely on these numbers, their presence appears to help models structure the patch: they act as scaffolding that encourages hunks to be segmented and emitted in file order.
bears_on: patch format design: familiar shape versus fewer global constraints

claim: Applying a given diff is conceptually trivial, yet only the strongest proprietary models did it perfectly; the others made mistakes in reproducing the target exactly.
quote: Although diff application is a conceptually simple task, only the strongest proprietary models solve it perfectly.
bears_on: patches should be applied deterministically by the compiler tool, never by asking a model to apply them

claim: The benchmark mixes Python with four brace languages but reports no per-language results, so it cannot say whether indentation or braces is easier to edit by diff.
quote: The final dataset covers five programming languages, with 200 examples each: Python, JavaScript, and Java, which are widely used and appear in most existing benchmarks, and Kotlin and Rust,
bears_on: adr:0005-significant-indentation: the evidence gap only the harness can fill

claim: Edits that name an entity and give only its new content cut output tokens sharply, because the model no longer copies the surrounding code verbatim as a search string.
quote: Structure-aware edits specify only the entity name and new content, avoiding verbatim reproduction of surrounding code. Output tokens decrease by 45.7% for GPT-5 and 72.4% for GPT-5-mini.
bears_on: token cost of `patch` addressed by symbol versus search-and-replace

claim: Without the structured edit, GPT-5-mini lost only 1.4 points of accuracy but spent 38.7% more: string edits eventually succeed, after more edit-and-check cycles.
quote: For GPT-5-mini, the w/o editCode configuration achieves only 60.6% Pass@1 (vs. 62.0% full) but requires 141.22$ in cost (vs. 101.83$ full)-a 38.7% cost increase for 1.4pp less accuracy.
bears_on: what structured edits buy: mostly cost and retries, less final accuracy

claim: Weaker models made more tool errors with the structured interface than capable ones (GPT-5-nano even more than with text; the small Qwen3 models still about a dozen per instance): AST operations have their own syntax that small models get wrong.
quote: This divergence highlights a capability threshold: while structured interfaces eliminate brittle text-level failures for sufficiently capable models, they impose additional syntactic and specification demands that smaller models struggle to satisfy consistently.
bears_on: keep a text search-and-replace path in `patch` alongside symbol-addressed edits

claim: The structured tools need a file that parses; a file already broken cannot be edited structurally. A tolerant parser that still yields symbols from a broken file would remove this limit.
quote: While our editCode tool includes syntax validation to reject malformed edits and preserve repository integrity (Algorithm 2), files that are already syntactically invalid prior to agent interaction cannot benefit from structure-aware operations.
bears_on: the tolerant parser as the base for `patch` and `rename`

claim: In a case study the agent without the structured edit hit repeated whitespace mismatches before an edit landed. The project's editing pilot saw no whitespace failures and identical strict and tolerant results on its twelve tasks; that is not a contradiction, but it suggests the pilot is too small and too short to see a failure that SWE-bench-scale editing on Python produces. The paper has no braces-language comparison.
quote: It performs 62 steps (1.7× the baseline) with iterative str\_replace attempts, encountering multiple failures from whitespace mismatches and scope errors before producing a working transformation through trial-and-error.
bears_on: research/experiments/editing: scale of the harness's editing test

claim: The paper is inconsistent about which text-edit failures occur: the introduction says string replacement frequently hits 'no occurrence' and 'multiple occurrence' errors, but the log analysis found neither pattern. The whitespace-sensitivity attribution is stated without per-category counts.
quote: No occurrence: Neither "duplicated text" nor "no text found" patterns appear in logs, suggesting these specific failure modes are rare in SWE-Bench tasks
bears_on: how much weight the whitespace attribution in claim text-edit-errors-are-whitespace can bear

claim: The taxonomy defines incorrect indentation as causing syntax errors or wrong semantics, but bugs were first sorted by interpreter output, so an indentation slip that still parses would most likely be counted as a functional bug: the A.2 rates are a lower bound.
quote: A.2 Incorrect Indentation Python relies on indentation to define the scope of loops, conditionals, functions, and other code blocks. Incorrect indentation violates the syntax structure, causing syntax errors or inconsistent semantics.
bears_on: silent indentation slips (the mutation experiment's 1% that parse and pass the tests)

claim: Consistent with the project's pilot (no indentation error in sixty whole programs): on real-world tasks syntax bugs remain the smallest class, and the real-world indentation rates in claim indentation-errors-real-world are compatible with zero in a sample of sixty programs.
quote: Similar to the existing benchmarks, the proportion of syntax bugs in RWPB is the lowest, indicating that LLMs can effectively avoid syntax bugs in real-world scenarios as well.
bears_on: lotml-syntax: indentation in generation (as opposed to editing) is not the risk

claim: Half of API-misuse runtime bugs were TypeErrors and a fifth AttributeErrors, the classes a static type checker reports before execution.
quote: There are three primary errors associated with API misuse: AttributeError (20.9%), TypeError (50%), and ValueError (26.9%).
bears_on: value of lotml's static types as compiler feedback

claim: On real-world functions runtime bugs rose for every model, led by wrong arguments and boundary checks; argument count and type mismatches are compile-time errors in a typed language.
quote: However, unlike existing benchmarks, the proportion of runtime bugs is higher for all LLMs, particularly for incorrect arguments and incorrect boundary condition checks.
bears_on: semantic-compiler: which runtime bug classes static checking removes

claim: Every benchmark in the study is Python, so the indentation figures have no braces counterpart.
quote: Another issue is that all benchmarks we used were monolingual, i.e., the programming language of the canonical code was in Python.
bears_on: adr:0005-significant-indentation: no indentation-versus-braces comparison in generation

claim: On the McEval prompts the gap holds: removing formatting cut input code tokens by 31.12% in C++ and 25.26% in C# but only 6.51% in Python.
quote: 31.12% and 25.26%. In contrast, Python achieves only a 6.51% average code token reduction, as formatting elements such as newlines and indentations are integral to its grammar and cannot be removed without compromising code functionality.
bears_on: token-cost: what significant indentation forecloses on the input side

claim: Removing just one formatting element (only spaces, only indentation or only newlines) significantly hurt Gemini-1.5 in some languages, which the authors attribute to partially formatted code being rare in training: half-formatted code is off the prior.
quote: We hypothesize that partially unformatted code is less common in training datasets, making it more challenging for some LLMs to process effectively.
bears_on: training-prior: keep one canonical layout and give the model fully formatted code

claim: Python is fragile when asked to compress output: with the detailed 'delete all spacings, newlines and indentation' prompt, GPT-4o's Python pass@1 fell from 71.5% to 59.7% (row shown), while its brace-language scores held.
bears_on: lotml-risks: never ask models to minify indentation-sensitive code

claim: Fifty training examples were enough to make two commercial models adopt an unformatted Java style, with no significant loss of pass@1.
quote: By fine-tuning with just 50 unformatted Java code samples, Gemini-1.5 and GPT-4o achieve substantial reductions in output tokens (35.9% and 24.8%, respectively) with statistically insignificant performance impact.
bears_on: training-prior: how cheaply a model adopts a new surface layout

claim: Their bidirectional formatter (YAPF-based for Python) round-tripped every McEval sample with an identical AST, so layout can be stripped for the model and restored for people.
quote: Specifically, we compare the AST of each code sample before and after the transformation and achieve 100% AST equivalence across all test cases, confirming that our transformations preserve semantic correctness while only modifying formatting elements.
bears_on: `fmt` as a lossless layer between the model's view and the stored source

claim: Only fill-in-the-middle completion was tested; editing existing code, where indentation risk lives, is outside the study.
quote: Due to budget and hardware limitations, our experiments were restricted to four programming languages and focused solely on the Fill-in-the-Middle (FIM) task.
bears_on: scope of the token argument for lotml-syntax

claim: Generative compilation checks partial programs during generation by sealing them into complete programs the real compiler can diagnose, and it works with black-box models because it only needs the streamed partial output.
quote: For frontier black-box models, this can be obtained through streaming API responses, where output is returned incrementally rather than only after completion.

claim: On repository-level Rust tasks across seven models, post-generation compiler feedback cut the average compiler error rate from 65.9% to 20.7%, and adding on-the-fly feedback on partial programs cut it further to 13.1%.
quote: Post-generation compiler feedback (PC) reduces the average compiler error rate from 65.9% to 20.7%, highlighting the strong repair capabilities of state-of-the-art LLMs. Even so, adding on-the-fly feedback with GC reduces the error rate further to 13.1%.

claim: Stopping at the first unrecoverable error yields smaller reports: 65% of on-the-fly reports hold one or two distinct diagnostics (mean 5.5), against 40% of post-generation reports (mean 13.8, sometimes several hundred).
quote: As shown in Fig. 12a, 65% of GC error reports contain only one or two distinct diagnostics, with an average of 5.5 diagnostics per message. In contrast, only 40% of PC reports are this succinct, averaging 13.8 diagnostics and, on Translation, sometimes reaching several hundred.

claim: For a prefix checker that feeds diagnostics back (rather than masking tokens), rejecting a completable prefix is the more harmful failure, so it should be globally complete and only selectively sound.
quote: For generative compilation, the priorities for soundness and completeness change, with incompleteness becoming the more harmful failure mode.

claim: Late detection on prefixes is dominated by references to items that might still be defined later: 90.5% of the slowest-detected errors involve unresolved names and imports (63.8%) or missing methods and functions (26.7%).
quote: Indeed, among errors in the top quartile of detection delay (≥ 25 lines; mean 99 lines), 90.5% involve such items: unresolved names and imports (63.8%) or missing methods and functions (26.7%).

claim: A semantic prefix checker owes two separate guarantees, safe pruning and dead-end freedom, and dead-end freedom holds when the language has productive syntax, type coverage (every demanded type has a closed inhabitant) and left-to-right semantic flow.
quote: Safe pruning holds independently. Dead-end freedom follows once a grammar has productive syntax, type coverage, and left-to-right semantic flow.

claim: Validated prefix by prefix against ocamlc and cc, a semantic prefix oracle had zero false prunes across 65 valid programs and caught 25 of 30 invalid programs mid-stream, where a syntax-only oracle caught none.
quote: Differential validation against production compilers shows zero false prunes across every prefix of 65 compiler-valid programs, and 25/30 invalid programs caught mid-stream where a syntax-only oracle catches none.

claim: Unannotated (inference-mode) recursion was dropped from the oracle because early unification on a streaming signature produced false prunes; only recursion whose signature is fixed before the body is checkable on prefixes.
quote: The problem is that the recursive call races the still-streaming parameter list to resolve the signature metavariable, and an early unification can commit it to a shape the header later contradicts, producing a false prune rather than a real error.

claim: In a matched ablation, typing rules on top of a grammar mask added +7.1 points on ML validity, +2.0 on STLC correctness and exactly 0 on the C-like fragment, so the semantic gain depends on how much the type system constrains surface choices.
quote: Aggregated within each language over the matched models, the semantic layer adds +7.1 points on ML (32.5% against 25.4%), +2.0 on STLC (40.4% against 38.4%), and exactly 0 on C (next paragraph).

claim: A syntax-only mask (with no false rejections) scored below unconstrained decoding on STLC (38.4% vs 44.4%) and ML (25.4% vs 30.2%).
quote: Syntax-only constraining can itself hurt: pooled over models it sits below unconstrained on STLC (38.4% against 44.4%) and ML (25.4% against 30.2%), fighting the model's prior with no semantic information to spend.

claim: Under a four-call cap, feedback with failure location, observed value and admissible alternatives raised terminal success over a raw diagnostic by 44 points for Qwen2.5-Coder-14B and 42 points for Llama-3.1-8B.
quote: feedback containing all three fields improves terminal success by 44 percentage points for Qwen2.5-Coder-14B (95% paired-bootstrap interval 28-60) and by 42 percentage points for Llama-3.1-8B (95% interval 28-56)

claim: The admissible alternatives carry the gain: location plus observed value without alternatives stayed near the raw baseline, and adding the alternatives added 36 points (Qwen) and 40 points (Llama).
quote: LocObs omits admissible alternatives and performs close to RawDiag. Adding those alternatives increases success by 36 points for Qwen and 40 for Llama.

claim: The same repair values in a keyed JSON record and in prose gave nearly identical success (+2 and 0 points), so JSON syntax itself did not improve repair; the keyed form only used somewhat fewer calls.
quote: TypedFields differs from the repair-value-matched SameNL by only +2 points for Qwen and 0 for Llama; both intervals include zero and both adjusted 𝑝-values are 1.

claim: With raw diagnostics, extra calls beyond four solved nothing more, while structured feedback kept improving one model through six calls: extra rounds pay only when the retry receives new information.
quote: In the 15-game budget subset, RawDiag is flat from four through eight calls. Structured feedback continues improving Llama through six calls. Extra calls are more useful when the retry receives new information.

claim: Across seven models on HumanEval and MBPP with up to four repair rounds, two repair rounds captured 76-95% of the total achievable improvement.
quote: Two rounds capture most gains: For cost-sensitive applications, two repair rounds (R0 through R2) capture the majority (76-95%) of the total achievable improvement.

claim: Error category predicts repair success: name errors were repaired about 77% of the time, assertion (logic) errors only about 45%.
quote: We present fine-grained error-type analysis revealing that error category is a strong predictor of repair success: name errors are repaired at ∼77% rates, while assertion errors succeed at only ∼45%

claim: Self-repair used 11% to 54% fewer tokens than independent resampling to reach comparable or better pass rates on HumanEval.
quote: Across all four models, self-repair uses fewer tokens than resampling to achieve comparable or better pass rates, with savings ranging from 11% (8B) to 54% (Qwen3).

claim: Prompt-only self-repair with raw error messages improved every model tested, by +4.9 to +17.1 points on HumanEval and +16.0 to +30.0 points on MBPP.
quote: self-repair universally improves pass rates: +4.9 to +17.1pp on HumanEval and +16.0 to +30.0pp on MBPP.

claim: In repository-level Java (CoderEval), 35.2% of compiling LLM outputs were less robust than the human-written code, and over 90% of the deficiencies were missing conditional checks, 70% of them at the first line.
quote: we find that 35.2% of their outputs are less robust than human-written code, with over 90% of deficiencies caused by missing conditional checks-70% of which occur in the first line.

claim: Among nine robustness-issue patterns, missing null checks were the most prevalent, ahead of missing specific-value, range and boolean-state checks.
quote: Statistical analysis of their frequencies revealed that over 90% of these issues are related to missing conditional checks, with Missing Null Checks being the most prevalent.

claim: The robustness gap lies in guard conditions rather than exception handling: try-catch was equally rare in human and generated code, and missing error handling was a low-frequency pattern.
quote: Robustness metrics further indicate that control expressions warrant more attention than exception handling, as they occur more frequently in real-world code and exhibit a larger performance gap.

claim: A batch of accumulated diagnostics can hinder the model; stopping at the first unrecoverable error gives smaller, root-cause reports that win after a few restarts, although all-errors-at-once gains more in the very first restarts. Reporting every error is not clearly better than reporting the root cause alone.
quote: Moreover, since the feedback concerns the entire output, the model receives a batch of accumulated diagnostics all at once, which can be large enough to hinder model understanding [10, 24].
wiki_says: Report every error at once (a tolerant parser), root cause first with cascades suppressed.

claim: Token masking needs white-box access, but prefix checking with diagnostics and restart works on black-box models through streaming APIs (evaluated on Claude Opus and Gemini Flash among others), so partial-program checking during generation is available for Claude and Gemini too.
quote: For frontier black-box models, this can be obtained through streaming API responses, where output is returned incrementally rather than only after completion.
wiki_says: Today, generation of lotml code can only be constrained on open models, on OpenAI and on Fireworks — not on Claude or Gemini.

claim: Saturation depends on feedback content: raw diagnostics were flat from four to eight calls, but structured feedback (location, observed value, alternatives) kept improving one model through six calls.
quote: In the 15-game budget subset, RawDiag is flat from four through eight calls. Structured feedback continues improving Llama through six calls. Extra calls are more useful when the retry receives new information.
wiki_says: The repair loop saturates in two or three rounds.

claim: Partially superseded: a controlled, paired study (TextWorld plans, not compiler diagnostics) compared a raw rejection message with location, observed value and admissible alternatives, finding a large gain, with the alternatives carrying it.
quote: On TextWorld, feedback with the location, observed value, and admissible alternatives works much better than a raw diagnostic.
wiki_says: No controlled study compares, for LLMs, rich Rust- or Elm-style diagnostics with terse ones.

claim: With current models, prompt-only self-repair improved all seven models, even at 8B, and used fewer tokens than independent resampling for comparable or better pass rates.
quote: We demonstrate that prompt-based self-repair is now effective across seven models from three families, even at 8B scale, updating the finding by Olausson et al. [5] that weaker models are harmed by self-repair
wiki_says: Once cost is counted, the gain from self-repair is "often modest" (Olausson et al., ICLR 2024).

claim: For program generation, a syntax-only mask that never falsely rejects still scored below unconstrained decoding on STLC and ML; only the semantic (typed) mask recovered the loss, and only on some languages.
quote: Syntax-only constraining can itself hurt: pooled over models it sits below unconstrained on STLC (38.4% against 44.4%) and ML (25.4% against 30.2%), fighting the model's prior with no semantic information to spend.
wiki_says: Constraining done well wins: in JSONSchemaBench, every engine beat free generation.

claim: On prefixes, the generative compiler reports an error a median 3 lines after the primary span of the eventual compiler error, and exactly at that span in a quarter of cases.
quote: In the median case, GC reports the error only 3 lines after the primary span of the eventual compiler error, and in a quarter of all cases it reports the error exactly at that span.
bears_on: checking partial programs: how close to the source a prefix check can localize errors

claim: Unrecoverable errors are reported at a mean of 33.3% of the file, so on-the-fly checking avoids generating the remaining 66.7% of output that could never compile.
quote: GC reports unrecoverable errors at a mean detection point of 33.3% of the file, nearly matching the timing-free upper bound of 32.7%. Thus, GC avoids generating the remaining 66.7% of unrecoverably non-compiling output.
bears_on: value of checking on every edit or prefix rather than only on complete files

claim: Some Rust features make prefix checking hard because well-typedness depends on later code — incomplete trait impls, calls to items declared later, types fixed by a later use — and those errors must be suppressed until end of file to stay complete.
quote: For example, a partial trait implementation may not yet contain all required methods, a call may refer to a function item declared later in the file, and an expression may have an ambiguous type that is resolved only by a subsequent use.
bears_on: which language features make partial-program checking hard (forward references, inference from later uses)

claim: Per restart, post-generation feedback gains more at first because all errors are in context at once, but from four restarts on the focused on-the-fly feedback overtakes it, resolving 4.4 points more generations at seven restarts.
quote: Per restart, PC initially gains more, as each of its restarts has all compiler errors in context at once; from four restarts onward, however, GC surpasses it. At seven restarts, GC resolves 4.4 percentage points more generations within the same budget.
bears_on: repair-round budget and whether to report every error at once or the root cause first

claim: The Rust sealor is about 5k lines, orders of magnitude smaller than rustc's frontend, because it delegates type, borrow and lifetime checking to the existing compiler instead of reimplementing them for prefixes.
quote: Our sealor is implemented in about 5k lines of Rust, which is orders of magnitude less than the ∼600k lines in Rust's compiler frontend [47].
bears_on: implementation cost of a partial-program check mode in lotml's compiler

claim: Despite intervening during generation, on-the-fly checking lowered total runtime overhead versus post-generation feedback (from +283% to +170% over plain generation), by interrupting files that could not compile.
quote: The average overhead over LLM drops from 233 seconds (+283%) with PC to 135 seconds (+170%) with GC.
bears_on: cost of checking during generation versus repair after generation

claim: Typing rules remove about a third of the syntactic branching: on ML the semantic oracle admits 16.8 candidate tokens per position against 26.3 for syntax only, and forced positions rise from 9% to 13%, without ever rejecting the gold token.
quote: Over the ML corpus the semantic oracle admits 16.8 candidate tokens per position on average against 26.3 for its syntactic twin, removing 9.5 candidates per position and raising the share of forced positions, where exactly one candidate is legal, from 9% to 13% (Figure 6b).
bears_on: how much a type-aware constrainer narrows generation beyond the grammar

claim: The Earley-based semantic oracle scales mildly superlinearly and stays under about 130 ms on adversarial inputs (450-token C declaration sequences), close to the latency target for checking on every edit.
quote: The largest inputs, 450-token C declaration sequences and 65-application STLC chains, the adversarial case for chart size, stay under ∼130 ms.
bears_on: latency budget for prefix/incremental checking

claim: Confining the mask to a late emission block after free reasoning (CRANE-style mixed mode) tracked full chain-of-thought within a few points while emitting 28-36 tokens instead of 1,100-2,000.
quote: Mixed mode avoids the cost by confining the mask to a late emission block, tracking full chain-of-thought within a few points while emitting 28-36 tokens instead of 1,100-2,000.
bears_on: when to apply constraints: reasoning outside the constrained block

claim: Constraints help weak and base models but can tax fluent ones: a 2B base model went from 0% to 50% in mixed mode while 9B and 27B models lost ground under the same mask.
quote: Constraint can repair weak and base models while taxing fluent ones: Qwen3.5-2B-Base rises from 0% unconstrained to 50% in mixed mode, while Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.6-27B both lose ground under the same mask.
bears_on: whether constrained decoding is worth it for frontier models versus small open models

claim: Without a closed inhabitant for every demandable type, a prefix can be accepted yet have no completion (a dead end); ML avoids this with `assert false`, a tool DSL with no literal for a type does not. lotml needs a universal inhabitant (a never-typed placeholder) for dead-end-free prefix checking.
quote: With an empty context, let s = summarize( is Live with no completion because the demanded docs argument has no literal form and no binding supplies one.
bears_on: type-system design for prefix checkability: type coverage / a typed hole or never-typed expression

claim: Definition-before-use lets a left-to-right oracle check calls with no lookahead, because the signature is exported before the call appears in the token stream.
quote: And definition-before-use holds at translation-unit granularity: a call is checked against a signature already exported by an earlier definition's rightbound effect, which a left-to-right oracle handles without lookahead because the definition precedes the call in the token stream.
bears_on: declaration order and forward references in lotml, for prefix checking

claim: With location, observed value and alternatives in the feedback, episodes ending on an invalid action fell from 35 to 2 (Qwen) and from 41 to 4 (Llama).
quote: Final invalid-action episodes fall from 35 to 2 (raw to same-information prose) for Qwen and from 41 to 4 for Llama.
bears_on: diagnostic content: listing valid alternatives (did-you-mean) at the failure point

claim: The keyed record reached the same success with fewer calls: 17 fewer than matched prose for Qwen and 12 fewer for Llama.
quote: It uses 17 fewer calls than SameNL for Qwen (paired mean -0.34 calls/game, interval -0.60 to -0.06) and 12 fewer for Llama (-0.24, -0.44 to -0.04).
bears_on: JSON diagnostics versus prose: format affects cost, not success

claim: The structured-feedback advantage grows with budget: typed-minus-raw gains rose from 20 and 27 points at budget 2 to 47 points for both models at budget 4.
quote: On 15 paired games, typed-minus-raw gains rise from 20 and 27 points at budget 2 to 47 points for both models at budget 4.
bears_on: how many repair rounds to budget

claim: The authors' prescription for validators maps to code as file and line, failing assertion, expected type or behavior, and observed exception.
quote: A validator should report where the failure occurred, what it observed, and what it expected when that information is available. In software, these fields may be a file and line, failing assertion, expected type or behavior, and observed exception.
bears_on: diagnostic schema fields for check --json and test --json

claim: Feedback cannot repair what the validator does not expose: on HumanEval every first answer passed the visible test, so no policy got a repair opportunity.
quote: Structured feedback can help only when the validator exposes a useful failure. It cannot fix behavior that the validator does not test, and passing one visible test does not guarantee hidden correctness.
bears_on: limits of the repair loop: the compiler and tests must expose the failure

claim: The evidence is narrow: TextWorld plans, two quantized open models, alternatives capped at 12 in environment order; longer, ranked or randomized lists were not tested.
quote: We cap admissible actions at 12 and keep the order returned by TextWorld. We did not test longer, ranked, or randomized lists.
bears_on: how many alternatives a diagnostic should list, and transfer to compiler diagnostics

claim: For three of seven models the fourth repair round added nothing over the third; the first repair round gave the largest single gain for every model.
quote: For Qwen3, Maverick, and Gemini 2.5 Flash, R4 yields no additional improvement over R3, indicating that these models have solved all problems amenable to self-repair by round 3.
bears_on: where repair-round gains saturate

claim: Name errors are repaired best because the message names the undefined identifier; assertion errors carry little diagnostic information about what was computed wrongly.
quote: Name errors are repaired at high rates (∼77%). These errors provide specific diagnostic information (undefined variable or function names) that guides the model toward the fix.
bears_on: diagnostic specificity drives repair success

claim: Assertion (logic) errors dominate first-attempt failures for every model, so most failures are code that compiles and runs but is wrong — outside what a compiler can report.
quote: Across all seven models, assertion errors dominate, indicating that most failures produce syntactically valid but logically incorrect code.
bears_on: limits of compiler diagnostics; need for test --json and contracts

claim: For the weakest model, independent resampling beat repair on pass rate (79.9% vs 76.8%), suggesting routing: repair diagnosable errors, resample assertion failures.
quote: For the weakest model (Llama 3.1 8B), resampling achieves a modestly higher pass@5 (79.9% vs. 76.8%); the diversity of independent samples compensates for the model's limited error comprehension.
bears_on: repair-versus-restart policy in the agent loop

claim: A chain-of-thought repair prompt (what the error says, root cause, fix) gave gains comparable to one or two extra repair rounds for models of 32B and up.
quote: for capable models (≥32B), chain-of-thought repair prompting is strongly recommended and can yield gains comparable to an additional 1-2 repair rounds.
bears_on: repair prompt design versus round budget

claim: Evidence limits: greedy decoding, a single run, Python only, easy benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP), and raw error messages as the only feedback.
quote: Our use of greedy decoding ensures deterministic, reproducible results but reflects a single point in the sampling distribution.
bears_on: strength of the round-budget evidence

claim: Where a needed conditional was missing, the `if` token was still among the model's top three predictions in 63% of cases (the introduction gives a different share), so the model often 'knows' a guard is due but greedy decoding drops it.
quote: in 63% of cases where a conditional statement is needed but absent, the "if" token still ranks among the top three predictions, suggesting implicit recognition of control flow.
bears_on: whether a compiler diagnostic or decoding nudge for unchecked inputs would be acted on

claim: Logit boosting of `if` at line starts (RobGen) cut less-robust code by 10% while keeping Pass@1 (43.57 average), at +33.4% time overhead.
quote: Experiments show that RobGen reduces the proportion of less robust code by 10%, achieves the highest average Pass@1 (43.57), and adds minimal overhead (+33.4%).
bears_on: decoding-time fixes for validation gaps, compared with type-level fixes

claim: Asking for robustness in the prompt was inconsistent and sometimes harmful: for one model, the share of code more robust than human code fell from 19.1% to 12.2%.
quote: Qwen2.5Coder-1.5B sees AvgABE drop from 1.38 to 1.05 and the proportion of code outperforming human-written code fall from 19.1% to 12.2%, indicating that prompt adjustment alone is insufficient to enhance robustness.
bears_on: whether validation can be left to instructions instead of the type system or compiler

claim: The study language is statically typed Java with strict exception handling, yet the null-check gap persists — static typing without null-safety does not close it; lotml's `T?` with compile-time checking targets exactly this pattern.
quote: Java's widespread use in enterprise applications [39], static type system, and strict exception handling [46] make it ideal for assessing robustness in LLMs.
bears_on: whether T? and typed errors (errors as values) address LLM validation gaps

claim: Larger models in a family had a higher share of first-line (function-entry) robustness issues, e.g. 73.0% at 1.3B rising to 79.6% at 6.7B — the missing checks sit at input validation on entry.
quote: As model size increases, the proportion of missing checks increases. For instance, DeepSeekCoder-1.3B has a 73.0% issue rate, which grows to 79.6% in DeepSeekCoder-6.7B.
bears_on: where validation belongs: preconditions at the signature (`where` contracts)

claim: Evidence limits: small open models, Java only, robustness judged by an LLM; the paper also reports its headline inconsistently — the introduction gives 37.8% while the abstract gives a different share.
quote: Our empirical study reveals that on average 37.8% of LLMgenerated code is less robust than human-written code, with significant room for improvement.
bears_on: strength of the robustness evidence

claim: On Cangjie, a short syntax reference in the prompt raised every base model by 22-46 points over direct generation, GPT-5 going from 4.8% to 50.4% Pass@1.
quote: On T2C average, every base model gains 22-46pp over Direct once given the grammar reference: GPT-5 climbs from 4.8% to 50.4%, Kimi-K2 from 15.3% to 40.7%, and Qwen3 from 2.8% to 39.5%.

claim: A 2,146-token grammar reference outperformed BM25 retrieval over the public Cangjie corpus, because retrieved examples cannot fix syntax the model has not yet seen.
quote: That a 2,146-token grammar reference outperforms BM25 retrieval over megabytes of Cangjie source shows that fixing the syntax model matters more than supplying example code, since retrieved examples cannot fix syntax the model has not yet seen.

claim: Adding the Python solution to GPT-5's syntax-constrained prompt cut HumanEval Pass@1 from 64.0% to 44.5%, pulling the model toward Python idioms the Cangjie compiler rejects.
quote: The most striking case is GPT-5 under Syntax-Constrained on HumanEval, where Pass@1 drops from 64.0% T2C to 44.5% C2C, a 19.5pp regression on the same tasks with the Python solution available

claim: Agent loops with documentation and compiler access gave the best Cangjie result only on the strongest backbone (Codex CLI on GPT-5: 66.9% and 77.0%); the other three agent setups scored 18-40%, no better than the syntax reference on the same model.
quote: Codex CLI on GPT-5 averages 66.9% T2C and 77.0% C2C, the best on every subset and modality and the only Agent configuration that dominates Syntax-Constrained on its own backbone, while the other three sit in the 18-40% range

claim: Once the syntax reference removed most foreign syntax, Cangjie failures shifted to API misuse (34-42%) and type or mutability errors (about 16%), which a grammar reference does not teach.
quote: Once Syntax-Constrained removes most foreign syntax, the mass shifts onto API/library at 34-42% and Type/mutability at around 16%, because the grammar reference teaches the parser-level shape of Cangjie but not the standard library or type rules

claim: With zero training exposure, Claude 3.5 Haiku learned the Anka DSL from the prompt alone, reaching 99.9% parse success and 95.8% task accuracy on 100 problems.
quote: Despite having zero prior training exposure to Anka, Claude 3.5 Haiku achieves 99.9% parse success and 95.8% overall task accuracy across 100 benchmark problems.

claim: A DSL designed for LLM generation, with one canonical form per operation and mandatory named intermediates, beat Python by 40 points on multi-step pipeline tasks (100% vs 60%).
quote: Critically, Anka demonstrates a 40 percentage point accuracy advantage over Python on multistep pipeline tasks (100% vs. 60%), where Python's flexible syntax leads to frequent errors in operation sequencing and variable management.

claim: In failing Python pipelines, variable shadowing - reusing names like df or result across steps - caused 42% of errors, the largest class, which Anka's mandatory unique INTO names prevent.
quote: Variable Shadowing (42% of errors). Python generators frequently reuse variable names like df or result across operations, losing intermediate state.

claim: Given the full specification and idiom snippets, Sonnet 4.5 solved 58% of problems in a language absent from pretraining against 88% in Python, a 30-point deficit.
quote: Even frontier models given the full language specification and starter code for input parsing fall well short with Sonnet 4.5 scoring 58% in PyLang versus 88% in Python, a 30% deficit.

claim: Showing idioms worked better than stating rules: code snippets added 24 points to Sonnet 4.5's spec-only score, and one explicit rule about a forbidden construct added a further 21.
quote: The results in (Table 7) show code snippets demonstrating correct idioms improve Sonnet 4.5 by +24%, while an explicit rule about unsupported chained indexing adds a further +21%.

claim: Frontier models given the complete spec plus an explicit list of constraints still routinely emitted for loops, chained indexing and built-ins the unseen language does not have.
quote: Despite receiving the complete PyLang specification through the interpreter in the prompt and an explicit list of constraints, frontier models routinely violate them and generate for loops the interpreter cannot parse

claim: When Sonnet 4.5 solved a problem in Python but failed in the unseen language, 77% of the time it had chosen the same algorithm: the gap is implementation fidelity, not reasoning.
quote: Among problems where Sonnet 4.5 succeeds in Python but fails in PyLang, 77% use the same algorithm in both languages.

claim: Fine-tuning drove syntax errors below 5%, yet the residual gap to Python was not syntactic: the models learned to write code that parses but does not pass tests.
quote: For fine-tuned models, syntax errors drop to less than 5%, confirming that the residual gap is not syntactic and that models learn to write code that parses in PyLang but not code that works, i.e., passes test cases.

claim: When the supplied semantics redefined familiar operators, models lost far more accuracy - often 40-70 points - than when the same rules were bound to novel symbols, even where standard-semantics accuracy was high.
quote: Across both tables, swap causes far larger drops than obf-often 40-70% points-even when standard accuracy is high.

claim: Even strong reasoning models such as GPT-5-mini and DS-Qwen 32B lost 20-70 points predicting final program states once familiar operators carried swapped meanings.
quote: On Human-Written programs (Table 4, left-side), GPT-5-mini and DS-QWEN 32B lose 20-70% points under swap, while obf causes modest degradation.

claim: Chain-of-thought lifted non-reasoning models by nearly 50 points under standard semantics, but the gain vanished when operator meanings were swapped.
quote: chain-of-thought (CoT) boosts nonreasoning models under standard semantics by nearly 50 points. However, these gains vanish under swap and shrink to ≈40 points for obf indicating that CoT aids long-horizon execution but does not overcome pretrained operator biases.

claim: Supplying formal semantic rules in the prompt helped reasoning models by 9-16 points but cost non-reasoning models 5-25 points on final-state prediction.
quote: reasoningoriented models gain 9-16% points (e.g., DS-QWEN 32B, DS-LLAMA 70B), pushing GEMINI-2.5-pro to ≥99% accuracy, while non-reasoning models lose 5-25% points.

claim: Asked for Scala, Haskell and OCaml, GPT-5 produced code with imperative patterns such as mutable variables, loops and in-place updates in 94%, 88% and 80% of outputs, the highest prevalence of the GPT models tested.
quote: Notably, GPT-5 demonstrates the highest prevalence of imperative patterns, with 94%, 88%, and 80% of the generated code in Scala, Haskell, and OCaml, respectively, containing such constructs.

claim: Error rates were significantly higher in purely functional Haskell and OCaml than in hybrid Scala or imperative Java for every model tested.
quote: however, error rates remain significantly higher in purely functional languages (Haskell and OCaml) than in hybrid (Scala) or imperative (Java) languages.

claim: Feeding static-analysis findings back with a hand-written fix instruction per issue type let models partly repair both correctness and functional-style violations.
quote: Finally, we showed that LLMs can partially self-repair both correctness and quality issues when provided with static analysis feedback and hand-crafted instructions for common types of issues.

claim: Anka, a DSL designed for LLM generation, reports a same-task, same-prompt-structure comparison against Python in which it scored higher (95.8% vs 91.2% overall; 100% vs 60% on multi-step pipelines, confirmed with GPT-4o-mini). The evidence is weak - two small models, a 10-task multi-step category, a lenient majority-of-samples metric, no per-feature ablation, a data-pipeline DSL - but it is controlled evidence the page should cite.
quote: Overall improvement: Anka achieves 95.8% overall accuracy compared to 91.2% for Python (+4.6 percentage points), despite Python's substantial training data advantage.
wiki_says: None of the languages built for agents has published controlled evidence that its design improves model accuracy.

claim: With the complete spec in the prompt (given as the interpreter's Python source), frontier models (Sonnet 4, Sonnet 4.5, GPT 5.4) still wrote constructs the language does not have; spec-only, Sonnet 4.5 passed 16.5% and Sonnet 4 produced 600 syntax errors, and syntax failures only receded once idiom snippets were added. The pilot's null result plausibly depends on lotml keeping Python's syntax wherever semantics match; where lotml removes or changes a construct, syntactic leakage should be expected.
quote: The model knows what PyLang does not support but it cannot reliably avoid using it, perhaps because its generation patterns remain anchored to the syntax it encountered during pretraining and its inability to adapt to the newer patterns.
wiki_says: For frontier models with the spec in context, the risk moves from syntax to semantics.

claim: On Cangjie the docs-plus-compiler agent beat a 2,146-token syntax reference only on the strongest backbone (Codex CLI on GPT-5); the other three agent configurations were comparable to or below the reference on the same model, at 10-120x its token cost, and ten syntax-guided samples with tests beat every matched agent run. A compact syntax reference is the first lever; the agent loop is a backbone-dependent escalation.
quote: The agentic loop amplifies what the backbone can already do, but does not lift a weak backbone past a stronger one running with the syntax reference.
wiki_says: Queryable documentation plus a compiler in the loop is the first way around the missing corpus and the largest effect measured without training anything.

claim: The pilot measured syntax, not correctness. In PyLang, frontier models given the full spec kept a correctness deficit above 25 points in every stdlib-dependence stratum, including problems where both languages have the same primitives, and extended thinking did not narrow it. Absence of syntactic leakage does not imply the corpus gap is closed.
quote: The gap in Sonnet 4.5's performance remains greater than 25% for all categories.
wiki_says: The no-training-corpus risk is medium for frontier models with the spec, because the pilot found no syntactic leakage.

claim: Without any Cangjie scaffolding, five of six large models scored under 7% Pass@1 and GPT-5, the strongest elsewhere, only 4.8%; the failures came before the tests ran.
quote: Without Cangjiespecific scaffolding, five of the six base models score under 7% Pass@1 in either modality, only Kimi-K2 breaks 10% at 15.3% T2C and 16.9% C2C on average, and GPT-5, the strongest model elsewhere, reaches only 4.8% on Direct T2C.
bears_on: Zero-shot baseline for a language absent from pretraining; why lotml cannot be used without the spec in context.

claim: Retrieval left 56-61% of failures as foreign syntax even with Cangjie text in the prompt, against 28-30% with the syntax reference: retrieved text does not override syntactic priors.
quote: Syntax-Constrained cuts foreign-syntax failures to about 28-30%, but RAG-Code and RAG-Docs still leave 56-61% despite putting Cangjie tokens in the prompt, because retrieval supplies surface text without overriding the model's syntactic priors
bears_on: Whether lotml should ship retrieval over documentation or a compact spec in context.

claim: Ten syntax-guided samples scored by tests beat the matched single agent run in every cell; even GPT-5 under Codex gained 11.5 points on HumanEval at about one-eighth of the agent's tokens.
quote: Even GPT-5 under Codex, the strongest cell in Table 2, gains 11.5pp on HumanEval and 10.8pp on ClassEval by switching to parallel syntax-guided samples within roughly one-eighth of Codex's budget.
bears_on: Mitigation choice and the evaluation harness: sample-and-test with the spec versus agent repair loops.

claim: In agent loops the Python reference helped instead of hurting, because extra turns let the agent repair Python-specific syntax that a single-shot prompt would emit verbatim.
quote: The multi-turn loop absorbs the negative-transfer pressure, since the extra turns let the agent revise Python-specific syntax that would land verbatim in a single-shot prompt
bears_on: Python-to-lotml translation for a synthetic corpus: run the translator in a compile-and-repair loop, not single-shot.

claim: The authors recommend a small, compiler-checked index with short examples for the constructs that break most often, explicitly including option types and mutability.
quote: A more useful index would be small and compiler-checked, organised by API signature and paired with short examples for the constructs that most often break, loops, string handling, option types, and mutability
bears_on: Content of the lotml spec and docs: worked examples for mutability (var, value semantics) and optionals.

claim: Per task, direct generation used about 1k tokens, the syntax reference about 3.3k, and agents 34k to 248k, roughly 220-250x direct.
quote: Direct generation consumes roughly 1k tokens per task, SyntaxConstrained about 3.3k once the 2,146-token grammar header is added, and the two RAG variants between about 1.7k and 4.6k, while Agent under iFlow CLI jumps to 34-36k and Agent under Qwen Code CLI to 221-248k, roughly 220-250x Direct.
bears_on: Token cost of each mitigation; a short spec is cheap relative to agent loops.

claim: Anka's core design bet is canonicalization: exactly one form per operation instead of Python's several equivalent idioms. The four principles were measured jointly, never ablated one by one.
quote: Rather than allowing the model to choose from Python's many valid patterns for filtering, mapping, and aggregating data, we can design a language where each operation has exactly one canonical form.
bears_on: lotml's single-canonical-form principle; which design features actually matter remains unmeasured.

claim: The advantage depended on program length: none on 1-2 operation tasks, +40 points on tasks with 5 or more operations.
quote: Figure 1: Anka advantage grows with task complexity. Simple tasks (1-2 operations) show no advantage; complex tasks (5+ operations) show +40% advantage.
bears_on: Evaluation harness design: short tasks may hide the effect of language design; include multi-step tasks.

claim: Anka gave no advantage on simple tasks and a slight disadvantage on 'hard' tasks with nested conditionals and edge cases, where the authors judge Python's flexibility an asset.
quote: Anka shows no advantage on simple tasks and slight disadvantage on "hard" tasks:
bears_on: Limits of constraining a language for LLMs; a general-purpose lotml must not lose on branching logic.

claim: The headline metric counts a task solved when at least 50% of its samples are correct, which is more lenient than pass@1, so Anka's numbers are not comparable with pass@1 benchmarks.
quote: Task Accuracy: Fraction of tasks where ≥50% of samples produce correct output (our primary metric)
bears_on: How much weight Anka carries as evidence on languages-for-agents.

claim: The Anka prompt carried a roughly 100-line syntax guide while the Python prompt only assumed pandas knowledge, so language design and prompt content are confounded.
quote: The Anka prompt includes a concise syntax guide (approximately 100 lines) teaching the language from scratch. The Python prompt assumes pandas knowledge, consistent with training data distribution.
bears_on: Size of an effective in-context spec, and confounds the lotml evaluation harness must avoid.

claim: The authors state that the benchmark covers only data-transformation pipelines and that generalization to other programming tasks is not established.
quote: Benchmark Scope. Our benchmark focuses on data transformation pipelines. Generalization to other programming tasks is not established.
bears_on: Transfer of Anka's result to a general-purpose language like lotml.

claim: Three verified exemplars in the prompt left Qwen3-32B at 10.2%, far below the 47.2% it reached after fine-tuning: a few examples do not override the pretraining prior.
quote: Three-shot in-context prompting leaves Qwen3-32B at just 10.2% on PyLang (Table 4), far below its fine-tuned 47.2%, showing that a handful of exemplars cannot override the Python pretraining prior.
bears_on: Open models: lotml needs fine-tuning or a translated corpus, not few-shot prompting.

claim: For Sonnet 4, adding rules without snippets lowered the score from 12.5% to 8.2%; snippets were the single most important prompt component.
quote: Table 12 reports prompt ablation results for Sonnet 4 on PyLang. The same qualitative pattern observed for Sonnet 4.5 (Table 7) holds: code snippets are the single most important component, and rules alone without snippets actually hurt performance (8.2% vs. 12.5% base).
bears_on: How the lotml spec should be written: worked idioms over lists of prohibitions.

claim: Base Qwen3-4B writing Python under the same restrictions (no stdlib, no for, no int/split) passed about 63%, against 36.1% for the model fine-tuned on PyLang: familiarity, not expressive power, explains the gap.
quote: On the 86 problems where Qwen3-4B complied, Restricted-Python pass rate was ∼63%, versus 36.1% for fine-tuned PyLang.
bears_on: Keeping Python's syntax where semantics match: writing in the familiar surface is worth tens of points.

claim: DPO and GRPO improved Python more than the unseen language because preference tuning only reweights correct samples the model already produces, and those are rare in a new language.
quote: The asymmetry arises because preference tuning can only upweight correct solutions that already exist in the model's sample distribution.
bears_on: RL with verifiable rewards as a lever: it needs a non-trivial base pass rate, so seed with supervised data first.

claim: The whole PyLang corpus was produced by Claude Opus 4.5 in an agentic loop against the real interpreter, keeping only fully test-passing programs, with a 30.4% yield.
quote: All 2,816 PyLang training and test examples were generated by Claude Opus 4.5 in an agentic loop and kept only if they passed every test case under the actual PyLang interpreter, out of 9,269 source Codeforces problems attempted (a 30.4% yield).
bears_on: Feasibility and yield of a test-validated synthetic lotml corpus generated by a frontier model.

claim: PyLang's interpreter inherits Python's runtime semantics (scalars by value, arrays shared by reference), so its semantic distance from Python is smaller than lotml's value semantics would be; PyLang does not test semantic divergence.
quote: PyLang's interpreter is implemented in Python and inherits Python's runtime characteristics (e.g., arbitrary-precision integers, dynamic typing), so the semantic distance between the two languages is smaller than it would be for a language with fundamentally different execution semantics
bears_on: Transfer of PyLang's result to lotml, whose value semantics diverge from Python's.

claim: Moving from human-written to LLM-translated and fuzzer-generated programs collapsed accuracy by more than 40 points; data-flow and size metrics, not control flow, were the main stressors on those splits.
quote: Moving from Human-Written to LLM-Translated and FuzzerGenerated programs (Table 5) induces systematic accuracy collapses-often exceeding 40% points-highlighting the fragility of long-horizon rule composition under scale.
bears_on: Long lotml programs: the semantic compiler, not the model, must track value semantics and mutation across long traces.

claim: Generating full execution traces under supplied rules was near impossible: only four of eleven models scored above zero.
quote: PredTrace sharply exposes the fragility of longhorizon rule conditioning: only four models achieve nonzero accuracy at all, and even these remain far from reliable.
bears_on: Whether models can be trusted to simulate lotml semantics step by step from a spec.

claim: Novel symbols also cost accuracy, and a single-token control ruled out tokenization as the cause; new syntax is cheaper than conflicting syntax but not free.
quote: Even when all obfuscated symbols are atomic tokens, models still fail to reliably apply the correct operational rules and compose them over execution.
bears_on: lotml-syntax rule 2: visibly different syntax for different semantics still needs the spec and diagnostics.

claim: Even single-step rule selection, with no state to track, stayed dominated by symbol priors for most models.
quote: most systems exhibit strongly negative ∆is, implying that even when state evolution is removed, local rule selection remains dominated by symbol priors rather than formal definitions.
bears_on: Short lotml snippets are not safe either: a single assignment or call with redefined meaning is read with Python's meaning.

claim: The authors name operator overloading and DSLs as the practical cases where supplied semantics conflict with the prior.
quote: complete operational semantics are supplied and we test whether reasoning conditions on those rules when they redefine standard operator meaning-a conflict that arises in practice with operator overloading, DSLs, and proof assistants
bears_on: lotml's value semantics reuse Python's assignment and argument syntax with copy semantics, and its traits allow operator overloading: both are the swap condition.

claim: The study measures reading code - predicting final states and traces of a featherweight C - not generating it; transfer to code generation is an inference.
quote: We use program execution as a lens for analyzing formal semantic rule-conditioned reasoning in LLMs.
bears_on: Scope of the evidence for lotml's semantic-leakage risk.

claim: GPT-5 trailed Java by nearly 18 points in Haskell and 9 in OCaml, a gap wider than GPT-4o's despite higher absolute scores.
quote: Specifically, GPT4o's pass rates in Haskell and OCaml lag those of Java by approximately 16.5 and 7.5 percentage points, respectively. This divergence even intensifies in GPT-5, where the performance gap widens to nearly 18 and 9 percentage points.
bears_on: Whether an immutable or functional style costs accuracy; the size of the paradigm gap.

claim: GPT-5 cut OCaml compile errors to 13.73% but stayed at 24.28% in Haskell, against 4.62% in Java.
quote: while GPT-5 successfully lowers the compilation error rate in OCaml to 13.73% and achieves a remarkably low 4.62% in Java, it fails to show similar improvement in Haskell, where the error rate remains high at 24.28%.
bears_on: Strict type systems raise compile-error rates; type-system strictness needs diagnostics with fixes.

claim: In Haskell and OCaml the imperative bias took the form of mutable references, in-place updates and effects inside pure functions.
quote: In Haskell and OCaml, we observe similar biases, such as the use of mutable references, in-place updates, or IO effects in pure function features that conflict with the declarative and immutable nature of these languages.
bears_on: Where models will break lotml's immutable-by-default rule: mutable locals and in-place updates of collections.

claim: In OCaml the static analysis also caught type errors and unintended mutation of immutable data structures, though less often than readability issues.
quote: We also observed several critical issues, including type errors and unintended mutation of immutable data structures, although these occurred less frequently.
bears_on: Semantic-compiler diagnostics for mutation of immutable values.

claim: GPT-5 passed more tests than GPT-4o but wrote less idiomatic code in all four languages, which the authors read as reward hacking.
quote: Specifically, in RQ1, we can see that GPT-5 consistently improve the pass@1 accross four studied programming languages. However, in this experiment, we found that GPT-5 consistently witness lower code style and maintainability in all these languages compared to GPT-4o.
bears_on: Tests alone will not enforce lotml idioms; the compiler must reject or flag them.

claim: GPT-4o dropped sharply after its cutoff in Java and Scala but stayed low and flat in OCaml and Haskell, so part of the paradigm gap reflects training-data frequency and contamination rather than the functional style itself.
quote: GPT-4o show show a substantial post-cutoff performance drop in Java and Scala, i.e., from 52.0% to 32.8% in Java and from 35.8% to 21.6% in Scala.
bears_on: Confound in reading the functional-language gap as a cost of immutability.
